With all of that being said, Mirror Sport will have the latest on City's possible punishment and appeal against the 114 financial charges...

News.title: 'Andy Burnham's state pension triple lock plans may scare many - but there is trade-off for ageing population'
News.content:
'Andy Burnham's state pension triple lock plans may scare many - but there is trade-off for ageing population'

Any leader serious about governing Britain faces the same uncomfortable question: as the population ages, how much more can younger workers reasonably be asked to pay to maintain promises made in a very different demographic era?

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Andy Burnham’s plan to lessen the state pension triple lock from 2030 will frighten many pensioners, and opponents will inevitably seize on the headline.

But the argument he set out at the Labour Party Conference deserves to be judged alongside what pensioners would receive in return: a National Care Service, free at the point of use, designed to stop older people being forced to burn through savings or sell homes simply because they need help washing, dressing or living with dignity. That is the real trade-off.

The triple lock has protected pensioners, but the long-term arithmetic is becoming increasingly difficult. The Office for Budget Responsibility says an ageing population and continuing the triple lock each add roughly 1.6% of GDP to state pension spending over the next 50 years. It is a colossal amount.

Other parties will attack Mr Burnham’s plan. Yet any leader serious about governing Britain faces the same uncomfortable question: as the population ages, how much more can younger workers reasonably be asked to pay to maintain promises made in a very different demographic era?

Britain has waited far too long for a Prime Minister prepared to say some uncomfortable things out loud. Social care has been ducked by successive governments. Water privatisation has left consumers furious over sewage, debt and executive rewards. Empty homes sit unused while families desperately need somewhere affordable to live. The electricity grid needs major reform if Britain is serious about cutting bills and rebuilding industry.

Then there was Brexit. Mr Burnham’s admission that it has done “more harm than good” was striking precisely because Westminster has spent years treating honest discussion of its consequences as politically radioactive. His call for a new post-Brexit relationship with Europe was another sign that this Government is prepared to reopen debates others would rather leave buried.

Add electoral reform and greater public control over essential services, and this was an extraordinarily ambitious programme. His ideas are bold, and some may prove transformative. But speeches are the easy part.

Building a care workforce, funding the promises, fixing infrastructure and turning sweeping reform into lower bills, better homes and greater security will demand years of relentless delivery.

Mr Burnham has finally confronted the problems Britain has catastrophically neglected. Now he has to prove he can solve them.

News.title: Andy Burnham tells Mirror readers: 'I'll tear down Thatcher's legacy and put Britain back in control of basics'
News.content:
Andy Burnham tells Mirror readers: 'I'll tear down Thatcher's legacy and put Britain back in control of basics'

EXCLUSIVE: Andy Burnham writes for The Mirror: 'I will build a country run in the public interest with power in every postcode, and we will begin with what matters most'

PM says he will repeal Margaret Thatcher's 'ideological' ban on the public ownership of water companies

Britain’s water industry is a leaking monument to everything that went wrong with privatisation. People lost control of their bills. Britain lost control of one of the essentials in life.

‌



Just look at the state of water in England right now. Private monopolies loaded with debt, paying out billions in dividends and failing to invest. Meanwhile, bills go up, pipes leak and our rivers and seas have been turned into open sewers. It is a national scandal.

‌



For me, nothing shows more clearly what has gone wrong in our country than water. It is failing households. It is failing businesses. The whole thing stinks. And I will not tolerate any longer a system where the public always loses.

‌



View Image The PM criticised the state of Britain's water companies (Image: SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

Enough is enough. Today, at Labour Party conference, I announced that we will bring in new laws that will allow us to take back control of water and put it back where it belongs: in the hands of the British people. Mayors will be able to hold water companies to account. Greedy bonuses will be stopped. Loopholes used to get round the rules will be shut. And companies that do not get their act together will face tougher consequences for failure.

‌



Thatcher banned the government from owning water companies. I will tear down that barrier. This new settlement for water will work on a very simple principle. Where private companies serve the public interest, we will work with them. Where they do not, we will take greater public control.

That means hope that bills can be affordable. Hope that investment in infrastructure can rise. Hope that our children can swim in rivers and seas that are clean, not clogged with filth. That is a Britain back in control of the basics.

After a decade of drift and division, today, I set out a clear path for Britain. A country run in the public interest with power in every postcode. We begin with what matters most.

Article continues below

Water, housing, energy and transport are the essentials of everyday life and the everyday economy. We rely on them. We pay for them. And we should have more power over them. This is how we give Britain hope again.

News.title: Cop who used baton on one-legged man, 92, 'wouldn't have done anything differently'
News.content:
Cop who used baton on one-legged man, 92, 'wouldn't have done anything differently'

PC Stephen Smith explained his authoritative approach had 'served him well' when attending previous incidents

Police bodycam shows Donald Burgess care home incident

A police officer who pepper-sprayed and used a baton on a 92-year-old wheelchair-bound amputee said he "wouldn't have done anything differently".

PC Stephen Smith, 52, demanded that one-legged widower Donald Burgess drop a dinner knife he was holding, saying if the pensioner failed to do so, he would be "sprayed or Tasered". The incident took place at Park Beck Care Home in St Leonards-on-Sea, East Sussex, in June 2022, when police received reports of an elderly man threatening staff with a knife.

PC Smith and his colleague, PC Rachel Comotto, arrived at the home at 1.15pm and confronted Mr Burgess, who had been isolated in his own room and was holding the dinner knife. A disciplinary hearing was told today that PC Smith "created a confrontation where there was none", with the officer claiming he wasn't aware Mr Burgess was wheelchair-bound.

View 4 Images Donald Burgess died three weeks after the incident (Image: PA)

He took an "authoritative approach" towards the vulnerable man as he said this had "served him well" in his work before. PC Smith admitted he had failed to ask care home staff about any medical or mental health conditions the pensioner suffered from before going into his room.

He then only realised the 92-year-old was a wheelchair-bound amputee after he had used force against him, the hearing was told. After he used the pepper spray and baton, his colleague PC Comotto fired her Taser on the vulnerable pensioner, causing him to scream out in pain and then tell the officers: "I'm dying".

Mr Burgess, a retired carpenter, was then handcuffed and driven to a police station. His condition quickly deteriorated and he was transferred to a hospital where he died three weeks later.

The disciplinary hearing in Lewes, East Sussex, was told the entire incident lasted less than 90 seconds. Giving evidence, PC Smith said he walked in and used "authoritative" commands and fully expected Mr Burgess to comply.

View 4 Images PC Stephen Smith said he 'wouldn't do anything differently' (Image: PA)

But Aaron Rathmell, lawyer for Sussex Police, said: "By drawing your spray and issuing an ultimatum, you created a confrontation between you and Mr Burgess where there had been no confrontation before."

He said: "You should have tried to establish a rapport with him." PC Smith replied: "No." Mr Rathmell said: "Why not ask him what is wrong and establish some basic information about his state of mind?"

PC Smith said: "Because he still had the knife in his right hand." Mr Rathmell said: "Were you frustrated Mr Burgess was not complying?" PC Smith said: "No."

Mr Rathmell said: "Are you embarrassed by your treatment of Mr Burgess?" "No," replied PC Smith. Mr Rathmell suggested that PC Smith knew Mr Burgess was in a wheelchair when he used physical force and to claim otherwise was "a lie". "No," replied PC Smith.

PC Smith, an officer with Sussex Police for 23 years, is facing allegations of using "excessive force" against the pensioner amounting to "gross misconduct". If the allegations are proven against him, he could be sacked from the force.

View 4 Images PC Rachel Comotto used a taser (Image: PA)

Asked why he took the authoritative approach, PC Smith said: "I was expecting that knife to be dropped. It has served me well before as an officer. I've given them a command I expect to be carried out."

He agreed it was the main technique he had used in similar situations in the past. Asked by his own lawyer, Denis Barry, why he didn't take a more compassionate, "softly, softly" approach PC Smith said: "I thought that would be the best option. I walk in, give that command. I was expecting the knife to be dropped."

Mr Barry also questioned PC Smith about why he didn't gather extra information about the pensioner from care home staff. PC Smith replied: "I didn't think it was necessary at the time. I didn't have the luxury of time in my opinion because of the way he was holding the knife. That knife, I wanted it out of his hand as soon as possible."

Mr Barry asked him: "Would you have done things differently on reflection?" PC Smith replied: "No, I don't think I would."

In body-worn footage taken from PC Smith's camera, the officer can be seen challenging Mr Burgess as soon as he enters the room. He said: "Do you want to put the knife down mate for me or you will be sprayed or Tasered. It's up to you. Do you want to put it down for me?

"Put it on the floor Donald don't be silly. Come on, don't be silly. We can solve this without having to resort to this."

‌



Raising his voice he says: "Do as you're told. Put it down. Put it down. Donald put it down. Seriously, put it down. Last chance. Put it down now. Drop the knife. Drop the knife!"

View 4 Images The moment Donald Burgess was tasered (Image: IOPC)

He then pepper sprays the pensioner in the face before repeating his demands for Mr Burgess to drop the knife. When Mr Burgess fails to do so he screams at the pensioner and hits him with his police baton.

‌



PC Comotto then shouts "Taser, Taser" before discharging the weapon at the wheelchair-bound pensioner who screams in pain. In the second video shown of PC Comotto's body-worn footage, she tries to tend to the pensioner, who is struggling to breathe following the pepper-spray.

She says: "Donald. How're you feeling?" "I'm dying," replies the 92-year-old.

The video footage shows the officers handcuffing the pensioner and then wheeling him out of the care home to give him fresh air. PC Comotto then had a conversation with the care home manager, Steven Cooper, and asks if Mr Burgess has any diagnosed conditions.

Article continues below

It is not alleged at the disciplinary hearing the officers' actions contributed to the subsequent death of Mr Burgess, who passed away after contracting Covid in hospital and suffering a cardiac arrest. Last year both officers were acquitted of charges of assault after a trial at Southwark Crown Court

The hearing continues.

News.title: Mum 'betrayed' as drink driver who killed teen son could be moved to open prison just a year into sentence
News.content:
Mum 'betrayed' as drink driver who killed teen son could be moved to open prison just a year into sentence

Toby Spiring, 28, could be eligible for day release and moved to a D category just a year into his sentence for causing the death of of 19-year-old Aidan Venison by dangerous driving

View 3 Images Tracy is campaigning for lifetime bans to be given to those who cause death by dangerous driving (Image: Sussex Police )

A heartbroken mother feels "betrayed" by the system after being told her son’s killer could move to an open prison.

‌



Tracy Venison's son, Aidan Venison, was just 19, when Toby Spiring, 28, ploughed into his motorcycle near Wisborough Green, West Sussex in June 2024. Now just a year into his eight-year sentence, Tracy has been told he could be considered for a move to an open prison.

‌



If moved over to the D category prison, there could be the possibility of day release. The grieving mother, describes feeling “utterly shocked” and “insulted” after receiving the email informing her of the news.

‌



View 3 Images Spiring was twice the legal drink-driving limit at the time of his arrest (Image: Sussex Police )

Daughter of Brit missing in France gives theory for disappearance READ MORE :

She said: "I felt betrayed by the system because it hit me so hard, it was like Aidan’s life didn’t count I'm still heartbroken, you wake up daily wishing you could turn the clocks back”

At the time of the fatal crash, Spiring, from Littlehampton, was twice the legal drink-driving limit. He later pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving and was sentenced in October 2025 and was also given a five-year driving ban from the date of his release.

‌



Spiring had one previous conviction for drug-driving and driving while insured from July 2018, which saw him disqualified for 12 months. Now, just a year into his sentence, he is eligible to be considered for the move to the less secure prison.

Tracy said: "He's had the chance to show that he can be a better person. He chose not to. It is not something that he just did once. It was a conscious decision he made to get in the car yet again, this time resulting in the death of my son."

Prisoners undergo regular reviews and risk assessments that are used to consider any changes. Just last month, the prime minister said those jailed for death by dangerous driving would not be eligible for the government’s early release scheme. However, Those in jail may be considered for an open prison within five year of their earliest release date.

‌



View 3 Images Spiring ploughed into Aidan's motorcycle in June 2024. (Image: Sussex Police )

Tracy is campaigning for lifetime bans to be given to those who cause death by dangerous driving, the petition has reached over 20,000 signatures - meaning the government will respond to the petition. Mark Day, deputy director of the Prison Reform Trust, said: "Somebody could be assessed as being suitable for open conditions but might not be assessed as suitable for release on temporary licence.

"We want people to progress in their sentence, we want them to be ready at the point of release to re-enter the community and to be equipped with the skills and experiences which will allow them to make a success of their resettlement."

Article continues below

An MoJ spokesperson said: "This was a horrific crime and our thoughts remain with Aidan Venison's family and friends. Public protection is our priority, and prisoners are only moved to lower-security conditions following a thorough risk assessment, informed by specialists in offender behaviour and psychology."

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said: "Public protection is our priority, and prisoners are only moved to lower-security conditions following a thorough risk assessment."

News.title: Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care
News.content:
Before turning to the pension triple lock changes, Burnham accepted he may "pay a political price" by trying to make the reforms but argued "someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off".

The triple lock was introduced in 2010 by the coalition government and designed to ensure the value of the state pension was not overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people.

It means the state pension rates rise every April by either inflation, earnings growth or 2.5% - whichever is the highest.

Burnham said this will stay in place until 2030, at which point he would like to "adjust it".

He said: "The state pension will continue to rise every year at least by prices or 2.5%. And it will hold its value relative to earnings over time so that pensioners will always share in the rising prosperity of the nation.

"But this change will generate significant savings which we will use to build up our national care service.

"Some may not realise it but older people with nothing more than the state pension, or only a little more, can find themselves paying care changes today from that small income. Under my plan, this will no longer happen."

Officials have suggested the change could save Â£15bn a year by 2040.

Jonathan Cribb, deputy director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said savings "are likely to be relatively small in the first few years, but rise substantially over time".

He also said "we should not expect this reform to save enough that it could fund universal social care in the next parliament".

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, told the BBC she believed the government should have "pulled another lever", such as a wealth tax, rather than making changes to the triple lock.

The political backlash was immediate.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "more tax rises are inevitable" under Labour's plan, while Reform UK's Nigel Farage accused the PM of "launching an offensive against our elderly".

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said families "cannot wait until after another election and it can't be funded from the pockets of our poorest pensioners".

News.title: Chris Mason: Burnham delivers deeply political speech with a personal core
News.content:
What stood out in this speech was its breadth. His pitch could, very broadly, be divided into the short term - what he hopes to achieve before a general election; and the long term - the prospectus he is beginning to assemble to put to the country when polling day comes around inside the next three years.

The biggest ideas have the longest timeframe and, perhaps, the greatest need for a lengthy debate in their gestation.

Take the headline grabber: revamping social care in England. Previous attempts to do so, by both Labour and the Conservatives, haven't survived the intensity of a general election campaign, having been announced close to an election.

The aim of Burnham's plan is to seed a conversation now about what a new system might look like â the idea being that the argument is won in advance.

Let's see. The debate is only just beginning.

The plan to fund this by making increases in the state pension from 2030 less generous than they are now was more detailed than some expected at this stage.

The triple lock means the state pension currently increases annually in line with inflation, average wage growth or 2.5%, whichever is highest.

But from April 2030, if Labour win the next election, the annual earnings link will be dropped. It would, Labour figures say, be increased further if needed, to ensure that it stays above 30% of the full time average wage.

Knowing they would face blunt criticism about binning the existing triple lock â note the reaction of the Unite union and Labour's political rivals â it would appear the prime minister was keen to offer as much of what he hopes will be reassuring detail to many.

Also going into the next Labour manifesto, he said, a change in the Westminster voting system and â after a review to come â the idea of a closer relationship with the European Union.

How much closer, with what trade offs and prompting what reaction, we don't yet know.

And from the longer term stuff to the here and now â including housing reform in England, more public control of the water industry and the electricity grid.

There was an energy and sense of urgency to Burnham's pitch and without question he has created a battalion of dividing lines with Labour's political opponents which are likely to dominate the debate ahead.

His cabinet and many in his party are relishing the battle of ideas the prime minister has set up and is enthusiastically leaning into.

It was noteworthy that beyond a broad reference to Labour's opponents on the Right, the party's rivals didn't get a mention in a speech lasting more than an hour.

The question is: does he and his government have the capacity to deliver?

And do they have the capacity to convince you, the voter, they have a vision you regard as coherent, appealing and affordable?

You hardly need reminding of the backdrop that contributed to thwarting many of his recent, many predecessors: a persistently sclerotic economy and a persistently turbulent international picture, for starters.

Neither will make turning all of this into a reality straightforward.

News.title: One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford called 999 himself
News.content:
One of five men arrested near RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday morning had dialled 999 himself, the BBC understands.

The suspect called the police at 00:45 BST, almost an hour before a female farmer also dialled 999 after seeing men in balaclavas.

The five were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later terrorism offences after three vans were spotted, sparking a major security incident around the Gloucestershire base which the US military operates.

They were released on bail on Monday in what police described as an "investigative decision" "grounded in experience and strategy".

Police say a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the vans.

Police were alerted to "three suspicious vehicles" in Whelford, a village which lies directly east of the base, by the farmer.

She told the BBC it was "pure luck" she had spotted them, having arrived home to find the road blocked and a "large group of hooded and masked men".

"I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had," she said.

A bomb disposal team arrived on scene shortly afterwards and a 400m (1,312ft) cordon was put in place.

But Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, told reporters on Tuesday that the police response that morning had been due to "a range of information".

Police cordons near the base are expected to be completely lifted on Wednesday, while residents from the 85 homes evacuated on Sunday have been allowed to return to their properties.

The five men are all UK nationals aged between 23 and 25. Four of them live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes are now complete.

Taylor previously said their bail was "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others" as they remained under investigation.

"The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision-making, and this was certainly the case yesterday," he said on Tuesday.

"I understand why this development was surprising to some, but I would like to reiterate that this is an investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy."

The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday told journalists he was "disappointed" the five men had been released on bail.

News.title: How did the RAF Fairford incident go from 'suspected bomb plot' to police bail?
News.content:
On Sunday morning, the world was watching as drama unfolded in the village of Whelford.

Before sunrise, residents were called from their beds and told to evacuate as a huge police operation unfolded in the village, which is next door to RAF Fairford, a base used by the US Air Force.

One villager managed to take a picture of five men sitting on the ground, stripped to the waist, handcuffed and under armed guard.

They were arrested for offences under the Explosives Act. But now counter-terrorism detectives say no explosives were found in their three vans, only an "accelerant" - petrol.

What some newspapers called a "suspected bomb plot" ended in the suspects being bailed. So what was going on?

The US President Donald Trump asserted that the men had been trying to do "big damage" to the base. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he declared.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involved the hands of a foreign actor."

But in a veiled criticism of that, the head Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK Laurence Taylor said that the worry that a lot of people had been experiencing had been "heightened by the international commentary".

He also defended his detectives' decision to give the suspects police bail with "very strict conditions". This had been criticised by President Trump.

Taylor said it was an "investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy".

This suggests there were good tactical reasons for releasing the men on bail, perhaps to encourage their cooperation.

News.title: Household energy bills forecast to see biggest rise in four years
News.content:
Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by Â£276, figures shared with the BBC reveal.

The 16% predicted increase would hit millions of households at the coldest time of year, and would mark the biggest rise in bills for four years.

The forecast from consultancy Cornwall Insight comes a day before prices go up under regulator Ofgem's October price cap and puts increased pressure on the government to support those who will struggle to pay.

Meanwhile, the boss of supplier EDF Simone Rossi has warned the UK is "walking into a second energy crisis" and called for an extension to the VAT cut on electricity which kicks in on Thursday.

News.title: Three teenagers die after car enters River Wear
News.content:
Three teenagers have died after a car entered the River Wear.

Northumbria Police said just before 13:30 BST a black Audi A3 came off the road at Panns Bank near Wearmouth Bridge, in Sunderland, and entered the water.

Four people were in the car at the time and a 17-year-old boy managed to reach safety. He is currently in hospital with non-serious injuries, and has subsequently been arrested in connection with the incident, the force said.

The bodies of two teenage boys and a teenage girl have been recovered from the water.

No other vehicles are believed to have been involved.

Ch Supt Scott Cowie, area commander for Sunderland, said it was "a truly tragic incident".

"Our thoughts are with their families, friends and all those impacted by what has happened," he said.

He added the investigation was at an early stage and the force was working to establish the circumstances.

News.title: Man City guilty of 'sham' contracts and misleading accounts
News.content:
Manchester City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than Â£830m, the Premier League says.

The League confirmed that City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

An independent commission found that, during that time period, the club arranged the "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs".

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

News broke last week that City had been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching, but on Tuesday the Premier League published a redacted version of the commission's report.

The commission's report said the charges "concerned well over 100 alleged individual breaches of Premier League rules across four broad charge categories".

It also found the club guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation and said that "a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence".

The sham commercial deals were described as being part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of Â£830.69m.

City recorded Â£360m in sponsor fees in the three seasons they won the Premier League - 2011-12, 2013-14, and 2017-18. Only Â£43m of it was legitimate - the rest came from their owners and was disguised.

"The relevant sponsorship agreements were found to be shams, or at minimum did not reflect their economic substance," the commission said.

It also describes "deliberate or reckless conduct intended to circumvent the Premier League rules" and that the "sham" scheme devised by City allowed the club "to avoid recording what would otherwise have been the largest single-season loss in Premier League history in 2009-10".

The commission highlighted the scale of evidence it had to consider by pointing out that the index alone ran to more than 750 pages, while the core bundle of documents "ran to many tens of thousands of pages".

City are owned by the Abu Dhabi United Group, who took over the club in 2008 and are referred to as "ADUG" in the commission's report.

News.title: It is time for Tuchel to offer Alexander-Arnold some trust
News.content:
England head coach Thomas Tuchel's apparent lack of trust in Trent Alexander-Arnold has been one of the defining features - and a constant narrative - of his time in charge.

The 27-year-old right-back has won a Premier League title at Liverpool then moved to Real Madrid since he last started for England, selected as a left-back by interim manager Lee Carsley when scoring in a 3-1 Nations League win in Finland in October 2024.

He was ignored for England's World Cup squad last summer, despite right-back being a cursed role for Tuchel, making it appear that whatever questions the German had about that position, Alexander-Arnold was never going to be the answer.

So Tuchel's decision to recall Alexander-Arnold for this four-game Nations League camp came as a surprise, so emphatically had he been marginalised by England.

It was against this backdrop that Alexander-Arnold became the ninth right-back used by Tuchel in 24 games when he finally got his start against Czech Republic in Prague as England tried to recover from the 3-2 loss to World Cup holders Spain at Wembley.

And, with perhaps something to prove according to Tuchel, Alexander-Arnold did exactly that in one world-class moment that might convince his coach to train his sights on what he can do rather than what he cannot.

It is time, in other words, for Tuchel to offer Alexander-Arnold some trust.

News.title: Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
News.content:
Andy Burnham has promised that Labour will fight the next general election on a pledge to change the UK's voting system.

In his first party conference speech as prime minister, he announced plans for a national commission to explore options for electoral reform.

He invited other parties to work with the commission to ensure "everyone's vote counts, and everyone's voice is heard".

He has previously supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model, telling last year's conference that "PR's time has come".

Westminster's first-past-the-post system, under which candidates with the most votes in each seat are elected, has been called into question as the UK political landscape has fragmented in recent years.

Debate over the system has intensified since Labour amassed a huge parliamentary majority with a 34% vote share in 2024.

Around 100 Labour MPs recently supported a parliamentary amendment in favour of setting up a commission to examine alternative options, a move Burnham himself supported last year when mayor of Greater Manchester.

In his speech Burnham told delegates: "We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote or less."

He added: "We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times."

News.title: Huel ad banned for suggesting its products could replace all conventional food
News.content:
An advert for Huel meal replacement shakes has been banned by the advertising watchdog for encouraging or condoning "irresponsible" dietary practices.

The ad featured Huel brand ambassador Spencer Matthews sharing an anecdote of a person he met who "only eats Huel" and who won a 260km race "by miles".

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said that viewers could assume from the ad that replacing all conventional food with Huel was "nutritionally appropriate" and was compatible with elite physical performance.

Huel said Matthews' anecdote was not "a recommendation or instruction" and the purpose of the ad was to challenge the misconception that Huel could replace every meal".

The video, which appeared as a sponsored Instagram post and YouTube pre-roll ad, featured Matthews speaking to Huel founder Julian Hearn in the style of a podcast.

The Instagram post included the caption: "Here's how our founder uses Huel. Spoiler alert it's not for every meal."

In the video Hearn said that he has Huel products for breakfast and lunch during the working week, but has a "traditional meal" when he goes home.

In response, Matthews said that when he was competing in an ultramarathon, he met a man who "only eats Huel".

Matthews said he was initially sceptical that the man would be able to manage the race, but then said: "He won it by miles, like literally just left us all in the dirt."

Hearn replied: "In an ideal world, you should have nutritionally complete whole food.

"Most people either don't do that or can't have the time to do that, and therefore that's where Huel fits in the gap."

News.title: Prince William and Catherine's surprise visit to Kevin Sinfield's charity run
News.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales made a surprise visit to support rugby league star Sir Kevin Sinfield, on the third day of his endurance challenge to raise funds for Motor Neurone Disease (MND) charities.

"What you're doing is so inspiring â the unity that you're building," Catherine told Sir Kevin.

Prince William and Catherine caught up with Sir Kevin in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, as he carries out what he says will be his final fundraising challenge.

Sir Kevin is aiming to complete seven ultra marathons in seven days, running between Hull and Manchester, in a challenge inspired by his former teammate Rob Burrow, who died from MND in 2024.

News.title: No 'deliberate' contact to stop car in A66 crash
News.content:
No evidence of "tactical contact" or the use of a stinger has been found before the A66 crash which killed five young men and two police officers, an initial investigation has revealed.

The crash between a Volkswagen Passat and a marked Cleveland Police vehicle happened at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August and followed a police pursuit which was abandoned.

The initial investigation by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said there was no evidence police had initiated contact with the Passat.

However, director of engagement, Emily Barry, said it will take the IOPC months to conclude its full investigation due to the amount of information to review.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, who had not been following the Passat, were killed.

The five people in the Passat were Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Robert Worthy.

News.title: Soho House venue under investigation for food safety
News.content:
A venue of private members club Soho House is being investigated by the local council after a former member of staff raised concerns about rats and out-of-date food allegedly being served.

The former staff member told BBC News he was pressured to replace labels on prepared food if it was not sold at the end of the day and said he regularly saw rats at the venue.

His contract was terminated two months after he first raised concerns, but Soho House said this was unrelated to his complaints.

It added that the food incident was isolated and re-labelling unsold food was not company policy, but it did not comment on the rats claim.

Hackney Council has confirmed it is investigating food safety and hygiene at Soho House's Shoreditch location.

Soho House is a popular haunt for A-list celebrities. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle reportedly had their first date at one of its London venues.

The former staff member at Shoreditch House, Kamran Khan, first raised concerns informally about the alleged re-labelling practice before formally filing a complaint with Soho House.

Khan was on probation at the venue when he raised the concerns in July, and his employment was terminated earlier in September.

Following his formal complaint, the company investigated and told Khan on 24 August there was evidence to support his claim and steps were being taken to address the matter.

Khan claimed the practice continued despite the assurances he was allegedly offered, leading him to complain to Hackney Council instead.

A spokesperson for the council said: "We have received a report about food safety and hygiene at Shoreditch House and have opened an investigation."

Speaking to BBC News, Khan said he was told in a probation meeting to continue the practice.

The 30-year-old, who told BBC News he has had several jobs in catering and hospitality said he was told "if I don't change labels on my own initiative, [they] would take that as a performance concern".

He said he felt compelled to raise the issue because he saw a lot of children and pregnant women at the restaurant.

"I told them that I don't want to be held personally liable for anyone that gets injured," he said.

Food served in a restaurant must legally be labelled with information including the best-before or use-by date.

Khan also said there had been rats at the venue for a long time and that cleaners were told to check daily for rat droppings.

A spokesperson for Soho House apologised for the incident, saying: "This is not how we expect our houses to operate and it is not company policy."

They said an external, independent investigation and audit was conducted.

"Delivering the highest level of food safety for our members and guests is incredibly important to us," they added.

"For clarity, the former employee's contract was terminated for reasons entirely unrelated to food labelling."

Soho House membership starts from Â£291.67 monthly or Â£204.17 for under-27s.

The group opened its first club in London in 1995, and now has 46 Soho Houses in Europe, North America and Asia, as well a string of other up-market hospitality businesses.

The company listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2021, but its share price dropped sharply in the following years as it struggled to make a profit and fought accusations it was losing its exclusivity.

It was bought by a consortium of investors last year, with actor Ashton Kutcher joining the company's board.

News.title: Sir Ranulph Fiennes' relatives tell BBC it's 'very painful' not being able to visit him
News.content:
Relatives of the British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said it is "very painful" he appears to have been hidden away from them.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his former sister-in-law told the BBC that she did not know where he was, and nobody had been able to see him.

It has been alleged that Sir Ranulph, 82, has been admitted to a number of care homes under assumed names, after a family rift involving his second wife, Louise Millington-Cotes.

Louise Millington-Cotes did not immediately respond to the allegations, or the BBC's request for comment.

Cheshire Police have said they are aware of the concerns regarding Sir Ranulph, and are satisfied he is living in an appropriate setting with suitable care.

They said there were "no immediate safeguarding concerns".

Sir Ranulph has not been seen in public for nearly two years, just months after opening up about a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease, a progressive disorder affecting the brain, nervous system, and muscle control.

He was the first person to visit both north and south poles by surface means in the early 1980s and has been described by Guinness World Records as "the world's greatest living explorer".

Spending his childhood between the UK and South Africa, he joined the British Army after leaving school, going on to serve in the SAS.

Sir Ranulph's stepson, Alex Millington-Cotes, told BBC Newsnight he wanted to see the power of attorney "removed from my own mother" and placed in the hands of people who "have fully his best interests in mind".

"He's not an isolated type of person, and so to see him isolated now is very painful," he said.

Last week, he launched a crowdfunding campaign for legal fees to "locate and safeguard" the explorer, and so far it has raised almost Â£26,000.

He wrote that the fundraiser had been created as "a result of our concern and desperation" after trying "multiple avenues" to locate his stepfather.

Questions about Sir Ranulph's whereabouts grew in prominence after a report in the Telegraph earlier this month, external in which "members of his inner circle" raised concerns about his whereabouts.

The paper also reported concerns about Sir Ranulph have been raised with the Office of the Public Guardian (OPG), the government agency which helps people to stay in control of decisions about their health and finances.

In a statement to the BBC, an OPG spokesperson said: "We have a strict duty of confidentiality to all individuals who have made a lasting power of attorney, and it would be deeply inappropriate to comment on a specific case.

"We take all safeguarding concerns seriously and investigate thoroughly where there is the evidence and legal basis to do so."

News.title: Body of newborn baby found on shoreline in Wales as police search for mother
News.content:
The force has not revealed any information about the baby's gender or age.

Giraud said they "have real concerns for the health of the mother".

"We recognise that she is likely to be extremely vulnerable. She may be fearful of seeking the support she needs through fear of identifying herself.

"You may feel you have nowhere to turn, or that you cannot speak to anyone about what has happened. Please do not feel that you have to face this alone.

"We don't yet know all the circumstances surrounding your baby's death but what is important right now is that we find you, make sure you are safe, and ensure you receive any medical attention and support you may need.

"I am asking you personally, to please get in touch with us. You can speak to a healthcare professional, approach a police officer or attend a police station.

"If you are watching or listening to this appeal, please know that we want to hear from you. Please take the first step and contact us. There are people to help you."

Det Sgt Kelly Wynne said they were concerned the mother "may not be in a position to reach out for support", and appealed to the baby's father and the mother's family, friends, neighbours or colleagues who may have information.

"If you have any information regarding a woman or girl you think may have been pregnant or whose behaviour has been unusual or out of character over the past few months including withdrawing from friends, family or social ties, please contact us.

"We appreciate coming forward is difficult, but inaction is not an option."

News.title: Daniel Thomas refused bail over alleged boat damage
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been refused bail during a crown court hearing over the alleged slashing of a dinghy in the English Channel.

Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, appeared via videolink at Portsmouth Crown Court accused of criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at the boat with a knife.

The 37-year-old, whose address was withheld by the court at a previous hearing, is also charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone.

He has been remanded in custody, with a provisional trial date set for 1 March.

The defendant, wearing a grey t-shirt and holding a copy of the Bible, did not enter a plea during the hearing but previously pleaded not guilty to both charges at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Friday.

The powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on Wednesday rejected South Korean findings that North Korea likely planted the land mines that injured three South Korean soldiers last week. She threatened to retaliate if the South fires at North Korean troops conducting border fortification work.

Three South Korean military officers were injured in two consecutive explosions Sept. 21 near the military demarcation line in the western section of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), a heavily fortified border buffer zone between the Koreas.

The statement by Kim Yo Jong came after South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff on Monday announced a preliminary assessment that the blasts were caused by North Korean mines following a joint inspection of the site with the U.S.-led United Nations Command.

South Korean Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul told lawmakers Tuesday that North Korea’s placement of the mines likely violated the armistice agreement that ended fighting in the 1950-53 Korean War, and that the South would consider unspecified “corresponding measures” if a finalized investigation confirms the North was responsible.

Kim Yo Jong, a top foreign policy official for her brother and possibly the second-most powerful figure in Pyongyang, called the South Korean assessment a “conspiratorial farce” and accused Seoul of making groundless claims to create a pretext for military provocation against the North.

North Korea in recent years has added mines, anti-tank barriers and other front-line fortifications as relations between the Koreas have sharply deteriorated, raising concerns in the South about the growing presence of North Korean soldiers near the DMZ.

Kim described North Korea’s efforts as a rightful exercise of its sovereignty to strengthen the border and accused the South of escalating tensions by broadcasting warnings and firing warning shots at North Korean troops involved in front-line fortification work, insisting that “our soldiers have never crossed the border.”

“When a single bullet is hit on our land, they must be prepared for a lot,” she said. “If the (South Korean) military gangsters fire at our soldiers carrying on the permanent project for the southern border, not warning shots, our border units will take immediate and merciless retaliatory action."

The recent explosions, which took place about 10 meters (yards) south of the military demarcation line, came during an operation to establish a patrol route through a densely vegetated area rarely visited for decades. The route was intended to allow future inspections with the U.N. Command after South Korea since last year detected “terrain changes” that may have resulted from North Korean minelaying.

Kwon Dae-won, vice chairman of South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, said there was a “very high possibility” that North Korean mines caused last week’s explosions, noting that there was no record of South Korean or allied forces laying mines in the area. Blast marks, forensic analysis of explosive substances and what appeared to be a third North Korean mine at the scene also pointed to the North, he said. Kang said South Korean and U.N. investigators found a possible fourth mine during a follow-up inspection Tuesday.

The DMZ, which is 248 kilometers (155 miles) long and 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) wide, is one of the world’s most heavily fortified borders. An estimated 2 million mines are buried in and around the zone, which is also guarded by barbed-wire fences, tank traps and combat troops on both sides. The zone is a legacy of the Korean War, which ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

The latest explosions came more than a decade after South Korea blamed the North for land mine explosions that maimed two South Korean soldiers and sharply raised tensions between the countries in August 2015.

The Koreas then traded threats, staged weapons demonstrations and resumed border propaganda broadcasts, before days of marathon talks eventually pulled them back from the brink. North Korea issued a vague expression of regret over the soldiers’ injuries but never clearly accepted responsibility.

Last week’s explosions came as South Korea’s liberal government sought to help revive diplomacy between Pyongyang and Washington as part of broader efforts to reduce tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

Since early 2024, North Korea has taken an increasingly hard-line stance toward South Korea, declaring its neighbor a permanent enemy and abandoning the concept of shared statehood in favor of a hostile “two-state” system. The North has so far rejected U.S. calls to revive diplomacy between the countries that collapsed in 2019, insisting that Washington must first drop its demand for the North’s denuclearization as a precondition for talks.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney accused the U.S. owner of steelmaker Stelco, a subsidiary of Cleveland-Cliffs, of betraying Canadian workers Tuesday after it announced layoffs it attributed in part to U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs — tariffs Cleveland-Cliffs’ chief executive has publicly championed.

Carney singled out Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves, noting that he had applauded Trump’s steel tariffs. Goncalves has called the 50% tariffs “a necessary step” to protect U.S. steelmakers.

“Our thoughts are with the workers and the families who have been betrayed by the company,” Carney said.

Carney also threatened legal action against Cleveland-Cliffs, saying the Ohio-based company has binding employment obligations stemming from its C$3.4 billion ($2.4 billion) takeover of Stelco in 2024.

Stelco said up to 500 workers could be affected as it indefinitely idles cold-rolled and coated operations at its Hamilton, Ontario, plant and shifts production to its Lake Erie facility in Nanticoke, Ontario.

Cleveland-Cliffs said Monday the move does not shift steel production out of Canada: Output will be concentrated at Stelco’s Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ontario, where it expects a significant number of affected Hamilton workers to be absorbed, with overall steel tonnage unchanged.

In a memo to employees, Stelco said U.S. tariffs had “significantly shrunk the market” for its cold-rolled and galvanized products. The company said demand in markets it traditionally serves fell almost 25% in the second quarter compared to the 2024 quarterly average, including a 10% decline in Canada.

The layoffs come amid an escalating Canada-U.S. trade war in which Trump has imposed 50% tariffs on Canadian steel and other goods and Canada has retaliated with tariffs of its own. At a White House event Monday announcing a new $15 billion steel plant in Iowa, Trump credited his tariffs with reducing foreign steel imports and attracting investment to the United States, saying companies were building plants there “because they don’t want to pay tariffs.”

Carney said the federal government had offered financial assistance to preserve jobs but did not disclose the amount or terms.

“There’s money on the table from the federal government,” Carney said. “The company made representations and has legal obligations for employment. We intend to use all powers that we have and pursue them to the fullest extent of the law.”

The Canadian government approved Cleveland-Cliffs’ takeover of Stelco in October 2024 on the condition that it meet legally binding five-year employment commitments, including maintaining at least the same number of unionized workers and the vast majority of nonunion employees.

Cleveland-Cliffs did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Carney’s remarks.

The suspected bomb plot targeting RAF Fairford was foiled after one of the suspects made a call to police an hour before their arrest, it has emerged.

One of the suspects is understood to have called police early on Sunday before he and four others were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorist offences. They were all released on bail on Monday.

Police are now looking into whether the men, who are all British nationals, were acting as proxies for Iran, according toThe Times. They are said to be probing whether the caller got cold feet or whether it was part of the plan.

The Independent has approached the Met Police for comment.

Officers discovered a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices in the three vans that sparked the major security alert near the Gloucestershire base being used by the US. Police had received a call from a farmer relating to “suspicious vehicles” travelling towards the base at 1.36am on Sunday.

open image in gallery Several men have been bailed following a suspected terror plot on Sunday ( Reuters )

On Tuesday evening, US president Donald Trump said he was “disappointed” at the decision to grant the five men bail.

He said: “We were involved in (the investigation), but as you know, your fellow countrymen, let them go.

“Well, they didn’t let them go. They put them out on bail. I assume they haven’t watched closely… they should not have done that.”

The head of UK counter-terrorism, Policing Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the decision to release the suspects on bail was an investigative decision.

Speaking outside New Scotland Yard, he confirmed on Tuesday that no improvised explosive devices had been found within the vans.

“A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information that we received,” he said. “This included a call from the member of public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford.

“Now, those vehicles, as I explained yesterday, have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices have been found.

“We have found a quantity of an accelerant, petrol, and we have recovered that as part of our investigation.”

He added the five suspects released “remain under investigation” and “must adhere to strict conditions” as the probe continues. “The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision making, and this was certainly the case yesterday,” he said.

“I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers.”

open image in gallery Head of Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the men are still under investigation ( PA )

The five suspects are a 24-year-old from Camden, north London; three men aged 23, 24 and 25 from Westminster, central London, and one aged 24 from Willesden, north-west London.

Villagers living near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, dozens of whom were dramatically evacuated from their homes on Sunday morning, were slowly returning to normal on Tuesday. Police cordons are expected to be fully lifted on Wednesday.

Questions over Iran’s potential involvement in the attack have continued as US secretary of state Marco Rubio claimed in a television interview that the suspected plot “clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor”.

Speaking to Fox News, Mr Rubio said: “It’s one that clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor. I won’t get into great detail about that yet.

“I do want to thank the authorities in the United Kingdom who have been very co-operative and on top of it.”

He added: “I know a lot of people are disturbed by the news that some of these people have been released on bail, as some of the people are being investigated, and obviously we’re engaging with them on all of that.

“Beyond that, I would argue that they’ve been very co-operative and very helpful on something that’s a very serious incident.”

Iran’s embassy in London has strongly denied any involvement in the alleged plot.

In Sen. Eric Schmitt's effort to trip up former Trump prosecutor Jack Smith on Tuesday, the Missouri Republican seemed to mistake basketball teams playing about 650 miles apart.

Schmitt accused Smith of perjuring himself during a Senate hearing after repeatedly prodding him about whether he'd attended an NBA game in Atlanta on the evening of Feb. 3, 2024. The hometown Hawks were playing the Golden State Warriors.

Schmitt appeared to be trying to set Smith in Atlanta at the time Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis was facing scrutiny for her romantic relationship with Nathan Wade, the special state prosecutor she hired for the county's election-interference case against Trump.

“So your testimony today is that you did not go to a Hawks game on Feb. 3, 2024. Is that correct?” Schmitt asks sharply. “What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta at a Warriors-Hawks game on Feb. 2, 2024?”

Smith said he didn't think he had visited Atlanta as special prosecutor, and was even more certain he hadn't attended an Atlanta Hawks game.

He did, however, recall attending a University of Iowa women's game at the University of Maryland on Feb. 3, 2024, recalling the game as one where then-Iowa star Caitlin Clark was playing.

“Could it then be that the University of Iowa was the Hawkeyes?” Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota interjected. “Perhaps you should have looked at it more carefully.”

Powerful cutters have whirred to life on a giant drill that will begin boring a new train tunnel under the Hudson River connecting Manhattan to New Jersey.

Officials gathered in North Bergen, New Jersey, on Monday to ceremonially flip the switch on the Gateway tunnel, one of the largest U.S. mass transit projects in generations.

“Our region is the beating heart of America, generating 20% of the nation’s GDP,” declared Democratic New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill. “And this 10-mile stretch of track is its main artery.”

New York and New Jersey officials said the tunnel is vital because the existing 116-year-old passage serves about 200,000 passengers daily. U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer said the “whole national economy could collapse” if the new tunnel isn't built.

“Did this matter to New York and New Jersey commuters? Yes,” the New York Democrat said. “But it mattered to all of America as well.”

The 1,680-ton tunnel-boring machine unveiled Monday is nearly the length of two football fields and armed with cutters harder than diamonds. It was custom made in Germany and sent in parts to the U.S., where it has been carefully reassembled on site in North Bergen the last few months.

Officials on Monday said the machine is still undergoing final testing but is expected to begin cutting through the Palisades Cliffs in New Jersey in the coming days.

The machine is one of two that are expected to carve a roughly 1-mile (1.6-kilometer) stretch through the dense, volcanic rock of the cliffs at a pace of about 30 feet (9.1 meters) a day. A second set of machines will then take over to carve the tunnel section under the Hudson River.

The $16 billion project is expected to take around a decade to complete but has already weathered years of political and financial setbacks.

President Donald Trump’s administration froze federal support last year, leading to a brief construction suspension before a federal judge ordered the payments restored while the legal fight continued.

“Nothing will stop us from digging this tunnel,” said New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, also a Democrat. “When you see New York and New Jersey working together, get out of our way.”

The U.S. Department of Transportation, the federal agency involved in the litigation, responded Tuesday that its appeal "against the possible use of taxpayer dollars for unconstitutional, discriminatory contracting practices is ongoing.”

___

Marcelo reported from New York.

Donald Trump continued his inexplicable embrace of artificial intelligence on Tuesday as he gave it the ultimate honor — a Trump-style rebrand with the flick of an executive pen.

With the signing of an executive order Tuesday afternoon, Trump directed the U.S. government to begin referring to artificial intelligence, which is now embedded across the federal government, as “super intelligence”. The effect will be immediate: Work will be needlessly complicated for federal employees, while millions of Americans will continue calling the technology “artificial intelligence”.

The renaming effort aside, Trump’s real purpose Tuesday was to help AI leaders shake off the somewhat self-imposed stain on their records by declaring “SI” the future of American business and innovation, and insisting that the concerns about the technology felt by Americans were overblown or overstated.

He made that clear when he denied claiming that those concerns were a “hoax”, then added: “That’s why I changed the name. A hoax sounds like, you know, when you were using the former name. But this is now ‘super intelligence.’ That’s not a hoax.”

The president hosted an outdoor press conference with leaders in the AI industry, including Elon Musk, Sergey Brin, Dario Amodei and others whom he hosted at a luncheon at the White House shortly before his order was signed. Surrounded by Amodei and others who have warned that the government needs to do more to establish guardrails around the technology, Trump poured all of his focus into the renaming and claimed that the companies had signed a “morally binding” accord to “self-police” the industry.

open image in gallery Donald Trump was surrounded by tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday as he announced that he wanted to rename 'artificial intelligence' to 'super intelligence' ( Getty )

“It’s almost like a kind of constitution, in a way,” said the president. “And the biggest people in the world signed it. And I signed it as president. And it really is a form of protection.”

Behold: The only “guardrails” for AI that are likely to emerge under this administration. A copy of the accord signed by the tech CEOs and Trump was posted by the president on Truth Social, vowing that the industry would “implement robust internal controls” around AI usage and development, while working to “ensure that its models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways”. The unwritten conclusion being that there will not be any new enforcement measures or punishments to stop companies that fail to uphold those standards.

The CEOs and business leaders around Trump spoke only briefly, with Amodei repeating his insistence that the technology carried both great benefits and “very real risks” to humanity.

open image in gallery Anthropic's Dario Amodei spoke only briefly at Trump's event on Tuesday, and did not mention his call for AI development to slow down ( Getty )

"What I've always said, which is that AI has incredible benefits. I've talked about the medical benefits of the technology. As the president has said. Whoever wins AI, wins,” said Amodei.

“We all need to work together to make sure that we can win, and we can win safely if we do this right; if we work with the president and everyone here, we can win safely,” he said.

Amodei’s remarks were a far cry from the alarming rhetoric that he and other AI leaders and developers have used in recent days amid reports of potentially thousands of instances where AI agents accessed unauthorized systems and information that were not previously reported to the public. The problematic behavior of AI agents, first reported in its scale by Axios, included “bypassing guardrails, creating message boards, escaping sandboxes, website hijacking, self-prompting or seeking to bypass monitors,” according to the news outlet.

"I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong,” Amodei wrote in a blog post earlier this month.

The report follows the now public Hugging Face incident in which experimental OpenAI tools breached containment and improperly accessed computational systems at Hugging Face. That July 2026 incident resulted in OpenAI taking steps to rework its AI agent containment and security strategies.

open image in gallery Meta's Mark Zuckerberg was one of the first to embrace Trump's 'super intelligence' label ( Getty )

A number of statements from prominent AI researchers and developers have also alarmed many over the past month. In early September, a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher wrote on X that the companies’ systems would soon be able to “hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources." Another researcher warned in response that there was at least a 10% chance that the technology could cause the end of humanity, though by which specific means was not explained.

“We do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” wrote Evan Hubinger in the latter post.

Trump, however, seems to think that he can reverse the trend of American public opinion on data centers and AI — both of which topics are quickly becoming unpopular — with vague pledges of responsible and generous behavior on behalf of America’s new tech billionaire aristocrats, whom he says will transform local communities and shower them with benefits as they make themselves rich winning a new technological race for the United States.

On this issue, Trump finds himself firmly isolated from American public opinion in a rare but not exclusive way. As with his war with Iran, the president is aiming to redirect a wave of populist anger which is currently poised to give Democrats a clear wedge to separate him from his working-class base of supporters. Time will tell if he’ll be successful; Joe Biden wasn’t when he sought to convince voters that the economy under his guidance was recovering at an acceptable rate. With the midterms just over a month away, there’s little time left for the White House to convince voters that their feelings are wrong.

Yes, for sure [this is as good as I’ve felt in an England shirt. My football IQ, I’m getting better and better, smarter and smarter. I need time to really feel at home, to feel comfortable and once I have that I don’t look back.

News.title: How vaccines and antibiotics can beat some cancers
News.content:
At least one in eight cancers worldwide are caused by viruses and bacteria, according to a new study published in The Lancet.

An estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 – out of a total of 20 million recorded worldwide – were caused by common infections, almost all of which could have been prevented with treatments such as antibiotics or vaccines.

Almost half of infection-linked cancers, around 760,000 cases, were caused by H. pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach, researchers from the International Agency for Research on Cancer found.

The pathogen, which is typically ingested through contaminated food and water and is carried by around 60 per cent of the world’s population at any given time, can remain relatively undetected in the gut for between 20 and 40 years without causing any symptoms.

If left untreated, it can trigger chronic inflammation in the stomach and cellular mutations that, in some cases, lead to gastric cancer.

Cases of stomach cancer linked to H. pylori are particularly common in East Asia, where roughly 80 per cent of the population carries the bacterium. This is due in part to the prevalence of a more aggressive strain of the pathogen, known as CagA, which is endemic to the region.

East Asian diets – which typically include salty, pickled or smoked foods – can also damage the stomach’s protective lining and accelerate the inflammatory processes that can contribute to stomach cancer, researchers have found.

While H. pylori infection is treatable with a course of antibiotics, its symptoms often mimic those of other digestive problems and can be difficult to distinguish without testing.

This means the infection can remain undetected for years, allowing inflammation and damage to progress.

News.title: ‘Pooled’ TB testing could save money and improve diagnosis, study finds
News.content:
Mixing phlegm samples from multiple patients in “pooled tests” for tuberculosis could halve costs and help find millions of missing cases, according to a major new study.

While most advances in fighting TB come with a large price tag, the shift in strategy could dramatically boost access to diagnosis and save money, experts said.

TB is the deadliest single infection globally, killing around 1.3m people every year, despite being both preventable and curable.

The gold standard in diagnosis is rapid molecular testing, which detects genetic material from the bacteria causing TB in patient sputum samples within hours. But each sample needs a specialist diagnostic cartridge that costs around US$8, beyond the budget of many poorer countries even before recent aid cuts.

In a pooled test, samples from multiple individuals are tested in one cartridge. If the result is negative then all of them are reported to be negative, but if the result is positive each is re-tested individually.

Results published in The Lancet Global Health found the strategy, with up to four patients in each pool, used half as many cartridges as individual testing – 7,028 compared to 14,362. It detected 84.9 per cent of people with TB compared with 88 per cent for individual testing.

The study involved more than 14,000 people whose symptoms suggested TB in Bangladesh, Brazil, Cameroon, Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria and Vietnam.

News.title: UK borrowing costs hit highest level since 2007
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2007 after Middle East tensions pushed oil prices above $108.

Yields on 10-year gilts, which determine the price the treasury pays to borrow money, rose above 5.43pc on Monday, before edging back to 5.42pc.

These are levels not seen in almost two decades, underlining the challenge facing John Healey as he prepares for next month’s Budget.

The Chancellor is coming under pressure to slash spending or raise taxes to bring Britain’s borrowing costs under control, against a backdrop of growing debt and rising inflation.

The surge in 10-year gilt yields pushes them above the 19-year high of 5.41pc recorded earlier this month, threatening to put a dent in Mr Healey’s fiscal headroom – a self-imposed guardrail to guide public spending.

Economists said high costs reflect the scale of Britain’s near-£3tn national debt and the rise in inflation facing the country.

“The uncomfortable truth for the PM and his Chancellor, John Healey ... is that the wide spread of gilt yields over peers is fair, in our view, given the UK’s dire fiscal position and the inflationary pressures stemming from high energy prices,” said Elliott Jordan-Doak, at Pantheon Macroeconomics.

“Gilt yields will fall if energy prices drop, but investors will continue to be driven by the economics and the Government’s willingness to take tough fiscal decisions, both of which point to yields staying high.”

UK borrowing costs are growing amid a wider bond market sell-off after Donald Trump rejected a peace deal with Iran over the weekend, pushing oil prices higher.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 3pc to just over $108 a barrel on Monday, adding to global inflation pressures. Bond traders reacted by demanding higher yields from governments to lend them money.

The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds rose to above 5.24pc, the highest level since 2007.
