In Group B1, Slovenia beat North Macedonia 2-0 with goals from Sandi Lovric and Aljosa Matko.

Moldova were held to a 1-1 draw at home to the Faroe Islands and Slovakia beat Kazakhstan 2-1, while Iceland were 3-0 winners in Luxembourg and Estonia drew 1-1 in Bulgaria. Finland and Belarus played to a scoreless draw in Helsinki.

Sports.title: Sham City: verdict on financial breaches is damning and punishment must be severe | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
How bad could it be, really? How serious can a breach of arcane financial regulations be, really? Just how damning can accountancy be? Even after Friday’s revelation that Manchester City had been found guilty of all but one of the charges brought against them by the Premier League, it was perhaps difficult to grasp the scale of what that meant. After the publication of the independent commission’s findings, there can be no doubt: the commission found that Manchester City cheated, that they did so deliberately, and that they have sought to cover that up with a campaign of calculated misinformation.

City continue to maintain their innocence and issued a statement insisting that “the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. It referred, once again, to “a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of all of its positions”, and, again, insisted that “the club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence”.

The chief executive, Ferran Soriano, released a video reiterating many of the same points and vowing that the club would appeal – it has until Friday to do so – and pursue “all other legal avenues” to prove its innocence. He dismissed the Premier League’s charges as “a conspiracy theory” – and pointedly referred to the independent commission as a “Premier League Commission” – claiming that they were based on “a single false accusation” of diverting funds from the owner to the club under the guise of sponsorship payments. This, he said, “could not happen and … did not happen”. The commission’s view, it’s fair to say, is very different.

Any sanction will be addressed separately in a further hearing with the independent commission, but it is impossible to read the verdict without thinking that it will have to be extremely severe. Everton were docked a total of eight points over two accounting windows for an inadvertent breach of profitability and sustainability rules amounting to around £20m, having cooperated with the investigation. Exactly what City’s breach would turn out to be remains to be calculated, but the verdict found that they overstated income by around £855m and understated outgoings by around £66m. And this was not a cock-up but a calculated attempt to circumvent the rules.

View image in fullscreen The Premier League is made up of its 20 constituent clubs. City have cheated each of the other 19. Photograph: Carl Recine/Reuters

The verdict makes for astonishing reading. The reputation and integrity of the Abu Dhabi United Group, the 81% majority owner of City, lies in tatters, shredded in careful, measured legal prose. The appendices, as and when they are made public, might make it even worse. Even if some technicality is found that mitigates the punishment, their standing cannot surely recover. The findings show this is the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on English football. This is not breaching the maximum wage and being caught when most clubs were doing similar, which lay at the heart of the three previous huge top-division financial scandals: Manchester City in 1906, Leeds City in 1919 and Sunderland in 1957. This was deception on a massive scale.

Sponsorship deals are described as “shams” to obscure investment and overstated by £830m over the nine years in question as part of “a plan to disguise shareholder funding … as ‘commercial partner revenue’”. The Fordham Agreement, an arrangement by which an entity bought player image rights, was “little more than a front”. Attempts to claim that the Premier League had misunderstood how the sponsorship deals worked were “an ‘explanation’ that the club concocted well after the event in an attempt to conceal and obscure the realities of the disguised funding scheme”.

The level of mendacity identified is extraordinary. In regards to the “sham” sponsorship arrangements there was “intentional conduct” to “disguise the true nature of certain revenues and liabilities/expenses, to give the appearance of minimising the club’s financial dependence on ADUG” and give “a misleading impression in the club’s financial statements that the club’s financial position was better than it in fact was”.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Having been charged, City “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation”. The panel found “evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses called to give evidence on behalf of the club was false in a number of key respects” and “certain of those factual witnesses had given evidence at the hearing that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest”. On occasions, the panel concluded it “should not accept the opinion of an expert”; the precise reasons why are set out in an appendix but, in context, an inference can be drawn.

The one charge on which City were not found guilty was of breaching “duties of cooperation” with the Premier League in relation to one tranche of accusations. That, clearly, is not the get-out many City fans have hoped for since Friday. The verdict is damning.

The Premier League is made up of its 20 constituent clubs. City have cheated each of the other 19. They have lied consistently and deliberately. The continued denials only enhance the sense that this is a club that has no respect for the regulations.

There must now be a very good argument for expulsion. How can City, at least under the current ownership, ever be trusted again? How can they go on playing even this season, pretending all is well, awaiting appeal and sanction, when they have been found guilty of charges of such magnitude?

When the club has behaved like this, how can its continued existence in the Premier League be tolerated? And when they have cheated as they have been shown to do between 2009-10 and 2017-18, how can their name appear on the Premier League’s roll of honour?

Sports.title: ‘The emperor is naked’: Uefa president Ceferin takes new swipe at Infantino
Sports.content:
The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, has attacked his embattled Fifa counterpart Gianni Infantino in a scathing takedown of the failed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) project and other recent scandals, saying “the emperor is naked” and declaring “it is time to say ‘enough’”.

In a pointed address to the European Football Clubs (EFC) general assembly, Ceferin did not mention Infantino by name but made clear his view that Fifa’s leadership must change. He drew on the event’s location, Copenhagen, to make a comparison to Hans Christian Andersen’s The Emperor’s New Clothes in assessing Infantino’s conduct, making clear reference to the peace prize awarded to Donald Trump and last summer’s Folarin Balogun affair along with the FFE scheme.

“An emperor is persuaded that he is wearing magnificent clothes – clothes which, he is told, only the foolish or unfit cannot see,” Ceferin said. “His court goes along with it. Until a child simply says aloud what everyone can see: the emperor is naked. Perhaps the moral of the story is this: convenient words cannot change uncomfortable realities.

“Selling part of football’s future does not become development because you call it development. Putting a fait accompli in front of national associations does not become democratisation because you call it democratisation, however big the cheque is. And secrecy does not become consultation because you call it consultation.”

Ceferin suggested to the ­hundreds of club representatives present that ­Infantino’s behaviour would not be tolerated at one of their organisations. “Imagine one of your senior executives secretly negotiating away control of your club’s crown jewels,” he said. “You didn’t know. Your board didn’t know. Your players and fans didn’t know. And by the time you find out, the deal is almost done. What would your board do?

“Imagine that he creates a peace prize for a political leader, without his own board having any say over its creation or its recipient. Then, that same political leader calls during the biggest competition in the world to complain about a decision on the pitch. The rules say one thing. The phone rings. Then the decision changes.

“How many times would this have to happen at your club before the board says: ‘enough’? I think it is time to say ‘enough’. No office, no title and no amount of power gives anyone the right to sell the future of football.”

The ongoing war of words between football’s biggest governing bodies had already intensified on Tuesday when Fifa accused Uefa of waging a “misinformation campaign” and trying to influence the race for its presidency, urging a US court to reject Uefa’s request to receive documents for use in a planned criminal complaint against Infantino.

Senior figures within Uefa remain adamant that a candidate to oppose Infantino in the Fifa election next March must be found before the 18 November deadline for nominations. The EFC chair, Nasser al-Khelaifi, has been mooted in the past as a future contender but conclusively ruled himself out of the Fifa presidency in the Danish capital.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“I have zero interest in Fifa, zero agenda or ambition to be there,” al-Khelaifi said. “I don’t think I’m the right guy for this position. I’m enjoying what I’m doing, having fun. Fifa, not for me.”

Al-Khelaifi has designs on expanding the scope of his own organisation. In his speech to the general assembly he said “now is the time to create World Football Clubs”, explicitly stating that a representative body including those beyond Europe should be formed. “We are more than proud and happy if we can help and contribute outside of Europe for our colleagues from different clubs in the world,” he said later.

Sports.title: Chloe Kelly and Ella Toone dropped by England after not hitting ‘expected’ level
Sports.content:
Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly have been dropped from England’s squad because of their performance levels by Sarina Wiegman, who has given a first call-up to the 20-year-old ­Chelsea midfielder Lexi Potter.

Toone and Kelly have played key roles in England’s run of three consecutive major tournament finals but Wiegman made clear on Tuesday, when announcing her selection for the Women’s World Cup qualifying playoff against Greece, that she wants to see more from them for their clubs.

“The main reason is that I think the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch,” Wiegman said. The head coach “still believes in them” but said: “We expect a bit more and we know they can bring more. That was the message.

“There is also competition going on. It’s about talent, it’s about playing minutes and it’s about the ­competition going on. I hope they can step up and show what they can do.

Quick Guide England squad Show Goalkeepers: Hannah Hampton (Chelsea), Khiara Keating (Liverpool), Anna Moorhouse (Manchester City on loan from Orlando Pride) Defenders: Lucy Bronze (Chelsea), Jess Carter (Gotham), Niamh Charles (Manchester City), Grace Fisk (Liverpool), Alex Greenwood (Manchester City), Maya Le Tissier (Manchester United), Esme Morgan (Washington Spirit), Leah Williamson (Arsenal) Midfielders: Laura Blindkilde Brown (Manchester City), Lucia Kendall (Aston Villa), Erica Meg Parkinson (North Carolina Courage), Lexi Potter (Chelsea), Georgia Stanway (Arsenal), Keira Walsh (Chelsea) Forwards: Freya Godfrey (London City Lionesses), Lauren Hemp (Manchester City), Lauren James (Chelsea), Beth Mead (Manchester City), Jess Park (Manchester United), Alessia Russo (Arsenal) Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

“I’m convinced they can do better, I think they are convinced about that, too. I think they took the feedback in a good and in a positive way but it’s hard to take at the same time of course; it’s not a nice message. I hope they respond to it really well. We will support them and of course they get the support at club, too. I hope they come back even better than they were before.”

Neither Toone nor Kelly has scored or provided an assist in the Women’s Super League this season, although Toone did score in ­Manchester United’s 10-1 League Cup victory against the second-tier side ­Sheffield United last week, after she had been left out of their draw at Arsenal. Toone has started three of United’s four WSL games. Kelly has started one of Arsenal’s league matches, their ­Champions League win against Køge and made three WSL substitute appearances.

There was also no place for the Chelsea forward Aggie Beever‑Jones. Wiegman has called up the uncapped 18-year-old midfielder Erica Meg ­Parkinson and the London City Lionesses winger Freya Godfrey, and there is a return after injury for the captain, Leah Williamson.

There had been growing calls for the inclusion of Potter this term after her strong form for Chelsea, ­including her starring role in the 1-0 victory against Arsenal on Sunday. “She’s grown a lot,” Wiegman said.

“Last season we kept a close eye on her because she was getting into the squad and playing really well. But I think she’s started the season so well. Her performances have really impressed us so she really deserves this call-up.

“She’s shown at Chelsea that she can start against any team. The last game I thought she did very well against a top Arsenal [team]. What I’ve seen from her is that she comes out on the pitch and no matter who she plays against, she’s just going to play and she’s comfortable. I hope to see that next week.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The Lionesses face Greece in the first leg at the Pankritio Stadium in Heraklion, Crete on Friday 9 ­October before the return at Leicester’s King Power ­Stadium the following ­Tuesday, needing victory to reach the second decisive round of the ­playoffs in December.

England are having to contest the playoffs despite winning five of six matches in their qualifying group, having missed out on top spot to the world champions, Spain, based on the head-to-head record from their meetings in April and June, in repeats of the 2023 World Cup final. England will be heavily fancied to progress to next summer’s finals in Brazil.

That tournament could be ­Wiegman’s last with England because her contract expires after the World Cup. She gave little away when asked about any contract discussions.

“We have regular conversa­tions together, and we talk about the future at moments, but at this point I’m just focusing on Greece. We want to get through and qualify for the World Cup. Of course I talk to Mark [­Bullingham], every two weeks, and we speak about what’s ­happening now, what’s in the future, but there’s nothing new.”

Sports.title: Aston Villa sack manager Natalia Arroyo with club second-bottom of WSL
Sports.content:
Aston Villa have sacked Natalia Arroyo as their women’s manager, with the side winless and second-bottom of the Women’s Super League.

Arroyo was let go on Monday night, after Villa endured a 4-0 defeat at Tottenham on Sunday. It was a second loss in their opening four games of the season, with a 4-1 defeat by Manchester City sandwiched between 1-1 draws with Chelsea and Brighton, with performances largely poor.

Arroyo was appointed in January 2025, signing a three-and-a-half-year contract with the club. The former Barcelona and Espanyol player, who spent time as a journalist before focusing on her coaching career, joined Villa following four impressive years in charge at Real Sociedad where she guided the club to a second-place finish in the 2021-22 season and a Copa de la Reina final in her final campaign.

The 40-year-old replaced Shaun Goater, who took temporary charge following Robert de Pauw’s departure amid allegations over remarks he had made to players. Villa had only two wins from their first 12 WSL games when Arroyo took charge. Five consecutive league defeats followed as the team adapted to the new manager and they won their remaining five games to finish sixth.

Villa finished ninth in Arroyo’s first full campaign, with 20 points from 22 games, but a poor run of form and four successive defeats blighted the end of the season. “Everyone at Aston Villa would like to thank Natalia for her efforts and wish her all the best in her future endeavours,” the club said in a statement.

Villa have confirmed that Brian Sørensen, the women’s technical adviser, will take temporary charge of the team, including for their Subway Players Cup tie against Newcastle on Wednesday. Sørensen joined Villa as technical adviser in March, following his exit from Everton in February after four years with the Merseyside club.

Sports.title: OLIVER HOLT: Man City have been exposed as the most famous cheats in English sporting history. The gory details revealed by the Premier League leave no doubt - nothing less than relegation will suffice for this sinister, dishonest club
Sports.content:
The Premier League shoved the owners of Manchester City into a beam of light on a dark stage on Tuesday evening. And the club that has dominated English football for much of the last 20 years stood there, defrocked and unmasked. Guilty of all charges, the League said. But that was not all it said.

In fact, it was the tone of the League’s statement that was the most startling thing about it. They are often circumspect and dull, these offerings. Not this time. This time, it was angry and it was vengeful.

It gloried in the gory details of the industrial-scale cheating it said City had indulged in for year after year as it duped the rest of football with a ‘disguised funding scheme’.

The anger was in the vocabulary, too. ‘Sham contracts,’ the Premier League statement hissed as it outlined the tactics of the Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.

‘Sham commercial deals,' it added later. Sham, sham, sham. Some had been expecting a conciliatory move from the League in the wake of its victory but this was anything but that.

To read that statement was to see the Premier League dancing on the grave of the club that had come to embody its excellence and its appeal. All the exasperation and all the frustration of years of obstruction and intransigence from City’s Abu Dhabi owners as they fought the 115 charges ranged against them came spilling out on that page.

This was an end to patience. This was an end to keeping one’s counsel. This was an end to diplomacy.

After the accusation, this was the confrontation. The most eye-catching part of it was the revelation of the extent of City’s wrongdoing. This was the juiciest steak the Premier League had to offer and they tossed it out into the public domain with uncommon relish.

‘The purpose of these schemes,’ its statement said, ‘was found to have been to artificially inflate the club’s revenues, and reduce its costs, by more than £900million during the affected period, to appear to comply with financial rules.’

The Premier League have accused Manchester City of 'artificially (inflating) the club’s revenues, and (reducing) its costs, by more than £900million'

To read that statement was to see the Premier League dancing on the grave of the club that had come to embody its excellence and its appeal under (from left) Khaldoon Al Mubarak, Txiki Begiristain and Ferran Soriano

This is English football’s civil war in all its ugliness and its violence and its ferocity. The League’s statement hinted at what is to come. City have until Friday to launch an appeal, which they will almost certainly do but when that is done, it appears the League will press for severe sanctions to quell the inferno of City’s misdemeanours.

The level of City’s duplicity, outlined by the Premier League, laid bare the extent of the advantage that they had gained over the period involved. The punishment will have to fit that. It is harder to see City escaping relegation than it was on Tuesday morning. Anything lesser than that, the League will surely believe, will not be enough to deal with the crimes uncovered.

In the hours that followed the release of the statement, television screens showed reruns of City’s moments of triumph – Phil Foden holding aloft the Premier League trophy on one of the club’s many open-top bus rides, Pep Guardiola and City’s chairman, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, standing together on the pitch at the Etihad Stadium, holding up six fingers to signify the number of leagues Guardiola won.

The footage did not speak of triumphs any more, though. It spoke of subterfuge and shame. Those scenes of jubilation, it now appears, were dishonestly earned. Those trophies were dishonestly won. The club had cheated and cheated and cheated to get to a position where it was held up as the exemplar of all that was good in the game.

The more we know, the worse this feels. The more we know, the more stupid we seem that we were duped, that we believed.

This is moving into Lance Armstrong territory now. This is Chicago Black Sox territory. City, a team once famous for hitting new heights of dominance, are now the most famous cheats in English sporting history.

Their owners are still sticking to their story, even in the face of the findings of the independent commission and the details now provided by the Premier League. Their response has not been humility or contrition. Their response has been, actually, the sinister language of threat and reprisal.

City’s owners are serious people. Al Mubarak, many say, is the equivalent of the prime minister of the UAE. Others equate his role to cabinet secretary. He wields much power and he is the guardian of much wealth. No one takes him on like this and now that someone has, he is fighting to the end.

For now, City are sticking to Al Mubarak’s insistence that they have ‘irrefutable evidence’ that proves their innocence.

It is a curious defence. If the evidence is irrefutable, why has it not been presented already? Why has it been hidden away? Were these men not so powerful and astute, it would be tempting to say that their stance is becoming faintly comical.

The more we know, the more stupid we seem that we were duped, that we believed. Some would say this whole affair is moving into Lance Armstrong territory now

City are sticking to Al Mubarak’s insistence that they have ‘irrefutable evidence’ that proves their innocence. If the evidence is irrefutable, where is it?

‘Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission,’ a City statement said. ‘The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

'The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.’

Relentless? That is redolent of Al Mubarak’s notorious assertion more than a decade ago, when City were fighting UEFA, that he would rather spend £30m on the best 50 lawyers in the world and sue UEFA for the next 10 years than lose the Financial Fair Play case in which they were adversaries.

I wonder if some of those who have lionised Al Mubarak for his statements will reconsider now. They said they would when it came to a point when City’s guilt was outlined for all to see. Well, it is out there now. It is there in all its sad and ugly detail. Perhaps some of City’s fans will start to realise now that they, too, have been deceived.

City’s owners, though, will not back down. It is not their style. After months and years of shadow-boxing, the gloves are off. And City stand alone in the ring.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's £150m mega-fight is back ON: Heavyweight rivals set to meet in London face off TOMORROW after Gypsy King claimed rival 'tried to pull out' amid Eddie Hearn's feud with Dana White
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's £150m mega-fight is back ON: Heavyweight rivals set to meet in London face off TOMORROW after Gypsy King claimed rival 'tried to pull out' amid Eddie Hearn's feud with Dana White

It's on. At last. Finally. Confirmed by the almighty Turki.

Reconfirmed by the late, late word sent out that the face to face stare down between our two heavyweight titans will definitely take place at a press conference launch this Wednesday.

The fight that almost got away. AJ versus the Gypsy King. So close to being another of boxing's lost jewels that we almost gave up hope.

May the lords of the rings be praised.

Whether or not Dana White, the American interloper from UFC cage fighting who is demanding a share of the action, is present despite the protestations of Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn, who won the battle for this fight to take place if not at Wembley but not as far, far west of London as New York.

Anthony Joshua v Tyson Fury has been rescued for the British fight fans, by Cardiff. Although like the 70-odd thousand in the Principality Stadium the TV majority will have to stay awake into the wee small hours on the Friday night of December 11.

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will face each other down at a press conference on Wednesday

Fury and Joshua's fight is due to take place on December 11 in Cardiff with the showdown set to begin at 2am so Netflix subscribers can stream it at peak time in America

Fury against Joshua was almost the fight that got away, with the heavyweights now set to sort out differences that should have been settled a decade ago

First bell about 2am so that the tens of millions of Netflix subscribers can stream at peak time in America.

Assuming they buy into this as being a mega fight for all time. Or are satisfied that it is a spectacle unto itself.

Maybe a world heavyweight title adding spice to the occasion. Maybe not. Maybe just two good old Brits sorting differences that should have been settled a decade ago.

And why not? Fury and Joshua may be past their prime but they are not yet the walking dead.

They have enough fight left in their late 30s to put on a show.

And a future to fight for. For the winner there can be challenges to meet from the new generation of champions and a few million dollars more to add to the 75 million each will receive as an early Christmas present.

Always assuming no more spanners are thrown into these on-off-on works.

Good luck to both. Even more so to the Welsh constabulary who will have to deal with all those fans spilling out into darkened streets on what will already be a typically wild Friday night in Cardiff.

Sports.title: Scotland dealt harsh lesson by Switzerland as new boss Sebastien Pocognoli's home bow ends in 3-0 defeat: Moment of madness proves costly on another sobering night
Sports.content:
To borrow an old line from Mike Tyson, everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face. Just eight minutes into his first match in charge at Hampden, Sebastien Pocognoli took one flush on the chin.

Whatever designs Scotland’s new head coach may have had on causing an upset against Switzerland in this Nations League clash, it all went to pot in double-quick time.

A moment of utter madness from Jack Hendry, with a crude and brainless last-man foul on Switzerland striker Dan Ndoye, saw Pocognoli’s side reduced to ten men.

Switzerland boss Murat Yakin had missed his pre-match media conference on Monday due to hearing problems caused by cabin pressure on the flight into Glasgow.

Hendry looked like he was towing a Boeing 747 in his efforts to run back and chase the jet-heeled Ndoye as he raced through on goal.

The fact that Switzerland defender Ricardo Rodriguez, a free-kick expert throughout his career, then curled one into the top corner from the subsequent set-piece poured salt into Scottish wounds.

Elvedi slides home the second goal at the near post in Switzerland's 3-0 victory at Hampden

Ricardo Rodriguez (far left) celebrates his free-kick opener against Scotland

Up against a slick and stylish Swiss side, this was always likely to be a tough assignment even with 11 players on the field.

Playing 82 minutes with a numerical disadvantage? Mission impossible. Scotland deserve credit for sticking to the task and not just capitulating after that horror start.

They briefly threatened an equaliser at times midway through the first half and the Hampden crowd were clearly appreciative of the effort.

But, ultimately, this was a damp squib. On what was supposed to be a thunderous Hampden bow for Pocognoli and his new-look Scots, it turned into a training exercise for Switzerland.

As such, it was impossible to properly gauge Pocognoli and the performance from his team. They spent the majority of the night operating with one hand tied behind their back.

They must now lick their wounds and dust themselves down ahead of a trip to face North Macedonia in Skopje on Saturday night.

A total of 123 days had passed since Scotland set sail for the World Cup with a 4-1 victory over Curacao in their Hampden send-off.

It doesn’t sound all that long ago when you put it like that. But the scale of the changes — both in terms of the players and a new head coach — have been significant.

As they made their way back to Mount Florida, the Tartan Army were probably still familiarising themselves with some of the new faces in Pocognoli’s squad.

Luis Binks was the latest player to be handed a debut, the Brondby captain coming in to replace Stephen Welsh in central defence.

That was one of three changes made by Pocognoli from the 0-0 draw away in Slovenia last Saturday, with Nathan Patterson and Kieron Bowie also coming in to replace Aaron Hickey and Robbie Ure.

Jack Hendry was given his marching orders early on and left Scotland with a mountain to climb

The first half in Ljubljana had been an eyesore, but Scotland were vastly improved in a dominant second half. On a different day, they could — and perhaps *should* — have won by two or three goals.

This was always likely to be a far stiffer test. Over the past 20 years or so, Switzerland have been a model of consistency in international football.

Back in the summer, they pushed Argentina all the way to extra-time in the quarter-finals of the World Cup and were unlucky to lose in the end.

Even without their captain Granit Xhaka, who withdrew from the squad due to an investigation into a fake Covid vaccine certificate, they were still expected to be formidable opposition.

The Swiss had opened their Nations League campaign with an emphatic 3-0 win over North Macedonia in Skopje, with Zeki Amdouni scoring two of their three goals.

Scotland were clearly intent on pressing the Swiss high up the pitch in the early stages. Picking up where he left off in Ljubljana, Billy Gilmour glided past a couple of red jerseys and fed a through ball for Bowie to chase.

The big striker outmuscled Leeds United defender Nico Elvedi and fired the ball across the face of goal before the visitors managed to clear the danger.

But the air of optimism around Hampden was soon shattered by a rapier-like attack from Switzerland right through the centre of the pitch that would ultimately see the home side reduced to ten men.

After a neat combination in midfield, the ball was played through for Ndoye to chase. One-on-one in a foot race with Hendry, there was only ever likely to be one winner.

Zeki Amdouni fires home the third goal as Switzerland cruised to a comfortable success

Ndoye was racing clear only to be clumsily hauled down just as he could see the whites of Angus Gunn’s eyes and was about to pull the trigger.

Serbian referee Nenad Minakovic initially gave a penalty-kick and booked Hendry. The fact he was blatantly the last man was offset by the double jeopardy law.

But when TV replays showed that the contact had initially started outside the box? Hendry was a dead man walking.

Red card. All day long and twice on Sundays. As he jogged off the field and headed for the tunnel, there was no acknowledgement from Pocognoli.

It was thoroughly dim-witted from Hendry. What on earth was he thinking? The smart play would have been either to let Ndoye shoot and potentially score, or make sure the contact was inside the box.

Either way, Scotland would have kept 11 men on the pitch in their efforts to mount a comeback. When Ricardo Rodriguez then curled a peach of a free-kick into Gunn’s top corner, it was the ultimate double whammy.

Open the touchline, Pocognoli urgently tried to reshuffle the pack. Off came Bowie and on came Welsh. It became a sort of 5-3-1 shape.

Gilmour was still having some excellent moments, drifting away from another challenge before firing the ball out wide to Andy Robertson.

Robertson’s low ball in was intended for Oli McBurnie, only for Elvedi to intervene at the near post. McBurnie also tangled with Remo Freuler on the edge of the box but threw himself to the ground too easily.

Against all the odds, another promising Scotland attack was undone by a clumsy touch from Robertson. Nonetheless, the Tartan Army roared their approval. There was still a game on here.

At the other end, Gunn made a good low save one-handed to deny Ndoye after a clever dummy from Amdouni on the edge of the box.

It became a bruising night for Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli in the Hampden dugout

Switzerland just had so much class and control, capable of flicking a switch and moving up through the gears at any moment.

The referee was needlessly picky at times and Pocognoli, decked out in a dark suit and shirt à la Diego Simeone, was booked towards the end of the first half for some fiery protestations on the touchline.

The mood of the new Scotland head coach wouldn’t have improved much when Switzerland doubled their lead just 10 minutes after the break, Elvedi converting an Ndoye cross from close range.

For Scotland, the final half-hour or so became an exercise in damage limitation. The game was gone. Switzerland continued to threaten, with Ndoye and Amdouni again going close.

The outstanding Amdouni rifled one into the top corner for 3-0 with just under ten minutes left to play. In the end, Scotland were soundly beaten.

That may well have been the outcome had they kept 11 players on the pitch for 90 minutes. We’ll never know. But this was a sobering night.

Sports.title: Roy Keane claims Man City stars should BIN their medals won during period of 'cheating' and hits out at owners after club found guilty of £900m 'sham' in seismic Premier League verdict
Sports.content:
Roy Keane says he would bin his medals if he was a Manchester City player after they were found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules for nine seasons.

The Manchester United legend fears it will be hard for the current crop under Enzo Maresca to maintain their elite levels of performance under the cloud of 'cheating owners'.

The Premier League has condemned City for making 'sham' agreements to manipulate their financial accounts to the tune of £900million over a nine-season period which saw them win eight trophies.

'They knew it would hurt a lot of people but they've still done it,' Keane told ITV Sport after England's 2-0 win over Czechia in the Nations League.

'If I was a player, I'd be 100 per cent sticking those medals in the bin. Of course you would, it's cheating.

'They won it on the pitch because cheating was going on.

Roy Keane has claimed he would throw away his medals if he was a Manchester City player

The Premier League have confirmed that Manchester City are guilty of the most serious financial rule breaches

'I think it's going to be very difficult for the players and the manager, the club, what they stand for, when you've got owners who are happy cheating. It's hard to maintain a level of excellence.'

Ian Wright added: 'They told them nothing bad is going on. If you're a player, something is not right.

'It's very unprecedented and sad for everybody. The owners and what they've done, terrible.'

Before the match, Wright had said: 'Unprecedented punishment is required here. It's a massive day for the Premier League.

'Very messy. It's a problem for them to be going to Liverpool (in their next fixture). In their real time, Liverpool were the team chasing them down. Look at what Jurgen Klopp went through to break them - it probably broke him.'

On Friday, Daily Mail Sport reported how City had been found guilty of 114 of 115 charges against them.

However, there had been no official comment from the Premier League on the findings of an independent panel who oversaw a hearing that concluded in December 2024.

That has now dramatically changed. In a lengthy statement, the Premier League say City arranged 'sham contracts (which misrepresented the true agreement between the parties) with a number of its commercial partners, as well as relying on "sham" agreements with others, to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs'.

It also says the club falsely altered the financial picture at the Etihad to the tune of £900m. The club had agreed exorbitant sponsorship deals with a number of companies, but those sponsors only paid part of the fee.

The rest was propped up by the Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.

Premier League CEO Richard Masters claimed that the commission's verdict had 'vindicated' the league's decision to pursue the charges

As the Premier League note, this allowed City to 'artificially inflate the club’s revenues' and therefore spend more under Premier League rules. The higher the revenue a club records, the more they are permitted to spend.

Moreover, further 'sham' deals, funded by ADUG, allowed the club to 'record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred'.

The Premier League say that revenues were inflated and costs reduced to the tune of £900m in an attempt to comply with spending rules. The result was that the club 'filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators'.

It added that the club was 'significantly in breach of both the Premier League's and UEFA's spending limits' during the time period in question, 2009-2018 when it won eight major trophies.

Had City reported accurately 'it would have been in breach of both the League's and UEFA's spending limits by a very substantial amount'.

The panel also found that City committed multiple breaches of its duties of co-operation and good faith in that it failed to assist the Premier League's four-year investigation, triggered by the emergence of club emails obtained by a hacker.

Indeed, City had 'made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation'.

Richard Masters, Chief Executive of the Premier League, said: 'The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade.

'It also vindicates the Premier League's decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently.

'It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously.

'This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the Commission's decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans.'

Manchester City have insisted on their innocence throughout the saga (Pep Guardiola pictured with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak)

In a statement released a short time later, City said it was ‘disappointed and surprised’ and referred to the ‘opinion of the Premier League Commission’.

It added: ‘The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

‘The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

‘The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

‘The club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete.’

City have until Friday to appeal.

Man City were first charged with the 115 breaches in February 2023. While that totemic number stuck, the figure – as they subsequently corrected – was actually 130.

Of those, 54 were charges of ‘failure to provide accurate and up-to-date financial information’ while there were 14 charges of ‘failure to provide accurate financial reports for player and manager compensation’.

Both sets related to alleged offences between 2009 and 2018 (2009-2018), an eight-year period which saw the club win four Premier League titles, the FA Cup, and three League Cup competitions.

There were also five charges of ‘failure to comply with UEFA’s regulations, including Financial Fair Play Regulations’ and seven charges of breaching the Premier League’s profit and sustainability regulations (PSR) between 2015 and 2018.

There were also 35 counts of failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations between 2018 and 2023.

The hearing into the 130 breaches began last September at London’s International Dispute Resolution Centre, with the Premier League sparing no expense and enlisting KCs Adam Lewis and Andrew Hunter to take its case.

Sports.title: Man City found guilty of HUGE financial 'sham' as Premier League confirm verdict in blistering statement: Club cooked their books by £900m - and now could be RELEGATED
Sports.content:
Manchester City cooked the books to the tune of £900m in a nine-year period peppered with ‘sham’ deals during which they became the major force in English football, a commission has found. In a damning 40-page verdict City, who won eight trophies during the spell involved, artificially inflated sponsorship agreements and pumped money into the club from its Abu Dhabi owners via disguised payments in a bid to swerve Premier League spending rules. The eight-times champions were found guilty of ‘all charges related to serious breaches’ of the regulations and the majority of those in relation to its failure to co-operate with the competition’s probe. City witnesses were also accused of lying in front of the three-person panel, in an explosive verdict that will further send shockwaves through football after news of the club’s guilt first leaked on Friday. All punishments, including expulsion, transfer bans and points deductions are open to the Premier League and a sanction hearing will take place in due course. However, City quickly confirmed that it would be launching an appeal ahead of Friday’s deadline and - amid extraordinary scenes - accused the Premier League of creating a ‘conspiracy theory’. The Premier League has confirmed that Manchester City have been found guilty of 'all charges related to serious breaches' of the league's financial regulations City's chief executive Ferran Soriano (centre) later circulated a video sent to club staff stressing that the allegations were false A fiery club statement branded the verdict ‘opinion’ and tellingly labelled the independent panel a ‘Premier League commission’. In a video sent to 1,000 staff and seen by Daily Mail Sport, infuriated chief executive Ferran Soriano said the allegations were ‘just not true’ and repeated the claim that they had provided ‘irrefutable evidence’. ‘Very soon we will look back at this as another time in our history when we dealt with adversity and overcame it together,’ he added. The bombshell statement was released late on Tuesday afternoon. In it, the Premier League said the panel found City arranged ‘sham contracts (which misrepresented the true agreement between the parties) with a number of its commercial partners, as well as relying on ‘sham’ agreements with others, to artificially inflate the club’s revenues and reduce its costs’. It added that the panel, whose hearing concluded in December 2024, had found that the club had falsely altered the financial picture at the Etihad to the tune of £900m. The Premier League said that City was actually ‘significantly in breach of both the Premier League’s and UEFA’s spending limits’ during the time period in question - 2009-2018 - when it won eight major trophies. Deals with a number of sponsors were part of ‘a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees’, the statement added, saying that ‘the remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club’. The panel also found further ‘sham’ arrangements, funded by ADUG, which allowed City to record lower operating expenses that it incurred, along with a ‘”sham” circular arrangement with Fordham, an entity that purchased the club’s players’ image rights, that was funded by ADUG’. The result was that the club had ‘filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators’. Premier League CEO Richard Masters claimed that the commission's verdict had 'vindicated' the league's decision to pursue the charges Had City reported accurately ‘it would have been in breach of both the League’s and UEFA’s spending limits by a very substantial amount’. The panel also found that City committed multiple breaches of its duties of co-operation and good faith in that it failed to assist the Premier League’s four-year investigation, triggered by the emergence of club emails obtained by a hacker. Indeed, City had ‘made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation’. The report noted that issues ‘were fiercely contested between the parties’. It added that proceedings lasted for 42 days and acknowledged that it had ‘taken us much longer than we would have wished’ to reach a conclusion, which ‘was regrettable’. Transcripts of evidence given ran to more than 7,000 pages. The lop-sided verdict also rounded on ‘a number of important factual witnesses’ who gave evidence on behalf of the club, saying such evidence was ‘false’ and stating that some gave evidence ‘they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest’. From 2009 to 2018 it found City claimed commercial income of £949.94m when only £119.25m had come from sponsors – which was the figure which should have appeared in the accounts. The statement added that City’s core defence was ‘untrue’, describing it as an explanation ‘concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the Disguised Funding Scheme’. Richard Masters, Premier League chief executive, said the competition had been ‘vindicated’ and that the club had ‘systematically broken Premier League rules for nearly a decade’. ‘It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition,’ he said. ‘It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously. ‘This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the Commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans.’

Your browser does not support iframes.

Premier League rules state that after City lodges its appeal the chair of the panel should appoint a three-person appeal board ‘as soon as reasonably practicable’. Any objections to the subsequent appointments should then be lodged within two working days. The whole process should be concluded within 12 weeks. Whether that will be the case remains to be seen. It is unclear whether a sanction will be handed down before an appeal takes place. In a statement released shortly after the Premier League, City said it was ‘both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission’. It added: ‘The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums. ‘The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.’ Soriano added: ‘The whole Premier League case against us is based on a single false accusation – that the owner’s personal money was somehow and secretly put into the club via some sponsors from Abu Dhabi. This is just not true. Irrefutable evidence has been provided that shows it could not happen and that it did not happen. This includes bank statements, money transfers, witnesses and everything necessary to categorically demonstrate the money did not come from the owner. ‘Surprisingly for us and our lawyers after nearly two years the Premier League’s commission has issued an opinion that supports the Premier League’s conspiracy theory.’

Sports.title: Anthony Gordon gives England lift-off in the Nations League with match-winning display against Czech Republic - but uncertainty in one key area still remains for Thomas Tuchel despite 2-0 win, writes IAN LADYMAN
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel is learning what it feels like to be an England manager. Expectation will always be sky high and the margin for error in the court of public opinion is mercilessly slight.

It was as well, then, that his England team won here. Defeat to Spain at the weekend had raised questions and made this a night when victory was imperative. After an uncertain start, England came through with a degree of comfort.

It was a big night for Trent Alexander-Arnold – restored to the team for the first time since June 2025 – and he had a decent game.

With hindsight it was a perfect night for the Real Madrid full-back to re-emerge. England ended the game having had 66 per cent of the possession and just as much territory. Question marks about his defending at this level will have to wait for another occasion.

Indeed it was Alexander-Arnold’s lovely cross that bounced nicely for Anthony Gordon – England’s best player – to stoop and head in the first goal early in the second half. It was a significant moment as England had not been always convincing until then. From that point, it was a stroll and the surprise was that there was just one more goal, from Harry Kane with 20 minutes remaining.

England’s victory was, however, undoubtedly shaped by an incident in the 24th minute when Czech Republic midfielder Pavel Sulc was sent off for a rather lazy and late challenge on Elliot Anderson. ‘An early red card always has a heavy influence,’ conceded Tuchel afterwards.

Anthony Gordon's superb display inspired England to a 2-1 win over Czech Republic in Prague

Harry Kane doubled England's tally in the 69th minute with a sharp finish in the penalty box

Up until that point, the Czechs had been in the game. From then on, they were not. It was pretty much that simple. The home team are going through a painful transition at the moment and had lost to Croatia here at the weekend. Their last win was in a World Cup warn-up against Guatemala and it may be a while before they experience another.

England, with Trevoh Chalobah winning his second cap as a replacement for the injured Ezri Konsa, had been a little uncertain early on, almost as though they were still shaking the memory of the Spain game from their minds.

But a Czech team asked to play for so long with one man fewer eventually ran out of gas and out of luck.

With Tuchel fielding a new central defensive partnership and the ninth different right back in England’s last 24 games, perhaps we shouldn’t have been surprised that there was some hesitancy once again in that department.

Early on, the home team broke quickly and regularly from their own half. England goalkeeper James Trafford was out quickly to foil Lukas Cerv before the same player volleyed wide from 18 yards. Then, soon after that, an Anderson slip let in Matej Radosta and his shot was blocked well by Chalobah.

Against this backdrop, England sought some control and though they were not always convincing, Morgan Rogers – playing ahead of the rested Jude Bellingham - turned to shoot against the far post in the 16th minute before Anderson and Bukayo Saka saw their follow ups come back from defenders in red.

The red card, when it came, was unnecessary. Suic was arguably not trying to hurt Anderson but his challenge was made on the stretch and had precious little control as studs made contact with Achilles. VAR was right to get involved and referee Umut Meler was right to upgrade from yellow to red.

Almost immediately the game changed. The Czech Republic retreated to the edge of their own penalty area and England’s puzzle was clear. How to break down a nine man defence.

For a while it was a challenge. Gordon ran one low cross right across the goal line while Kane was denied by Matej Kovar in the Czech goal.

Trent Alexander-Arnold was given his chance by Thomas Tuchel after almost 500 days in exile

England's task in Prague was made easier when Czech Republic's Pavel Sulc was sent off





At half-time England looked a little below the required levels. Happily that soon changed as Alexander-Arnold delivered a super and very familiar cross for Gordon to convert.

‘We never doubted that he can produce those moments,’ was Tuchel’s assessment.

With their game plan now out of the window, the Czech Republic were in trouble. Damage limitation wasn’t really an option and as spaces appeared, English players ran into them.

Indeed Lewis Hall almost scored his first England goal after the irrepressible Gordon set him up before a low Hall cross was poked on to the post by Rogers.

The Chelsea player was in the midst of it all again with 20 minutes left as he protected the ball with his back to goal in the area. That show of strength allowed Kane to run in and drive a low shot across Kovar and in.

With some breathing space established, Tuchel handed a debut to Bournemouth’s Alex Scott from the bench and a first competitive appearance to Liverpool teenager Rio Ngumoah.

Bellingham, meanwhile, came on for Kane and wore the captain’s armband.

A glimpse into the future, conceded Tuchel. ‘It shows that he could be captain one day,’ he said.

Sports.title: Trent Alexander-Arnold has kept up his end of England bargain - but return might be short-lived
Sports.content:
Trent Alexander-Arnold has kept up his end of England bargain - but return might be short-lived

CZECH REPUBLIC 0-2 ENGLAND: The Three Lions are off the mark in the Nations League with Trent Alexander-Arnold having laid down a marker to Thomas Tuchel after returning to the squad

View 3 Images Alexander-Arnold made his first start under Thomas Tuchel in Prague (Image: Getty Images)

Trent Alexander-Arnold turns 28 next week. He has two Premier League winners’ medals, one Champions League winners’ medal, one FA Cup winners’ medal, two EFL Cup winners’ medals, a UEFA Super Cup winners’ medal, and a FIFA Club World Cup winners’ medal.

‌



He plays for Real Madrid. But he will turn 28 having started 27 matches for his country. Boy, England must have been good over this past decade.

‌



To be fair, he has had strong competition for his role, Kyle Walker being a formidable obstacle to his inclusion in starting line-ups down the years.

‌



But the bottom line is that first Gareth Southgate, and now Thomas Tuchel, have given the impression they would rather play themselves at right-back than trust Trent.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



This was Alexander-Arnold’s first start for Tuchel. England’s German coach has used eight different players as starting right-backs before a lack of options finally persuaded him - kicking and screaming probably - to give Alexander-Arnold a start.

Had Ben White, Reece James, Djed Spence and Tino Livramento been available, the Real Madrid defender would not have got a look-in.

Had Gary Neville, Phil Neal and Viv Anderson been available, he would probably not have got a look-in.

‌



Alexander-Arnold knows that. You can tell. For one half of football, this was not Alexander-Arnold with a point to prove. This was Alexander-Arnold on autopilot.

This was Alexander-Arnold - making his first international start in 716 days - knowing that Tuchel is not having him. But he is too good, too professional, to let that mindset take root. His natural-born brilliance takes over.

View 3 Images Trent Alexander-Arnold played an inch-perfect cross to Anthony Gordon for England's opener (Image: Getty Images)

‌



His assist for Anthony Gordon’s opener was not just about the trademark, whipped delivery. It was not just about a right boot that does not so much strike the ball as persuade it.

It was about his sense of adventure, because that is what got him into the position to execute the assist in the first place. It was a very accomplished finish from a team-mate brought up just down the road in Liverpool, but the pass was a thing of beauty.

It was a pass that took three defenders out of the game. It was a pass that gave the goalkeeper no chance of interception. It was an extraordinary pass. But ordinary for Alexander-Arnold.

‌



Will one assisting masterpiece be enough for Tuchel to trust Trent? This is the manager who could not get Alexander-Arnold into a 26-man World Cup squad, don’t forget.

View 3 Images Gordon celebrates with Alexander-Arnold (Image: Getty Images)

Probably not. Tuchel will have to swallow some serious pride. Against the Czechs, Alexander-Arnold came up with a peach of an assist and Lewis Hall was excellent. Neither were on hand to help England at the World Cup.

‌



Tuchel must have had one hell of a squad. You never know, Tuchel might now make Alexander-Arnold an essential part of his plans for Euro 2028.

Tuchel might decide he is the manager who can get the very best out of an outrageously talented player. Tuchel might say to Alexander-Arnold that the right-back position is his to lose.

But don’t hold your breath. Just enjoy moments like such a gifted footballer provided in Prague.

Sports.title: Roy Keane sends brutal 'medals in the bin' message to Man City stars after 115 charges verdict
Sports.content:
Roy Keane sends brutal 'medals in the bin' message to Man City stars after 115 charges verdict

Roy Keane has given his verdict on Manchester City being found guilty of financial breaches following a statement released by the Premier League

View Image Roy Keane (Image: ITV)

Manchester United legend Roy Keane has claimed that he would put his medals "in the bin" if he were a Manchester City player after the club was found guilty of financial breaches. The Premier League issued a statement on Tuesday confirming that City had been found guilty by an independent commission, following charges first issued back in 2023.

‌



City issued a statement in response, maintaining their innocence, and outlined their intention to appeal the verdict, with a deadline set for Friday (October 2).

‌



The charges brought against City by the Premier League relate to a nine-year spell between 2009 and 2018, during which time the club won three league titles, one FA Cup and three League Cups, and regularly competed in the Champions League.

‌



Keane has already called for City to be punished following the verdict, and has now sent a message to the players who have won major honours for the club.

Ian Wright demands 'unprecedented' Man City punishment after Premier League statement READ MORE :

Man City chief's secret message to staff after bombshell Premier League verdict emerges READ MORE :

"Well, do you know what? They [City] knew it would hurt a lot of people, and they've still done it," Keane told ITV Sport.

"And if I was a player with that bit of success and praise that we've given a lot of credit for - but if I was a player I'd be 100% sticking them medals in the bin."

‌



ITV presenter Mark Pougatch then asked: "You would feel let down by the club?" Keane then responded: "Oh, 100% of course, of course you would. It's cheating."

Keane went on: "You're hearing nonsense from ex-players saying, 'Oh well, they won on the pitch'. Because there was cheating. There was cheating going on."

The United legend added: "I think it's going to be very difficult for the players, for the manager. The trust, the belief in whatever's gone on at the football club, what they stand for when you've got owners who are quite happy cheating.

‌



"It's very difficult for these players going forward to try and maintain the level of excellence that they've been [displaying]."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Arsenal legend Ian Wright was alongside Keane in the ITV studio, and added that the club had let down players and fans, in a situation that is sad for everyone involved in football.

"You know what it is as well, they've told the players," Wright said. "The players, the fans, they've all believed them, they've tried to stand behind their club, but they told them that nothing bad's going on.

"And now what is it? 115 charges, 114 charges? And they've been telling people. So if you are a player, something's not right with you, you're thinking this ain't right."

‌



Wright added: "We're not meant to be seeing this, it's unprecedented what we're seeing right now and it's sad for everybody.

"But in respect of the owners and what they've done? Terrible, terrible."

City issued a statement on Tuesday evening which read: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission, that has been published today.

‌



"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

Article continues below

"The Club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Sports.title: Man City chief's secret message to staff after bombshell Premier League verdict emerges
Sports.content:
Man City chief's secret message to staff after bombshell Premier League verdict emerges

Manchester City have been found guilty of the Premier League charges and the eight-time champions have now hit out at the allegations ahead of a possible appeal over the coming days

View 2 Images Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Ferran Soriano (Image: Getty Images)

Manchester City's chief executive, Ferran Soriano, has sent a video message to staff members claiming that the club will continue fighting their guilty verdict.

‌



The Premier League confirmed on Tuesday that the club had been found guilty of all charges, with the process now moving towards an appeal. That is an avenue that City will take advantage of. Before that, CEO of the City Football Group Foriano has got in touch with club employees.

‌



He sent a three minute video message, obtained by the Manchester Evening News, to staff members and said that they will continue attempting to clear their name and suggested that the Premier League's verdict is based on a 'single false accusation'.

‌



"I want to share some information related to the ongoing disciplinary process between Manchester City and the Premier League. A document has been made public with an opinion of the Premier League commission that is negative to our interests. I want to explain exactly what this is, the next steps and how we are going to continue to defend the club, and finally be vindicated in this process.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



"This has gone for so long that it is important to remind ourselves that the whole Premier League case against us is based on a single false accusation - that the owners' personal money was somehow and secretly put into the club via some sponsors from Abu Dhabi. This is just not true.

"Irrefutable evidence has been provided to the Premier League commission that shows that it could not happen and that it did not happen. This includes bank statements, money transfers, witnesses and everything necessary to categorically demonstrate that the money did not come from the owner. Every other false charge that has been thrown at us - and aggressively marketed and promoted - comes from the simple, central, and completely false accusation.

"Surprisingly for us, and for our lawyers, after nearly two years the Premier League Commission has introduced an opinion that supports the Premier League's conspiracy theory. To do so, the opinion had to ignore the extensive evidence provided by the club in order to reach a conclusion that is clearly wrong.

‌



View 2 Images Ferran Soriano has sent a message to Man City employees (Image: Getty Images)

"Our lawyers will now file an appeal that sets out the opinion contains clear material errors of law, principle and fact and it is unsafe. Remember we have been here before. In 2020 we were also wrongly ruled against for many of the same issues. We appealed to an independent body in CAS and we won.

"We will now be relentless in our work. We will focus on the independent appeal process and also all other legal avenues available to us in order to win the case, and we will take all necessary action to protect the club and seek compensation from any party that tries to damage it now, and in the future.

‌



"I know this can be a bit of a distraction but please remain focused on our business and take care of our extended City family as we always do. Please follow the normal protocols in referring to fan, partner and media enquiries. Very soon we will look back at this and recognise it is another time in our history when we dealt with adversity and overcame it together."

Soriano's message comes in the aftermath of a strong statement from City in response to the Premier League's verdict. It read: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission, that has been published today.

Man City 115 charges delay explained as commission lay out Premier League timeline READ MORE :

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

‌



"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence. The Club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Elsewhere, Premier League CEO Richard Masters has claimed that the Premier League are attempting to wrap up the proceedings as soon as possible. In a statement, he said:“The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade.

‌



“It also vindicates the Premier League’s decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently.

“It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously.

“This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the Commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans.”

Sports.title: Man City 115 charges delay explained as commission lay out Premier League timeline
Sports.content:
Man City 115 charges delay explained as commission lay out Premier League timeline

Manchester City have been found guilty by the independent commission who have now explained the reason behind the delay

View 3 Images Manchester City have been found guilty by the independent commission following their legal battle with the Premier League. (Image: PA Wire)

The independent Commission has explained the reason behind the 20-month delay following the end of the 42-day hearing into the Premier League and Manchester City's 115 charges. The investigation into Man City began in December 2018, and a complaint was subsequently issued under Section W of the League’s rules in February 2023.

‌



The Premier League announced in a statement today (Wednesday) that City were found guilty of 'all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules over a nine-season period, and the majority of charges in relation to its failure to co-operate with the League’s investigation.' The club still maintain their innocence.

‌



In a statement, the independent Commission explained the reason behind the lengthy delay and wrote: "It has taken us much longer than we would have wished, and much longer than we had anticipated would be the case when the hearing concluded, to produce our Decision. That is regrettable.

‌



FOLLOW OUR MAN CITY FB PAGE! Follow our Manchester City Mirror Football Facebook page

"However, we were fortunate to have available to us throughout the period in which our Decision has been being prepared not only all of the documents that were used at the hearing but also (a) verbatim transcripts of the evidence given by each witness and expert at the hearing.

"Those transcripts ran to approximately 7,000 pages, and (b) extremely detailed written submissions from the parties (that they had supplemented orally over four days at the end of the hearing) on the evidence and each of the numerous issues that we were tasked with determining in the proceedings."

‌



Premier League chief executive Richard Masters also broke his silence on the investigation and said: "The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade.

View 3 Images Richard Masters, CEO of the Premier League, has released a statement on Manchester City's rule breaches. (Image: PA Wire)

"It also vindicates the Premier League’s decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently.

‌



"It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously.

"This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches.

"Now we have the Commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans."

‌



View 3 Images City have been found guilty (Image: Getty Images)

City however, maintain their innocence and have until the end of this week, Friday, October 3 to lodge and appeal. They released a statement which read: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission, which has been published today.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.
