You may be having second thoughts about eating the berries in your fridge after CBC News spoke with a whistleblower who made a startling claim about the amount of chemicals on fruit that a U.S. company allegedly shipped to Canada.

David Harada, a former employee for California-based Driscoll's, alleged in a lawsuit that about half of the company's exports to Canada contained pesticide levels that exceeded Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) standards.

Driscoll's supplies raspberries, strawberries, blueberries and blackberries that are largely grown in California and Mexico, but with some products coming from other places seasonally — including parts of Canada.

Harada says the excess chemical levels were due to over-spraying and the removal of food safety compliance parameters for berries sent to Canada.

The CFIA confirmed higher-than-permissible levels of pesticides on the company's berries. Driscoll's has said that it's amended its controls to comply with Canadian standards.

But that may not be enough to put some Canadian consumers' minds at ease, especially parents. Meanwhile, food safety experts say this has prompted an important conversation about the chemicals used on the produce we eat.

Here's a quick look at what you need to know.

Are the berries in my fridge safe to eat?

Harada's lawsuit alleges that millions of pounds of berries with chemical levels exceeding CFIA guidelines were imported between 2022 and 2024, so it's highly unlikely those would have survived in your fridge since then — and you certainly shouldn't eat them if they are still in there.

Maria Corradini, an associate professor in the University of Guelph's food sciences department, says the chemical compounds sprayed on produce do degrade over time.

But the issue, she says, is ensuring that the right amount is applied and that enough time has passed so that there isn't leftover residue come harvest time.

WATCH | Driscoll's berries shipped to Canada with excess chemicals, lawsuit alleges: Driscoll's sent berries with excess chemicals to Canada: whistleblower | Duration 3:06 A whistleblower lawsuit in California alleges millions of trays of fruit containing non-compliant levels of pesticides and chemicals crossed the border between 2022 and 2024. The suit also accuses Driscoll’s fruit company of trying to cover it up.

Environmental toxicologist Daniel Green says that even if you actually consumed berries with higher than permissible levels of chemical residue, it probably wouldn't be enough to harm you.

You would likely need to eat something like 19 kilograms of berries in a short period of time to really feel any adverse effects.

"This issue isn't one serving of berries," he told CBC Montreal's Gloria Henríquez, explaining that it's like "one speck" of the chemicals to which people are exposed in their daily lives.

What chemicals were found on the berries?

The three chemicals found were bifenthrin, iprodione and captan.

Iprodione is used to prevent and control mould, mildew and stem and root rot on a variety of crops. Captan is also a fungicide that is used on field, greenhouse and orchard crops.

Bifenthrin is an insecticide that accounts for more than a quarter of commercially used pesticides globally. In addition to various produce, it is used on certain flowers, shrubs and trees. It attacks insects by targeting their nervous systems, eventually paralyzing them and causing death.

A worker at an unidentified farm in Mexico's Guanajuato state sprays a field of strawberries that will be distributed to different states in Mexico and exported to the U.S. (Mario Armas/AFP/Getty Images)

Bifenthrin is considered to be of low toxicity to humans, though large quantities can induce adverse effects, including headaches, dizziness or skin or nasal irritations when inhaled, or a sore throat, nausea and vomiting if ingested.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also classifies it as a possible human carcinogen, but only based on incidences of tumours in mice.

However, Corradini says that workers on berry farms would be more likely to face any sort of health risks from acute exposure.

Can I wash these chemicals off berries?

It may not do much, Corradini says, especially when it comes to berries, because of how soft they are and all of the tiny crevices in their skin.

She says there have been some studies showing that soaking them for a few minutes in a mixture of water and sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) may help, but that there's not enough evidence to conclusively say it's effective.

Are organic berries better?

Buying organic is your best bet in avoiding these chemicals, but it's not foolproof, Corradini says.

"If you are in a facility that is having half of the production organic and half not, well, there is always a risk that there is a mistake," she said.

Driscoll's also markets a line of organically grown berries, including strawberries, that it says adhere to U.S. Department of Agriculture standards. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

She also pointed out that chemical pesticides are why fruits and vegetables can be grown so plentifully and at a relatively affordable cost.

Organic crops, she says, may also be more prone to infestations. And like non-organic produce, organic foods are not immune to pathogens and parasites that can cause food-borne illnesses such as E. coli and norovirus.

WATCH | The parasite that caused a nationwide outbreak in the U.S.: What is cyclospora? A diarrhea-causing parasite | Duration 2:37 A diarrhea-causing parasite has led to a growing outbreak in the United States that has sickened more than 1,000 people and sent dozens to hospital. As of Wednesday, multiple states had reported cyclospora infections, which can cause watery diarrhea, bloating, fever and nausea. While cases are common in the spring and summer, the current outbreak has led to an unusually high number, making it one of the largest the country has seen. No deaths have been reported.

Is Driscoll's facing any sort of investigation?

Driscoll's says that it "never knowingly shipped product that we believed to be unsafe."

Harada's lawsuit is still in progress and the company wouldn't comment on it other than to deny his allegations.

Driscoll's is also facing a separate class-action lawsuit filed earlier this year by six plaintiffs living in New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts and Illinois.

SFGate reported that the suit accuses the company of consumer fraud and deceptive practices by allegedly "greenwashing" the amount of so-called forever chemicals, known as PFAS, on its strawberries.

World.title: Trump trade adviser says Canadian lobbyists should 'get the hell out of our country'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of U.S. President Donald Trump's trade advisers is threatening repercussions for Canada if it "interferes" in the upcoming midterm elections — though it's not clear what he anticipates the country would do to impact the vote.

Peter Navarro, who has lashed out at Canada in the past, made these latest remarks during a talk at an economic conference in Washington on Tuesday.

Navarro was speaking generally about the Trump administration's trade policy when the conversation turned to the ongoing dispute with Canada. He blasted Canadians on "K Street" — an area in Washington known as a hub for lobbyists — telling them to "get the hell out of our country."

"The problem you have is you lobby this country and you've been successful in the past and you think you can keep doing that," Navarro said of Canada's approach.

"Memo to Canada: You cannot do that. That game is up and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan you will pay even more dearly."

WATCH | Navarro tells Canadian lobbyists to 'get the hell out': Trump adviser says Canadian lobbyists should 'get the hell out' of U.S. | Duration closed caption 1:26 U.S. President Donald Trump's adviser Peter Navarro said on Tuesday that Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford 'just talk trash' about Trump for domestic political gain. 'You just can't trust them,' Navarro said about Canada's trade negotiators.

Navarro said he "loves" the Canadian people but has had no love for Canadian negotiators since 2016.

"You just can't trust them," he said.

During the talks that led to the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) in Trump's first term, Ottawa leaned on U.S. labour and business groups to help make its case. More recently, a number of Canadian provinces have hired their own representatives to be present for ongoing trade discussions in D.C. since Trump returned to the White House in early 2025.

Navarro didn't elaborate on what he meant by suggesting Canada could interfere in the election, but the ongoing trade war has become an election topic in the two border states he mentioned.

Asked about Navarro's comments during a Tuesday afternoon news conference in Vancouver, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he has "no response."

WATCH | Maine is a critical state to determine control of U.S. Senate: Trump’s tariffs loom over pivotal Maine Senate race | Duration closed caption 2:40 The Canada-U.S. trade war is hitting Maine’s economy as voters grapple with rising costs. The fallout could shape a key midterm race that will help determine which party controls the U.S. Senate.

The Democratic nominee for Michigan's open Senate seat, Abdul El-Sayed, has sought to make trade with Canada a central ballot issue for the vote in November. Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, has opposed the trade war.

Navarro made the comments on the same day that Trump's latest trade escalation came into effect.

As of Tuesday at 12:01 a.m. ET, some Canadian alcohol products, dairy byproducts, motorcycles and molasses have been shut out of the U.S. market.

The White House announced the bans and some additional tariffs a few days after Canada slapped counter-tariffs on U.S. goods earlier this month. Both moves came after trade talks collapsed in August.

WATCH | These Canadian goods now officially banned: These Canadian goods are now officially banned in the U.S. | Duration 2:59 Washington’s ban on several Canadian goods, including alcohol, molasses, motorcycles and select dairy products kick in as of Sept. 29. The list of items might come across as a head-scratcher to some but one trade lawyer suggests there’s more to this collection than meets the eye.

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Monday, Trump said he expects Canada to return to the negotiating table in the coming weeks with an apology.

"I think what's going to happen is over the next three or four weeks, they're going to come to us and they're gonna say, 'We're gonna get rid of all the tariffs,"' the president said.

Trump also repeated claims that Canada has treated the U.S. "unfairly" and said it's been "one of the worst countries in the entire world" when it comes to trade.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said during an unrelated news conference on Tuesday that the government has no intention of apologizing for "standing up for Canadian workers, Canadian businesses [and] defending our economy."

WATCH | Carney laughs at Trump's claim that Canada will soon apologize: Carney laughs at Trump's claim that Canada will apologize to U.S. | Duration closed caption 0:45 Asked by CBC News about U.S. President Donald Trump's comment on Monday that Canada will soon apologize to get a trade deal, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada 'stands ready to negotiate in good faith' for a deal that 'respects both our countries' sovereignty.'

"We are having conversations with our American counterparts. We're not negotiating detailed texts as we were five, six weeks ago. But we remain in contact with them," he said.

"If the prime minister concludes at some point that there's a deal possible, that protects the sovereignty of our country, that would be in the economic interest of the country, then we would obviously be in a position to have that conversation."

During his Tuesday remarks, Navarro suggested that Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford were acting to promote their political self-interests as opposed to "what's good for the Canadian people."

"Mark Carney and Doug Ford just talk trash about Donald Trump. That's what they do and then they go up in the polls and they think that's a winning strategy," he said.

"We look at that and go, 'Oh, that's not smart. OK, do your thing. You got tariffs now.'"

Last year, Ford's government paid to run an anti-tariff ad featuring former U.S. president Ronald Reagan that sparked backlash from the White House. U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra has since likened the  to foreign meddling.

Navarro has taken heat for past comments on Canada. In 2020, he questioned Canada's role in the U.S.-led multilateral NATO mission in Afghanistan, suggesting the country's role was motivated more by a desire to curry favour with the U.S. than to support the global fight against terrorism.

Those comments spurred a former chief of the defence staff to call Navarro an "idiot."

World.title: Matthew Mayich's Arizona teammates dispute school report on workout before Hamilton NHL prospect's collapse
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An anonymous letter by members of Arizona State University's hockey team that was sent to the school's president disputes aspects of ASU's official report into events that led up to Canadian NHL prospect Matthew Mayich's collapse.

In the review released last week, ASU official James Rund wrote that the Hamilton-born 21-year-old collapsed just before 8:30 a.m. during Aug. 20 training at Sun Angel Stadium on ASU’s Tempe campus. It also determined ASU h ockey coaches didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before the training session.

The players said in the letter that they had it sent anonymously Monday to ASU president Michael M. Crow through their lawyer, Timothy J. Casey, as they feared retribution.

It alleges that Mayich "received no water" during the outdoor workout on a hot day last month, and calls for the university to place the trainers "responsible for approving, conducting and supervising the session" on leave pending an independent investigation.

The players' letter says that, to "our knowledge, no one involved has been placed on leave, suspended or disciplined. The head coach who selected the instructor and scheduled the session continues to lead our program."

It urges that the team's coaching staff be replaced "for the period of the investigation if the facts set out in this report, together with what the investigation finds, indicate that step is appropriate."

Also on Monday, the Arizona State Legislature's House and Senate education chairs, Republicans Matt Gress and Hildy Angius, announced on X that they're calling for an independent investigation into the Aug. 20 training session. In a news release, they said they have asked the state's Board of Regents to retain an independent investigator.

Mayich struggled near end of workout, ASU report says

According to Rund's report, during the workout, a "break was taken approximately 20 minutes into the event for the student athletes to drink water." However, the letter from the players alleges "Matthew, and many of us, did not get water at any point."

Rund, ASU's senior vice-president of educational outreach and student services, said coaches asked permission for Timothy Ziesel, who was there for the workout and had "spoken with the ASU hockey team in the 2025-26 season about topics of leadership and teamwork," to speak to the team.

However, the coaches didn't "submit a plan of training activities for review by ASU’s strength and conditioning coaches" before training began, Rund said.

Near the end of the workout, "Matthew appeared to struggle, and then in rapid succession stumbled, dropped the medicine ball and fell to the ground," Rund wrote. "He attempted to get up and resume running, but fell to his knees."

Rund also announced that ASU would have a panel of experts provide best-practice recommendations.

The players' letter alleges that when "those of us who reached the water drank, Ziesel stood behind us and declared that he did not get water in combat."

The players also ask for answers to 19 questions, including:

Who approved Ziesel to work with the team and when?

Why was the strength and conditioning coach, who head coach Greg Powers says runs the team’s workouts, excluded from planning or reviewing the Aug. 20 session, and who made that decision?

Why was no one assigned to monitor each player for signs of heat illness, including altered consciousness?

Was the team physician contacted? If not, why not?

Why did the ASU review rely on an off-site weather station?

Did anyone verify Ziesel’s first-aid, CPR and automated external defibrillator (AED) certifications?

Arizona State University in Tempe is seen in a drone shot on Sept. 17. (Andrew Hernandez/CBC)

Mayich family 'grateful' to teammates

In a statement shared with media Tuesday afternoon by Rob Carey, the Mayich family's lawyer, Matthew's parents, John and Christina, said they were “so grateful to Matthew's teammates. A lot of you have come by, sent messages and kept Matthew in your thoughts every day. It means more to us than we can say."

The family said they "want this [hockey] team to have a great season, and we'll be cheering for you. But the coaches who ran that workout on Aug. 20 need to be removed while an independent investigation gets to the truth. The players shouldn't have to worry about retaliation from the people they report to every day."

In their letter, the players also made several requests, including that:

Written findings be issued on whether each requirement of the Outside Consultants and Exertional Heat Illness policies was met on Aug. 20.

The staff responsible for approving, conducting and supervising the workout session be placed on administrative leave pending an independent investigation.

The investigation be referred to an agency outside the university.

There be confirmation in writing that no player will lose a scholarship, roster position or playing time for participating in any investigation or in this report, and that each will be protected from retaliation if their identities are revealed.

When asked for comment, Chris Fiscus, ASU vice-president of media relations and strategic communications, told CBC News on Tuesday afternoon that the university "will respond later today." At the time of publication, no response had been provided.

Family 'praying for a miracle'

Last week, Carey said "Matthew is in stable but critical condition still. The family is still praying for a miracle, but nothing has significantly changed. But even if that happens, we will never have the young man who came to Arizona last month, a hockey star and ... a wonderful person."

According to Carey, "when Matthew went down [during the workout], there was no plan and no preparation, so he was treated in a way that hurt his chances rather than helped them."

"A month later, nobody's been named, nobody's been suspended, nobody's been fired for violating the very policies ASU published today, and the university wants to appoint a committee."

Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020. He was selected in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft by the St. Louis Blues.

Doug Armstrong, the Blues' president of hockey operations, said in a news release in late August, "The entire Blues organization is keeping Matthew Mayich close to our hearts as we pray for his comfort and recovery while he continues to undergo medical treatment in Arizona."

The organization also extends its "deepest support" to his family, friends and teammates during this difficult time, Armstrong said.

World.title: Sask. drone company says no 'special rights' attached to $10M US investment linked to Trump Jr.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saskatoon drone maker Draganfly Inc. says there are no "special rights" attached to a $10-million US investment from an unnamed U.S. investment fund and Unusual Machines Inc., a company linked to Donald Trump Jr.

Draganfly is headquartered in Saskatoon and was founded in 1997. Unusual Machines and the unnamed fund are each investing $5 million US.

Unusual Machines, a supplier of drone components, named the U.S. president's son to its advisory board in November 2024.

"No board seats or special rights are attached to these investments," a Draganfly spokesperson said in a statement emailed to CBC News.

"In response to rising demand for Draganfly's proprietary products and technology in Canada and other allied countries, we have recently attracted investment to facilitate new hires and expand manufacturing capability."

The investment took the form of a purchase of 1,869,159 common shares of the company at a price of $5.35 US, according to a news release by Draganfly. As of market close on Tuesday, the stock was trading at $6.20 US on the NASDAQ, a one-day increase of $0.60 US.

The stock also trades on the Canadian Securities Exchange. As of closing Tuesday, it was trading at $8.81, a one-day increase of $0.92.

The company said it plans to use the investment money to accelerate development and fund general working capital.

Draganfly manufactures drones in Saskatoon and Vancouver, and is planning expansions in Edmonton and Ottawa. It also operates in Tampa, Fla.

The drones are used around the world in search and rescue operations, agriculture and by the U.S. military. In 2025, Draganfly won a contract to provide the U.S. Army with drones.

Earlier this month, Draganfly secured a five-year contract with Ottawa to supply the Canadian Armed Forces with up to 5,000 drones. The deal includes a firm commitment to buy 100 drones, with the option to purchase another 4,900.

The federal government approved Draganfly as a qualified supplier under Ottawa's Defence Drone Initiative.

In 2015, Draganfly was acquired by TRACE Live Networks, California-based tech firm.

Draganfly has a market capitalization of about $285 million, according to the company's statement.

The company is often cited as the maker of the first civilian drone to be credited with saving a life. A Draganfly drone was added to the collection of the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum.

World.title: Conservative MP Scott Aitchison expected to resign this fall: sources
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

MP and former Conservative leadership candidate Scott Aitchison is expected to resign his seat later this fall, three sources tell CBC News.

A senior Conservative source said Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was told last week that Aitchison plans to leave at the end of the fall sitting.

The MP's departure was expected to be announced next week, one source said.

The resignation would add Aitchison to a list of Conservative MPs exiting electoral politics in recent months.

Prime Minister Mark Carney appointed former Conservative MP Richard Martel to the Senate early in the summer. Martel was sworn into the Red Chamber earlier this week.

Former MPs Cathay Wagantall and Larry Brock both stepped down in the past month.

Aitchison has been the MP for Ontario's Parry Sound-Muskoka riding since the 2019 election.

CTV News first confirmed the news of his departure.

Pierre Poilievre and Aitchison hug as Poilievre is announced winner of the Conservative leadership race in 2022. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

The former Huntsville, Ont., mayor launched a leadership bid in the 2022 Conservative campaign that saw Poilievre chosen as the party's chief. Aitchison finished fifth.

Housing was a key feature of Aitchison's leadership campaign and Poilievre named the MP as his housing critic.

Aitchison's office did not immediately return a request for comment.

The resignation would create another vacancy in the House, where six seats are currently empty.

In addition to Brock and Wagantall, former Liberal cabinet minister Steven Guilbeault officially resigned last month. Former Liberal MP Shaun Chen resigned in mid-August.

Former NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice and the Bloc Québécois's Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay both left federal politics to run in Quebec's provincial election.

World.title: 'It's devastating': Hundreds of Stelco workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke face uncertain future due to layoffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hundreds of Stelco workers in Hamilton are facing an uncertain future after the company announced Monday it will indefinitely idle its cold-rolled and coated operations at its Hamilton Works plant.

Ron Wells, the president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, says the wind-down is expected to begin Oct. 9, with about 350 workers from the Hamilton plant expected to be laid off.

He said the total layoffs could be up to 500 in total, between the Hamilton and Lake Erie Works plant in Nanticoke, Ont. Stelco has also said up to 500 workers could be affected.

"I hate using 'we're disappointed' — we're disgusted," Wells told CBC Hamilton Tuesday morning.

For families connected to the plant, the uncertainty is already taking a toll.

Jillian Watt's husband is a line worker, and has worked at Stelco in Hamilton for 21 years. She said he has not yet been told whether he will be among those laid off.

"They haven't spoken to individuals, so it's kind of still up in the air," she said Tuesday morning. Watt, who is a union representative for a Canadian Union of Public Employees heath workers local, spoke to CBC from the entrance to National Steel Car, just down the road from Stelco.

National Steel Car workers have been on strike for a 48 days and have been regularly joined on the picket line by other unionized workers.

Watt is particularly concerned about whether her husband's experience with the company is enough if layoffs are decided by seniority. She said the possibility of losing the family's main source of income is particularly stressful.

"He's a breadwinner for our family. We have four kids, you know, trying to make it by," she said. "It was a bit of a kick to the gut for both of us."

Jillian Watt says she's nervous about what will happen to her husband following the news that Stelco will be laying off about 350 workers. As of Tuesday, they have not received any notice. (Claude Beaudoin/CBC)

Watt said her husband had already been concerned about the plant in recent months, as operations were idled and orders slowed. Now, they are awaiting the verdict of what happens next. "It's very stressful," she said.

Union questions job commitments

Wells said the union was told about the layoffs during a meeting with the company Monday morning.

He said he has been talking with workers concerned about how long the layoffs could last because the company has not provided an end date.

"They're asking how long is this going to last? Should we start looking for another job?" Wells said. "People are concerned."

Ron Wells, president of USW Local 1005, says he is "disgusted" by the decision to lay off approximately 350 workers. (Meagan Fitzpatrick/CBC)

The company has said some affected workers could be offered jobs at Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke.

But Wells said the union was told there are only roughly 40 to 45 openings there — a number he says falls well short of the potential layoffs in Hamilton.

Wells is also questioning the commitments Cleveland-Cliffs made when it acquired Stelco in 2024.

He said the agreement included a commitment to maintain the number of unionized employees for five years, and he wants the federal government to enforce it.

"You have people making these decisions in Cleveland and they have no ties to our community," Well said. "If 350 Hamiltonians lose their jobs, they don't care."

Pat Persico, the senior director of corporate communications for Cleveland-Cliffs, told CBC News in an emailed statement that while Stelco is idling some of its operations in Hamilton, the company's total output of steel will not be impacted as it consolidates production at its Lake Erie Works.

"Very importantly, job opportunities at Lake Erie Works will be offered to Hamilton employees," Persico wrote in an email. "We expect that a significant number of employees affected by the indefinite idle at Hamilton should be absorbed at Lake Erie Works."

Company 'betrayed' workers: PM

At a news conference in Vancouver Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the Stelco situation, saying his thoughts were with the "workers and their families who have been betrayed by the company."

He did not directly answer when a reporter asked if Ottawa was considering legal action over the company appearing to break its employment commitment.

Cleveland-Cliffs "has legal obligations for employment," Carney said, adding that the government intends to use "all powers that we have and pursue them to the fullest extent of the law."

WATCH | Carney says company betrayed workers at Stelco: Stelco 'betrayed' Ontario workers with layoffs, Carney says | Duration closed caption 1:16 Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada will 'use all the powers that we have' to ensure that Stelco meets its 'legal obligations for employment.' The company, which is owned by U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs, announced plans on Monday to idle some production at its Hamilton plant, putting hundreds of workers out of a ‌job.

Carney added that U.S. tariffs caused the situation, noting that Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves has praised them. In 2024, Goncalves told CBC Hamilton that tariffs on imports into the U.S. were "a great move."

'Devastating' news for Hamilton

Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath said Monday the city had been working with the federal and provincial governments in response to the announcement.

"The fight is not over," Horwath told CBC's As It Happens radio program on Monday.

LISTEN | Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath reacts to layoffs: As It Happens 6:54 Hamilton steelworker layoffs 'painful for our community,' says mayor As of next Friday, about 350 Hamilton, Ont., steelworkers will be out of work, according to their union. Stelco, the U.S.-owned company that operates the Hamilton plant, blames the layoffs on trade disputes between the U.S. and Canada. But Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath says the fight isn't over. She spoke to As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.

She said she believes Cleveland-Cliffs is not living up to commitments made to workers and that she has asked city staff to review commitments made during the company's restructuring process.

"We're going to fight tooth and nail to have them basically live up to their commitments and protect these jobs," she said.

Karina Gould, the Liberal MP for nearby Burlington, called the decision "devastating news" for Hamilton and said the federal government is prepared to provide support to maintain operations and protect jobs.

"This is a very difficult time," Gould said.

Hamilton mayoral candidate Keanin Loomis, who is the president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction, also called the announcement "devastating."

"Steel jobs have supported generations of Hamilton families and remain vital to our local economy," Loomis said in a statement on social media.

The impact of tariffs has been a discussion topic on the municipal election campaign trail, with several candidates sharing proposals on how to respond to trade uncertainty.

For Watt, the announcement represents another difficult moment for a city where steel means so much.

"My grandfather, my dad, my uncles, they all worked at Stelco," she said. "My husband and my brother are there, and this is going to have a huge impact."

"It's scary times."

World.title: N.S. senior killed ailing wife after promising to help her take her own life, court hears
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story includes references to suicide and details a killing.

A 75-year-old man smothered his ailing wife in their Kingsport, N.S., home more than four years ago after she made him promise to help her take her own life, a court was told Tuesday.

Douglas Smith was sentenced in Nova Scotia Supreme Court in Kentville, N.S., to six years in prison for the death of Iris Dodd, 72, on April 30, 2022. He pleaded guilty to manslaughter in April days before he was set to stand trial for second-degree murder.

Smith and Dodd, who had serious health issues, had been married for 33 years but faced eviction and had nowhere to go, according to an agreed statement of facts.

Court documents illustrate a harrowing situation the couple, who had a "long, supportive and happy life together," found themselves in that night.

Dodd’s health had been deteriorating since she suffered a stroke in 2018 and they were going to be kicked out of their home the next day, the documents say.

She used a wheelchair, was losing her eyesight and lived with chronic pain from arthritis and fibromyalgia — a long-term condition that causes muscle pain, extreme fatigue and sleep difficulty.

She had just had a long stay in hospital due to bouts of pneumonia.

On the night she died, court documents say Dodd told her husband she didn’t want to spend her final years in a health-care or long-term care facility.

She told Smith she planned to take all of her medication at once in an attempt to overdose and Smith should leave the house so he wouldn't be culpable.

Douglas Smith and Iris Dodd lived in this home in Kingsport, N.S., for nearly eight years. They were going to be evicted the day after Smith killed Dodd. (Paul Poirier/CBC)

The only thing she needed from her husband was for him to arrange the pills because she couldn’t see them very well.

Initially, the documents say, Smith didn’t support his wife’s plan when she raised the topic abruptly.

However, “The victim was very upset and made Mr. Smith promise to help her with her plan and he promised he would,” said the agreed statement of facts.

The couple agreed they’d go ahead with the plan the following day, which helped Dodd calm down and go to sleep.

Smith couldn’t sleep, though, worrying about his wife dying alone. He became increasingly concerned her plan might fail and leave her with permanent brain damage.

“Mr. Smith resolved all these thoughts and fears in his head by getting up and holding a pillow over the victim’s face,” the agreed statement of facts said.

‘She was in distress and I eased her distress’

The day after Smith killed Dodd, he drove to the local RCMP detachment to turn himself in.

After discovering the office was closed, he called 911 from the parking lot and admitted to taking her life.

A recording of Smith's 911 call was released by the court.

The call began with a dispatcher asking Smith what emergency he was reporting. The senior replied that he wanted to report a death.

WATCH | N.S. senior killed ailing wife after promising to help her take her own life, court hears: Annapolis Valley senior sentenced to 6 years in prison | Duration closed caption 2:25 Douglas Smith killed his wife, Iris Dodd, at their home four years ago. As the CBC's Josh Hoffman explains, the couple was facing eviction, Dodd's health was failing and she had asked her husband to help her end her life. This story includes references to suicide and details a killing.

The dispatcher asked if the death had been sudden or unexpected and Smith said that his wife had died and he was responsible.

Smith said he didn’t want to provide any details but the dispatcher said she required some information before an officer could be sent to meet him.

“She was in distress and I eased her distress,” Smith replied.

An officer came out of the detachment, arrested Smith and took him to a cell inside the building where Smith confirmed it was his voice on the 911 call, according to court documents.

Emotional day in court

Smith was emotional in court Tuesday, holding his head in his hands while the agreed statement of facts was read.



He wept when Crown prosecutor Daniel Rideout reached the part detailing how Smith had smothered his wife.



Smith was asked if he wanted a break but replied: "Let's get this over with."

During submissions, Rideout noted the case differed from the spate of domestic homicides in Nova Scotia in recent years.



Smith was driven by compassion when he took his wife's life, but he still broke the law and had other options available, Rideout said.

The Nova Scotia Mental Health and Addictions Crisis Line can be reached 24/7 first at 902-429-8167, or 1-888-429-8167, or by dialing 911.

World.title: Polo makes 2nd landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tropical Storm Polo weakened over northwestern Mexico on Tuesday after making a second landfall and drenching the Baja California peninsula, while a strengthening Tropical Storm Rachel churned offshore, threatening more dangerous weather for Mexico's ​Pacific coast.

Polo again came ashore earlier on ​Tuesday near the port city of Guaymas as a Category 1 hurricane after crossing the peninsula the day before, the U.S. National Hurricane ​Center said.

By 2 p.m. MST, Polo's maximum sustained winds ⁠had fallen to 100 km/h, with rapid weakening expected ‌as it pushes farther inland.

Though Polo is fading, forecasters warned its moisture could continue fuelling heavy rain well beyond Mexico.

PHOTOS | Hurricane Polo hits Mexico:

Hit Baja California as Category 2 storm

The NHC said Polo could dump 10 to 15 centimetres of rain across southern and central Sonora state, with isolated maximum totals of 20 centimetres, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

Private forecaster AccuWeather said Polo's remnants could trigger a broader deluge across the U.S. Southwest and Plains.

Before its second landfall, Polo tore across Baja California Sur as a Category 2 hurricane, flooding crossings, toppling palm trees and utility poles and sending police to block inundated roads.

"At my house we tied all down. ⁠We prepared very well," resident Bertha Lopez said. "We expected it to be stronger, but thank God it wasn't ⁠so disastrous."

Baja California Sur Gov. Víctor Manuel Castro said no deaths had been reported.

Even as Polo weakened, Rachel was intensifying to the ⁠south.

The ⁠NHC said Rachel, about 435 kilometres west-southwest of port Lazaro Cardenas, had strengthened to 110 km/h winds and ​was forecast to ⁠become a hurricane on Tuesday night and a major hurricane by Thursday, moving parallel to, but remaining off the coast of southwestern Mexico.
