World.title: Budapest police apologise after journalist receives insulting, misogynistic internal email
World.content:
The Budapest Police Headquarters has apologised to an HVG journalist after an internal email describing her as a “screaming blue stocking” was apparently sent to her by mistake.

Journalist had requested interview on street harassment

HVG journalist Noémi Martini first contacted the communications department of the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK) in early September to request an interview with Budapest police chief Colonel Norbert Tamás Baricska about street harassment in the capital.

The request was initially turned down. Martini subsequently began collecting accounts from people who had experienced harassment on the streets through an anonymous questionnaire.

According to HVG, more than 300 stories were submitted within a few weeks, 93% of them from women. Most described sexual harassment on Budapest streets or on public transport.

The journalist then contacted the police again, asking whether another representative could discuss the issue, as the responses appeared to point to a broader problem.

BRFK spokesperson Soma Csécsi subsequently called Martini and asked her to send specific questions so that a suitable police representative could be found. The National Police Headquarters (ORFK) later responded in writing, but only answered some of the questions.

Martini then asked why she could not put her questions directly to a police representative and, if written answers were the only option, why only some of her questions had been addressed.

Internal email apparently sent to journalist

According to HVG, an email was sent to Martini a few hours later that appears to have been intended for police staff rather than the journalist herself.

The message began with “Dear Attila!” and included three police employees among the recipients. Discussing Martini’s interview request, it reportedly said that, according to Soma, “a screaming blue stocking” would not be given an interview by the Budapest police chief.

The term “blue stocking” is a derogatory expression traditionally used for a woman portrayed as overly intellectual or opinionated.

BRFK launches internal investigation

In a statement published on Tuesday, BRFK acknowledged the incident and apologised for the tone of the internal correspondence.

The police said the language used was “unacceptable” and did not reflect its communication standards or the ethical requirements associated with them. It stressed that respectful and factual communication is expected when dealing with journalists, members of the public and colleagues alike.

BRFK also addressed the underlying issue raised by the journalist, stating that street harassment of women is a real problem. It said both reported and unreported cases must be taken seriously and that all legally available means should be used to prevent such incidents.

“We apologise to the journalist, everyone affected and the public,” the police said, adding that an internal investigation would be launched into the incident.

The statement did not identify the employee or employees responsible for the wording of the email.

World.title: Fidesz: ‘Ukrainian mafia’ operatives have infiltrated Hungarian state institutions
World.content:
The Fidesz party claims that the “Ukrainian mafia” is paying dozens of people in Hungary who have already infiltrated state institutions. The opposition party also said that people allegedly “paid by Ukrainians” and making false accusations would eventually face legal consequences.

Fidesz made the claims in a statement sent to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) on Tuesday, accusing the “Ukrainian mafia” of transferring huge amounts of money through Hungary without restraint.

According to the party, Hungarian authorities put an end to this activity under the previous “national government”, and therefore deserve recognition rather than accusations. Fidesz added that the authorities would receive this recognition once the party “restores the rule of law in Hungary”.

USD 40 million and EUR 35 million in cash, plus gold, seized

According to the MTI report, officers from the National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) and the Counter-Terrorism Centre (TEK) seized two vehicles on the M0 motorway on 5 March on suspicion of money laundering.

The vehicles, owned by Ukraine’s Oschadbank, were reportedly transporting USD 40 million and EUR 35 million in cash, as well as 9 kilograms of gold, from Austria’s Raiffeisen Bank to Ukraine.

The seven-member, unarmed crew was questioned the following day and subsequently expelled from Hungary. They later filed complaints alleging inhumane treatment and violations of their rights.

Former prosecutor says ‘gold convoy’ case was politically created

Pál Fürcht, former head of the Central Chief Prosecutor’s Office for Investigations, also commented on the case on Tuesday in an open letter published on the Facebook page of authorised lawyer Lóránt Horváth.

Fürcht wrote that experienced prosecutors at the Budapest Investigative Prosecutor’s Office concluded in May, based on the evidence collected up to that point, that the so-called “gold convoy case” was a case created for political reasons.

According to Fürcht, the investigation at the time indicated that then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán himself had instructed the intelligence services on 3 March to arrest the Ukrainian cash couriers on 5 March. (Read more details HERE.)

He claimed that, while carrying out the task allegedly set by politicians, the intelligence service consulted a department head at the Office of the Prosecutor General on 4 March, as well as the Prosecutor General himself.

Fürcht said that on 5 March, the intelligence service’s criminal complaint reached the investigative authorities within a record four to five hours, instead of the three-day period provided by law. He said this happened with the involvement of the Prosecutor General, the deputy Prosecutor General and another senior prosecutor.

The complaint reportedly came with an instruction from the prosecution service that an investigation had to be launched.

According to Fürcht, even this process was almost too slow, as the operation against the alleged gold convoy was already well underway.

He argued that if the leadership of the Office of the Prosecutor General had sent the instruction to launch the investigation even half a day later, the Ukrainian cash couriers would already have safely returned home and the task allegedly set by the prime minister could not have been carried out.

The Fidesz statement and Fürcht’s open letter offer different interpretations of the background to the case. The claims made public so far do not in themselves establish that “Ukrainian mafia” operatives had infiltrated Hungarian state institutions, or that the people referred to by Fidesz had made false accusations.

World.title: Exclusive interview: “The ‘N’ still stands for non-governmental, doesn’t it?” – Máté Hajba on EU-funded lobbying
World.content:
Máté Hajba is the director of Hungary’s Free Market Foundation, which has published a new report examining what it calls “circular lobbying” in Brussels: public institutions funding NGOs that, among their activities, seek to influence the policies of those same institutions. The report examines nine organisations, identifies roughly €12.8 million in annual public funding, and says around 96.8% of the public funding it identified came from the European Commission. Daily News Hungary spoke with Hajba about whether Brussels has created an echo chamber financed by European taxpayers.

Daily News Hungary: Let’s put this crudely. Brussels gives NGOs taxpayers’ money, some of those NGOs lobby Brussels, and Brussels then hears supposedly independent civil society demanding policies it helped finance. Is that really the system?

Máté Hajba: Put that way, it does sound exceptionally efficient, doesn’t it? You provide the money, help finance the advocacy, receive the advocacy, and then point to civil society as evidence of public demand for the policy. As a Hungarian, I saw how self-servingly such a practice worked in my country under the Orbán regime, which the EU so often and rightly criticised.

Of course, reality in the EU is more complicated, and we should not pretend that every euro in an EU grant is paying somebody to knock on an MEP’s door. Lobbying is legal, advocacy is legitimate, and EU funding does not automatically make an organisation a puppet of the European Commission.

But that is precisely why transparency matters. If these relationships are entirely proper, there should be no problem showing taxpayers exactly where the money goes and what activities it supports. “Trust us, it’s civil society” is not really a substitute for a receipt. This lack of transparency erodes trust in public institutions and NGOs, at a time of global turmoil when justly earned trust is most needed.

Daily News Hungary: You found roughly €12.8 million in annual public funding among just nine organisations, with about 96.8% of the public funding you identified coming from the European Commission. At what point does “independent civil society” start sounding like a rather creative accounting term?

Máté Hajba: The “N” in NGO still stands for “non-governmental,” as far as I am aware. That does not mean an NGO stops being independent the moment it receives a public grant. Plenty of organisations receive government or EU funding for perfectly legitimate work.

But when a public institution becomes a significant financial supporter of organisations that are simultaneously trying to influence public policy, taxpayers are entitled to ask whether the relationship is transparent enough. It is basic due diligence the EU owes to its taxpayers.

And there is a very simple way to test whether people genuinely believe the principle they are defending: reverse the politics. Imagine the Commission giving millions to organisations lobbying against climate regulation, against further tobacco restrictions, or for dramatically tighter migration rules. Would everyone who currently sees no problem suddenly become fascinated by the details of EU grant agreements?

If your standard of transparency changes depending on whether you like the cause, then you do not have a transparency standard. You have a favourite team.

Daily News Hungary: Brussels spends quite a lot of time telling member states how to manage public money. Are you essentially saying the EU should try some of its own medicine?

Máté Hajba: I would phrase it more politely, but since you have already phrased it for me: yes, consistency would be refreshing.

The European Union is right to demand transparency when public money is spent. The European Court of Auditors has itself identified shortcomings in the transparency of EU funding to NGOs. So the answer is not to abolish NGOs, ban lobbying, or silence organisations whose politics somebody dislikes. The answer is almost embarrassingly boring: publish the information properly.

Create one genuinely searchable system where a taxpayer can see how much public money an organisation receives, who provided it, under which program, what it was supposed to finance, and which advocacy activities are connected to that funding.

Then let everyone lobby. Environmentalists, businesses, trade unions, health campaigners, free-market organisations, everyone. Democracy is supposed to contain competing voices.

But when taxpayers are paying for some of those voices, taxpayers should be allowed to see the bill. If everything is above board, putting the receipt on the table should be the least controversial idea in Brussels.

World.title: Russian-linked forensic technology reached Hungarian police, US case reveals
World.content:
A company selling powerful digital forensic tools to law-enforcement agencies across Europe — including the Hungarian police — has been accused by US authorities of concealing its Russian ownership and the fact that its software was developed in Russia. The case has raised fresh questions over Russian surveillance software in Europe and the security of technologies used to access highly sensitive digital evidence.

As The Hungary Insider reported based on a POLITICO investigation, Virginia-based Oxygen Forensics worked with EU-backed projects and supplied technology to law-enforcement agencies across several European countries.

The company develops digital forensic software designed to extract, preserve and analyse information from electronic devices such as smartphones and computers. Such tools can be used by investigators to recover messages, photographs, location information and other data relevant to criminal investigations.

US prosecutors now allege, however, that Oxygen Forensics concealed significant aspects of who actually controlled the company and where its technology was developed.

Hungarian police bought Oxygen Forensics technology

Hungary is directly connected to the case.

According to a Hungarian government procurement document cited by POLITICO, Hungarian police signed an IT contract with Oxygen Forensics in December 2024 worth HUF 10.14 million (approximately EUR 26,000). The contract ran until December 2025.

The Hungarian example is significant because Oxygen’s technology is not an ordinary office software package. Digital forensic systems are specifically designed to work with information extracted from computers and mobile devices during investigations.

POLITICO reported that Oxygen products have also been used or recognised by law-enforcement authorities elsewhere in Europe, including Germany, Spain, Italy and Poland.

The company’s presence extended to EU-backed initiatives as well. Public records reviewed by POLITICO show that Oxygen was involved with two projects aimed at improving the handling and analysis of electronic evidence in criminal investigations.

The European Commission told the publication that Oxygen was not a member of the project consortia and therefore did not receive Commission funding through them.

If you missed it: Hungarian intelligence services undergo sweeping reorganisation after Orbán era

Why Russian surveillance software in Europe raises security concerns

For foreign readers, the significance of the case lies largely in what digital forensic software is capable of doing.

Unlike conventional business applications, forensic tools can operate close to some of the most sensitive information handled by police and investigative authorities. Their purpose is precisely to extract and analyse data from devices, potentially including communications, photographs, documents and other evidence.

This means that the identity of a supplier’s owners, the location of its developers and control over its software-development environment can become important security considerations.

The US Department of Justice alleges that Oxygen Forensics presented itself to American government customers as an independent US-based company, while five Russian nationals actually owned and controlled it through a Cyprus-based holding company. Prosecutors also allege that the software was developed by a team working in Russia.

The same five people also owned a Russian company which, according to the US authorities, sold versions of the technology to customers reportedly including Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), Investigative Committee and Interior Ministry.

These allegations are particularly sensitive in Europe following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which fundamentally changed the EU’s security relationship with Moscow.

No allegation that the software contained malicious code

There is an important distinction in the case. The US criminal complaint does not allege that Oxygen’s software contained malicious code or that it was used to gain unauthorised access to customers’ computer systems or data, the US Department of Justice explicitly stated.

In other words, the current case should not be interpreted as evidence that Russian authorities obtained information from Hungarian police systems or from other European customers through Oxygen software.

The allegations instead concern the company’s ownership, control, development arrangements and representations made to government customers.

US authorities have charged Oxygen Forensics CEO Lee Reiber and Russian national Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov with conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Reiber was arrested in Idaho, while Davydov was detained at London’s Heathrow Airport, with the United States seeking his extradition. Both defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

A wider European supply-chain question

The affair nevertheless highlights a broader challenge for European governments: understanding who ultimately controls the technology used inside sensitive public institutions.

This is particularly important for Russian surveillance software in Europe, as software supply chains can involve developers, owners, cloud infrastructure and corporate structures spread across several jurisdictions.

For Hungary, the procurement identified by POLITICO now provides a concrete domestic dimension to what might otherwise appear to be a distant US criminal case.

The key unanswered questions include what exact systems Hungarian police used, what information those systems could access, and whether Hungarian authorities carried out any subsequent security review after concerns emerged about Oxygen Forensics’ Russian connections.

For now, the publicly known allegations do not establish that Hungarian data were compromised. They do, however, put the Hungarian procurement into a much wider debate over how European law-enforcement agencies vet the companies entrusted with technology designed to handle some of their most sensitive digital evidence.

What’s next? Only one year left to use Russian gas: will the Hungarian economy truly grind to a halt without it?

World.title: 5-year high in Hungary: New-build homes flood the market as prices show signs of cooling
World.content:
The supply of new-build homes for sale in Hungary has reached a five-year high, with buyers currently able to choose from around 10,700 advertised flats and houses across the country, according to fresh data from property website ingatlan.com.

At the same time, price growth is slowing in the cheaper segment of the new-build market. The cheapest 10% of newly built flats nationwide can now be bought for up to HUF 59 million, just HUF 1 million more than a year ago.

New-build prices vary sharply across Hungary

The cheapest 10% of new-build properties cost up to HUF 71 million in Budapest, HUF 48 million in county capitals and other major cities, and HUF 41 million in smaller towns and villages.

There are significant differences between individual cities. Among new-build flats, Zalaegerszeg currently has the lowest prices, with the cheapest 10% of the market available for less than HUF 34 million. The equivalent threshold is HUF 46 million in Győr, while it stands at HUF 47 million in both Veszprém and Szombathely.

For new-build houses, Nyíregyháza has the lowest threshold among the cities highlighted by ingatlan.com, at HUF 69 million. The figure is HUF 77 million in Kecskemét and HUF 87 million in Székesfehérvár.

Within Budapest, the lowest entry price is currently found in District XIX, where the cheapest 10% of new-build properties are priced from HUF 50 million. The threshold rises to HUF 62 million in Districts X and XVIII and HUF 64 million in District VIII.

If you missed it: Green light for 280 new Budapest homes as huge development acquires permits

Affordability becoming increasingly important

László Balogh, chief economic expert at ingatlan.com, said affordability is becoming an increasingly important factor in the competitiveness of new-build properties. While new homes have continued to become more expensive compared with last year, the slower increase in the cheaper segment could give buyers more room to choose from the growing supply.

Balogh also said the future of Hungary’s preferential 5% VAT rate on new homes is becoming an increasingly important issue for both buyers and developers. The reduced rate is currently due to expire at the end of the year.

According to the expert, raising the rate to the standard 27% VAT would not appear realistic at current property prices. He therefore expects the preferential VAT rate for buyers of new-build residential properties could remain in place after 2026, potentially continuing into 2027. This is an expert expectation rather than a confirmed government decision.

World.title: More Resorts Planned in Protected Area at Heart of Albanian Protests
World.content:
Documents obtained by BIRN from the National Territorial Planning Agency, AZHT, under Albania’s freedom of information law, shed more light on the three planned projects that were previously unknown to the public.

According to some of the documents, Green Investment, a company whose majority shareholder is Kreshnik Malaj, the son of former Socialist MP Mezan Malaj, is set to develop the Arte Marea 1 tourist complex in the village of Zvernec.

Meanwhile, Turi M.Z.P, owned by businessman Artur Haxhi, plans to build a hotel.

A conditional permit has also been granted to Concord Investment, owned by the Dulaku brothers, which plans to build a tourist complex near the Vlora Thermal Power Plant.

However, final decisions on permits have not yet been formally issued, because the developers have not completed all the required documentation.

“We were granted a conditional development permit but it has not yet been formally issued, and now I don’t know where the process has stalled,” Artur Haxhi, the sole shareholder of Turi M.Z.P, told BIRN by phone.

“The procedure hasn’t moved forward,” he added.

His company’s project is called SALTERRA 2, and documents show that the KKTU conditionally approved a “tourist complex comprising hotel and service facilities”. The footprint of the structure is expected to cover 4,250 square metres.

Haxhi told BIRN the project was still pending and there was no confirmation yet of the building’s final size.

“We applied for 11 storeys but I’m not sure how many were approved – seven, six or five plus one. We are waiting for the process to move forward,” he said, insisting that the investment would protect the natural environment.

The second-largest project is Arte Marea 1, developed by Green Investment. Three-dimensional plans published on a website show a resort village with villas and large-scale buildings along the seafront, covering 49,985 square metres, of which 8,424 would be occupied by structures.

The project is located on land that residents say was once agricultural, although it is currently not cultivated. The company’s main shareholder is Kreshnik Malaj, son of former Vlora MP Mezan Malaj.

Kreshnik Malaj and the company could not be reached for comment, while his father, former MP Malaj, distanced himself from the project. “It has nothing to do with me,” he said, declining to comment further.

The largest project on this group of development permits granted a year ago belongs to Concord Investment sh.p.k. It covers a roughly 13.6-hectare strip of forest in the area known as Pylli i Sodes, behind the Vlora Thermal Power Plant.

Concord representative Artan Dulaku defended the investment, arguing that the protected-area status of the surrounding area is absurd given the industrial degradation caused by the nearby power plant.

“The protected area is a massive distortion of what the term means,” Dulaku told BIRN.

“When there is a barren environment with no value whatsoever, no vegetation and nothing else, why is it a protected area?” he asked, claiming that protesters and the media were inflicting economic damage on Albania.

Environmental experts warn that the procedures followed for development permits in Zvernec are sidestepping obligations to protect ecosystems and opening a Pandora’s box for Albania’s entire coastline.

Olsi Nika of EcoAlbania says the large-scale interventions are part of a broader trend set in motion by the example of Kushner’s project.

“Across the entire coastline, permits have been granted and plans are in place … Once that door is opened, all these areas will be dismantled and turned into urban zones,” Nika said.

Zydjon Vorpsi of PPNEA said the plans undermine the very essence of the protected area, threatening wildlife and the unique hydrodynamics of the Vjosa Delta.

“If we interfere with these factors, lay down asphalt, dig for sewage systems and concrete foundations and light up the entire area, the protected status is no longer worth anything,” Vorpsi said.

World.title: Belgrade Mayor Denies Punching Opposition Councillor in Street Altercation
World.content:
Belgrade Mayor Aleksandar Sapic on Tuesday denied physically assaulting an opposition city councillor, Tatjana Micic, the night before, insisting he had “only defended” himself after being verbally attacked.

The Kreni-Promeni (Move-Change) movement said Sapic, a senior official of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, assaulted their councillor, Micic, and her husband, while they were walking their dog near their home.

The movement said Micic sustained suffered a broken nose and jaw, which it said was confirmed by medical documentation. BIRN could not independently confirm this.

“The Mayor rushed at me, claiming I had brought people outside his home [to hold a protest], and got right in my face. When I took out my phone and tried to film him, he started hitting my arm, and my husband tried to protect me. I stepped between the two of them to prevent things from getting out of hand, when he [Sapic] hit me on the nose,” Micic told media outlet N1.

A friend called the police, she said, but did not initially say Sapic was involved.

“When they [the police] realised who it was, two more patrols arrived, followed by the head of the New Belgrade [district] police department,” she told N1.

Sapic denied the claims at the press conference on Tuesday, saying he had “always condemned every form of violence”, particularly against women.

“My personal code, as a man and as a human being, has never allowed me to do such a thing, nor would I ever allow myself to do it,” Sapic said.

He said that during his evening walk with a friend, he had encountered “a person who had distributed leaflets, called on people to gather outside my home, gathered people there and, in every possible way, endangered both my safety and my peace”.

When he recognised her, he had asked “why she had been coming to his home”. He claimed he was then verbally attacked, first by the man and then by the woman.

Sapic said he had only defended himself from the woman’s husband.

“I have never attacked anyone first in my life … I believe I acted correctly. I did not touch the woman in question, except that at the moment when he came towards me and they started pushing, I moved her away from me precisely so that I would not come into any kind of contact with her,” he explained.

He said he then went to the police station, where he remained until the early hours, to cogive his accont of the incident.

He said that he was sorry if the woman was injured. “I would like to know how she was injured and who injured her. Because I certainly did not injure her, and that is what I am asking the competent authorities to establish,” he added.

A friend of Sapic also addressed journalists, confirming Sapic’s version of events.

The Prosecutor’s Office said Sapic was released after being questioned and more steps would be taken once the facts were established.

Prime ministerial candidate Aleksandar Vucic, who stepped down as president on Sunday to run in elections scheduled for October 25, said that Sapic “should have stepped away” when the incident happened.

“You hold public office; as a public official, you should have removed yourself from the situation. Cross to the other side of the street if necessary, but you must not take part in something like that. The responsibility lies entirely with Sapic. There is no doubt that there was a provocation, but you cannot respond in that way,” Vucic said.

The Kreni-Promeni movement said it will file a criminal complaint and demand the arrest of Sapic.

World.title: Mayor’s Resignation Deals Fresh Blow to Turkey’s Fragmented Opposition
World.content:
Ankara Mayor Mansur Yavas’ resignation from the Republican People’s Party, CHP, has further fragmented Turkey’s opposition, leaving open the political future of one of the few figures who polls suggest could mount a strong challenge to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Yavas on September 23 announced that he was leaving the CHP following months of turmoil that have split the party between the leadership, restored to Kemal Kilicdaroglu, and the New Party, Turkey’s new main opposition party, established by former CHP leader Ozgur Ozel.

“I am resigning my membership of the CHP and will continue my political path as an independent,” Yavas said, adding that the decision followed a period of legal and political disputes that had deeply divided the opposition.

The decision leaves Yavas outside both major camps that emerged from the CHP’s crisis. It also raises a larger question for an already fractured opposition: whether the Ankara Mayor is gradually withdrawing from national politics – or positioning himself as an independent figure who could eventually unite different opposition constituencies.

World.title: Powerful, Plugged-in: Czech Arms Maker CSG Cashes in on West’s Rearmament
World.content:
Smoking guns

The extent of CSG’s political connections has raised eyebrows and fuelled suspicions in some quarters about the group’s business practices.

In Slovakia, where the group has been expanding since 2013, several deals between CSG and the Slovak Defence Ministry announced in late 2025 were mere framework agreements rather than actual orders, and regarded by some as a ploy to artificially hype up the group’s prospects before its IPO the following month.

Investigative journalists also uncovered financial ties between Slovak Defence Minister Robert Kalinak and companies owned by Strnad. According to Snidl, the Dennik N reporter, CSG made a winning bet early on to foster close ties with the ruling Smer party of Prime Minister Robert Fico. “Defence Minister Kalinak has been acting as if he were a hidden shareholder in CSG,” Snidl claims.

And just last week, Kalinak admitted that his company Kallan Consulting had done lobbying work for a CSG subsidiary in the UAE but denied any conflict of interest, claiming the cooperation and financial payments ceased when he became defence minister in late 2023.

“We see no basis for connecting this commercial project in the UAE with contracts subsequently concluded between CSG companies and the Slovak Ministry of Defence,” dismisses CSG spokesman Cirtek.

Snidl disagrees, insisting that “it’s an incredible conflict of interest, and we still don’t know the whole story”, adding that while it is, to some extent, a topic of scrutiny in Slovakia, “it would have been a much bigger scandal ten years ago.”

Further controversies have emerged over the past several months, putting a dent in CSG’s success story narrative.

Just days before the IPO launched, long-time minority shareholder Petr Kratochvil began exercising his right to sell his stake in key parts of the business – a process CSG did not mention in its prospectus for investors ahead of the IPO, before then “invisibly” adding it to its annual report in white text over a white background.

Strnad has also been locked in a long-running dispute with a minority shareholder in Tatra Trucks, which is part of CSG. Denisa Materova claims the management of the historic Koprivnice-based manufacturer only acts in favour of its majority shareholder amid concerns that Strnad is seeking to take full control of the company.

From an initial reputation as something of a “shy heir” to his father, “Michal Strnad is said to be even more predatory than his father,” says Snidl – a reputation sources familiar with the company’s dealings have also highlighted to BIRN.

“[Strnad] has become such an omnivore, he simply devours whatever he sees,” Seznam Zpravy journalist Janek Kroupa assessed recently.

This appetite, sources told BIRN on condition of anonymity, has led the Czech arms manufacturer to roll out what they have described as unusually aggressive business practices to expand its reach and consolidate its dominance.

The most telling case perhaps relates to Czech aircraft engine manufacturer PBS which, after rejecting an offer by Strnad to be bought outright, has since accused former employees of leaking sensitive and strategic information to CSG about their technical know-how and industrial processes.

“We respect the right of any company to protect its intellectual property,” says CSG spokesman Cirtek. “At the same time, this matter should be seen in the broader context of a competitive dispute between two companies operating in the same technological segment.”

Yet in October 2025, the group founded a new subsidiary AviaNera focused on the production of drones and unmanned aerial vehicles to be headed up by PBS’s former CEO, Pavel Cechal.

Pointing to the recent departure of “a handful of our former technicians and managers… under non-standard circumstances”, the current PBS chief executive, Petr Kadner, has questioned CSG’s ability to produce in such a short time “such sophisticated technology as aircraft engines without prior experience”.

CSG, on the other hand, has rejected the accusations of intellectual property theft. “AviaNera develops its own technical solutions and has access to its own know-how and propulsion system designs through its R&D, investments, partnerships and acquisitions,” including through its acquisition of Serbian company MUST Solutions in 2025, according to CSG spokesman Cirtek.

World.title: Letter from Washington: Cornered Trump Reaches for Balkan Playbook
World.content:
Greetings from the East Coast, where this month has been particularly busy – from the annual gathering of world leaders at the UN General Assembly in New York, where everyone gets a photo op and a stage to air their grievances (for the audiences at home), to Chinese President Xi Jinping’s official meeting with Donald Trump, in Washington – a visit that, much like the UNGA, was heavy on pomp and light on concrete results.

On the domestic front, the midterm elections are approaching, and the campaign is increasingly starting to look a lot like the ones back home in the Balkans. Trump is escalating the war with media outlets who criticize him, and, while another war, in Iran, is making Trump more unpopular, he has reached for another Balkan political trick: when things get difficult, hand out the taxpayers’ money!

Trump has promised that, if Republicans remain their majority in Congress, every American adult will receive $5,000. Still, such a measure would have to get the green light on Capitol Hill, so it is far from certain that Americans will actually get the money – unlike in Serbia, where the outgoing President distributes money from the state budget ahead of elections, despite having no authority to do so.

World.title: Montenegrin Women Suffer Sexual Dysfunction in Silence, Often Untreated
World.content:
“My first-time having sex, at 19, was horribly painful,” said one of the women in the survey.

She thought pain during first intercourse was normal, so she said nothing. It continued to hurt, however.

Too ashamed to seek help and worried that any treatment might be too expensive, the woman said she continues to suffer from pain during intercourse to this day.

Others spoke of believing sexual pain and dissatisfaction to be a normal part of a woman’s life.

Almost a quarter of the 90 women said they were embarrassed to talk about their issues, more than a dozen said they did not know whom to turn to; a similar number said they did not believe they would find help within the healthcare system. Many cited financial reasons for not seeking treatment.

The Montenegrin public healthcare system is financed from public funds and mandatory health insurance contributions, which means treatment is usually free of charge.

However, long waiting times and a lack of specialised treatment mean many Montenegrin citizens turn to the private sector, which can be costly.

The Clinical Center of Montenegro, the country’s largest healthcare institution, said that women rarely consult doctors when facing sexual dysfunction issues.

The Institute of Public Health of Montenegro, IZJCG, does not collect statistical data on patients reporting sexual dysfunction.

None of the local gynaecology clinics within the public healthcare system responded to requests for comment, except for Herceg Novi, on the coast, which said that, according to the estimates of their gynaecologists, some 15-20 per cent of patients of the Women’s Health Department present with symptoms that can lead to sexual dysfunction.

“In the majority of cases, the aetiology of these symptoms is either infectious in origin or related to the menopausal transition,” the clinic said. “Occasionally, patients present with these symptoms and are subsequently diagnosed with premalignant or malignant lesions of the genital tract. Congenital anomalies of the genital tract are a very rare cause of these symptoms.”

As they point out, treatment for infections is available within the public healthcare system; however, “patients undergoing menopause have to purchase most of the medications and other products used for their treatment themselves.”

Almost half of those who responded to the questionnaire said they do not believe the Montenegrin healthcare system offers any help when it comes to sexual dysfunction.

Vuksanovic Bozaric called for more training of health professionals to recognise sexual dysfunction early, for the development of therapies and their availability, and for closer cooperation between gynaecologists, physiotherapists, psychologists/psychotherapists and other specialists.

“The cause of the pain needs to be identified, as it may be the result of various conditions,” she said. “The causes can vary – gynaecological, hormonal, infectious, urological, musculoskeletal, neurological and psychological – so treatment should be individualised and, where necessary, multidisciplinary.”

The existence of individual specialists or private clinics providing a particular service does not automatically mean that there is an organised model of care for women with sexual dysfunction and chronic pain that is available to everyone, Vuksanovic Bozaric said.

A shortage of specialists, treatments unavailable

World.title: Kosovo MPs Voice ‘Deep Concern’ Over Guerrilla Leaders’ Conviction
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Kosovo MPs in session on September 28, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

In a rare show of unanimity, Kosovo MPs on Monday adopted a statement expressing “deep concern” over this month’s Hague court conviction for war crimes of four former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA – Hashim Thaci, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi.

The statement supported by 99 MPs calls on Kosovo’s institutions to take action “to protect the truth and purity of the liberation war of the people of Kosovo”. Ethnic Serb MPs from the Belgrade-backed Srpska Lista party were not present for the vote.

The text calls for the drafting of a common state strategy that would coordinate actions “for the protection and affirmation of the full historical truth about the just war for freedom and liberation of Kosovo.

“[Parliament] considers the conclusion [of the verdict] on the existence of a common criminal intent unacceptable,”= the statement added.

Kosovo’s ex-President, Thaci, and his co-defendants, former parliament speakers Krasniqi and Veseli and former MP Selimi, were sentenced to 25, 25, 18 and 13 years in jail respectively on September 16.

All four were found guilty of responsibility for crimes carried out while they were senior officials of the KLA during the 1998-99 war with Serbian forces.

They were found not guilty of crimes against humanity, of persecution, imprisonment, other inhumane acts, torture, murder and enforced disappearances.

Thaci, Veseli, Krasniqi and Selimi all pleaded not guilty to all charges and will appeal the verdict.

Since the verdict was announced, hundreds of people have been protesting in the capital, Pristina, and in other cities in Kosovo and abroad. Many Kosovo Albanians deem the Hague verdict an attack on the KLA’s just war for liberation.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA, under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies. The court is widely disliked in Kosovo, where it is seen as denigrating the KLA’s struggle.

Parallel with the statement, the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, is urging parliament to support amendments to the law on Specialist Chambers, approved in 2015, which would limit the scope of the chambers.

“Parliament has done its job, now it’s for the government to address the draft law [on the Specialist Chambers] responsibly. It should address it with urgency because there is no reason for delays. We saw with the Statement that there is a will. We expect the government to work on it today and send it to parliament tomorrow, or the day after,” Arian Tahiri, head of the PDK parliamentary group, said on Monday.

World.title: Serbia’s Vucic Pardons ‘Novi Sad 12’ as ‘Act of Mercy’ Before Resigning
World.content:
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic on Sunday said he had pardoned 12 anti-government activists from the city of Novi Sad who are on trial for allegedly preparing “acts against the constitutional order”, in one of his final decisions as President as he announced his resignation before next month’s elections.

Vucic said he had pardoned a total of 49 people, including 23 who are connected to what he called “all these terrible events over the past year and a half” – a reference to mass student-led protests that have shaken his government – including the so-called ‘Novi Sad 12’.

“I made the decision to pardon 12 people from the Novi Sad group led by [activist] Mila Pajic, just as I decided to pardon 11 people who, on the other [pro-government] side, took part in incidents against protesters involved in the blockades,” Vucic said in a speech in Belgrade before submitting his resignation.

He described the decision as an “act of mercy because of their age, not because they are not guilty of something or did not do something. I did so because I know they would have been sentenced to several years in prison in any country, in any other country in the world. And I want to protect every young person because I believe there is hope that they will change and behave much more responsibly in the future,” Vucic said.

He said he had made the decision despite advice from the security services.

The 12 activists, linked to the opposition Free Citizens Movement, PSG, and the activist group Students Against Authoritarian Rule, STAV, were charged with preparing acts against Serbia’s constitutional order and security.

The charges arose from a recording of the meeting between the indictees ahead of a March 2025 rally that became the largest in Serbian history.

Six of them spent more than seven months in detention and house arrest before being released to defend themselves at liberty.

The other six were outside Serbia when the arrests took place and have remained abroad, with proceedings against them conducted in absentia.

One of the six activists in exile, Doroteja Antic, told BIRN that none of them wanted the case to end with a pardon from Vucic, who she claimed was again using the group “for his own political purposes, to score political points”.

“He did not do this out of kindness but solely because it is politically advantageous for him at this moment. And this is the final proof that the case was fabricated and politically constructed from the very beginning, and that there was never really a case at all,” Antic said.

She acknowledged that this should end the court proceedings being conducted against the 12 activists.

“We are now waiting for the final confirmation and official notices from the court that the proceedings have been discontinued, but that is expected to happen soon, at least according to our lawyers,” Antic explained.

However, she said that her plan is to remain outside Serbia while Vucic remains in power, to ensure she is safe.

“My plan is to stay here at least until the elections, in the great hope that after October 25 we will all meet again in a free Serbia, because this really feels like the final moment, the last gasp and cry of a government that people have long wanted to see the back of,” she said.

World.title: Uber CEO Comes to Zagreb and Tries Out Rimac’s Robotaxi
World.content:
September the 30th, 2026 – Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi arrived in Zagreb and tried out Mate Rimac’s famed robotaxi without a safety driver.

Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi visited Verne and the Rimac Campus in Zagreb yesterday and rode in a robotaxi without a safety driver, Mate Rimac announced. “Uber is an investor and strategic partner in Verne. Dara tried out the robotaxi without a safety driver in Zagreb and was delighted with the experience. We talked about further cooperation and expanding Verne beyond Croatia with the ‘final’ Verne car without a steering wheel and pedals,” Rimac wrote on Facebook.

Index reports that Uber and Verne have otherwise been cooperating for months now on an autonomous taxi project. Back in March, Verne, China’s Pony.ai and Uber announced a strategic partnership to launch a robotaxi service in Europe, starting in Zagreb. Uber also announced an investment in Verne at that time.

driverless rides are already being tested out in zagreb

At the beginning of September, Verne and Pony.ai began testing rides with passengers in Zagreb without a safety driver or other staff in the vehicle. The tests are taking place on a 22-kilometre route connecting Verne’s headquarters with the area of Zagreb Airport. However, these are vehicles from the Chinese manufacturer BAIC with Pony.ai autonomous driving technology, not the final Verne vehicle without a steering wheel and pedals that Rimac mentions in today’s post. Since August, Uber has also enabled the ordering of autonomous rides via its app in Zagreb. In that phase a licensed operator was still behind the wheel, while fully driverless rides were introduced as separate tests.

the final report for the eu-funded project has been submitted

Mate Rimac’s announcement comes on the same day that Project 3 Mobility, the company developing Verne, submitted its final report to SAFU on the last day of the deadline for the robotaxi project financed from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan. According to what remains unofficial information, the company is not requesting recognition of the remaining part of the already paid advance in the final documentation. Verne had 179.5 million euros in non-repayable EU funds approved for the project, and back in July 2023 it received an advance of 89.75 million euros. SAFU earlier confirmed to Index that of that amount around 8.77 million euros had been justified so far, while around 80.98 million euros had not been justified.

The project formally ended on the 30th of August, after which a 30-day deadline for submitting the final documentation began. SAFU now has 60 days to check the reported costs and documentation, and during the procedure it may also request additional information. Only after the check is completed will it be known how much of the paid advance will be recognised and how much money, if any, Verne will have to return.

the primary contracted goal was not completed in time

The key problem of the EU-funded project remains the fact that by the deadline it was not confirmed that a fully autonomous Level 5 vehicle had been produced and homologated, which was one of the main contracted results of the project. Prime Minister Andrej Plenković said after the deadline expired that the project had not received final homologation from the competent institution in Germany and that it had not been completed by the end of August.

At the beginning of September, Verne revealed that it was ready to return the funds if the final evaluation showed that the contracted obligations had not been fully met. At the same time the company claimed that during the project test prototypes of fully autonomous electric vehicles had been confirmed and appropriate tests carried out. Mate Rimac’s meeting with Uber’s Dara Khosrowshahi therefore concerns the continuation of Verne’s commercial development and cooperation with Uber, while the final evaluation procedure for the EU-funded project continues separately.

World.title: EU Raises Retirement Age, Here’s What Awaits Croatia
World.content:
September the 30th, 2026 – As the EU raises its retirement age and multiple countries now expect their work forces to work for longer, what exactly awaits Croatia?

Working life across the European Union is lengthening significantly, and for younger generations the difference could be as much as ten years. Croatia is not currently going to raise its retirement age above 65. The retirement age is rising across Europe, and for some of today’s younger workers a working life could last until the age of 70 or even longer. The OECD estimates that the average retirement age will increase further in the future as life expectancy rises, while numerous countries have already legally adopted gradual increases.

Denmark stands out the most. There it has already been decided that the statutory retirement age will rise to 70 by 2040, while the OECD projects an even higher threshold for generations that have only just entered the labour market if the current method of linking the pension age to life expectancy continues. According to the latest edition of the OECD’s Pensions at a Glance report, the average normal retirement age for people who retired in 2024 is around 64.7 years for men and 63.9 years for women.

For those who have only just entered the labour market, the OECD expects a significantly longer working life. The average future retirement age is estimated at 66.4 years for men and 65.9 years for women.

denmark is taking it the furthest

Denmark is at the top of the European ranking. The current normal retirement age there is 67, and parliament has already adopted an increase to 70 years from 2040. The OECD projects that if the current formula linked to life expectancy continues to be applied, the future retirement age in Denmark could rise as high as 74 years. It is important to emphasise, however, that 74 is not a legally set limit for a specific year, but a projection that depends on whether Denmark continues to link the pension age to increases in life expectancy. The country is already discussing possible easing of that formula after 2040.

High future thresholds are also expected in other European countries. Estonia could reach 71 years, while the OECD projects a normal retirement age of around 70 for Italy, the Netherlands and Sweden. Under current rules, Finland could reach around 68 years and Slovakia around 69, while in a number of other countries the future normal retirement age is approaching 67.

many countries are adopting reforms

The changes are no longer just projections. In several European countries reforms have already been adopted that gradually increase the retirement age or link its future movement to life expectancy.

Belgium will reach a retirement age of 67 years, while the United Kingdom has planned a further increase towards 68. The Czech Republic has also adopted a gradual increase of the statutory age to 67. Slovenia has reformed its pension system and raised the statutory age, but in international comparisons the possibility of full retirement with a sufficient number of contribution years must also be taken into account. The main reason for such reforms is demographics. Europeans are living longer, while at the same time in many countries the share of the working-age population that finances pension systems is shrinking.

Countries are therefore trying to achieve a balance between longer life expectancy, the number of years spent in retirement and the financial sustainability of the system.

men and women are moving towards the same threshold

Differences in retirement age between men and women are gradually narrowing. In most European countries men and women already have the same statutory retirement age, while differences have been retained only in some countries. Some countries where the difference still exists have already decided on its gradual abolition, so the number of systems in which women can take full retirement earlier than men will decrease further.

where does croatia fall here?

Croatia is currently among the countries that do not have a legally determined increase in the regular retirement age above 65. Men in Croatia acquire the right to an old-age pension at the age of 65 with at least 15 years of pensionable service. For women a transitional period is still underway. In 2026 a woman can acquire the right to an old-age pension at 64 years of age and at least 15 years of service.

The threshold for women then increases by three months each year. In 2027 it will be 64 years and three months, in 2028 64 years and six months, and in 2029 64 years and nine months. From the 1st of January 2030, the conditions will be equalised, so both men and women in Croatia will acquire a regular old-age pension at the age of 65. There are also special rules for long-term insured persons. A person who has 60 years of age and 41 years of insurance service in effective duration can acquire the right to an old-age pension for a long-term insured person.

For early old-age pension the general rule is 60 years of age and 35 years of service. For women a transitional period is still underway, so in 2026 they can acquire the right at 59 years of age and 34 years of pensionable service.

will people in croatia have to work for longer?

So far no decision has been taken according to which the regular retirement age in Croatia would be increased above 65. This currently distinguishes Croatia from countries that have already legally linked the retirement age to life expectancy or adopted increases towards 67, 68 or 70 years. Nevertheless, the demographic pressure that is driving reforms in other European countries is also present in Croatia. The population is ageing, and the ratio of the number of employed people to pension beneficiaries is one of the key factors in the sustainability of the system.

That is why the question of how long future generations will have to work before retiring will remain one of the more important topics of European, and also Croatian, social policy. The difference between today’s and future generations can be large. While in a large part of Europe today’s normal retirement age is around 65, in some countries those who are only just starting work could, under current rules, retire only after the age of 70.

World.title: Wellovar – Bjelovar Geothermal Complex Now Open
World.content:
September the 30th, 2026 – Wellovar, the much anticipated Bjelovar geothermal complex is now open, with the ceremony attended by approximately 600 guests.

The ceremony was attended by around 600 guests, and alongside Mayor Dario Hrebak and Bjelovar-Bilogora County Prefect Marko Marušić, the highest-ranking state guests included Prime Minister Andrej Plenković, Speaker of the Croatian Parliament Gordan Jandroković and Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina.

Poslovni reports that after years of planning, preparation and 23 months of intensive construction, Wellovar opened its doors today. The ceremony was held as part of the celebrations of Bjelovar’s 270th birthday, and the new complex in Veliko Korenovo was presented as the largest project in the city’s history.

The way Wellovar was opened was particularly symbolic. Instead of the classic ribbon-cutting, 18 Bjelovar residents of different generations jumped into the Olympic pool. The youngest was a kindergarten-age girl, and among the participants were also well-known Bjelovar athletes, swimmers and pensioners. This “Generational Jump” was meant to symbolise the decades during which the people of Bjelovar had waited for an indoor Olympic pool, as well as the fact that the project is intended for the generations to come.

Wellovar was built as a geothermal sports and recreational complex and contains a total of 10 pools – five indoor and five outdoor. The complex also has four saunas, a gym, sports and recreational facilities and a restaurant. The outdoor pools will be presented to the public next spring.

Terme Bjelovar Director Zvonimir Žarec emphasised that behind the project were 23 months of intensive work, numerous challenges, but also a large team that in recent months prepared the complex for its first guests. Terme currently employs 47 people, and the number of employees will continue to grow. For Bjelovar, the opening of Wellovar also marks the beginning of a new tourism and economic story. With the project, the city aims to position itself as a destination for geothermal, sports and health tourism, and the new complex should also attract visitors from outside Bjelovar.

World.title: Split to Construct a Totem at the Entrance to the City
World.content:
September the 30th, 2026 – Split is set to construct a totem at the very entrance to the city, with 130,000 euros to spend on it.

Split will announce a public competition for a spatial marker, or totem, with which it wants to mark the entrance to the city. A total of 130,000 euros has been allocated for the project through 2026 and 2027. Index reports that on the 25th of August, Split Mayor Tomislav Šuta issued a conclusion on conducting a competition that should result in a “high-quality, recognisable and feasible design solution” for marking the city entrance.

The competition will seek proposals for the appearance, materials, basic dimensions, method of installation, visual identity and how the marker will fit into the immediate space and urban context. The final appearance, material and dimensions of the totem have therefore not yet been determined. The competition does not cover only the conceptual design. The official conclusion also states that its subject includes the production of the marker itself by the author of the winning solution.

130,000 euros have been allocated

In the budget, 80,000 euros has been earmarked for the activity “Marking the city entrance” in 2026, and a further 50,000 euros in 2027. The competition will be prepared and conducted by the city’s Department for City Development and the Croatian Designers’ Association, with the participation of other city departments. Official documents so far do not indicate exactly how much the production of the totem itself will cost, as other project costs are also financed from the same budget item.

World.title: Nations League: Spain Hand Croatia 4-1 Defeat in Seville
World.content:
Spain and Croatia met in Seville on Tuesday for matchday 2 of Group 3 in the Nations League A division.

The reigning world and European champions opened the campaign with a 3-2 win in England, while Croatia came from behind to beat the Czech Republic 2-1 away. Spain were heavy favorites, both in the group and the competition as a whole. Following this match, both sides return to action on Saturday — Croatia host England at Rujevica, while Spain welcome the Czech Republic.

Slaven Bilić made several changes from Prague, with only five players retaining their places. Dinamo Zagreb duo Dion Drena Beljo and Josip Mišić were handed starting berths, with Beljo leading the attack. Behind him, Ivan Perišić, Marco Pašalić, and Petar Sučić provided support, while Mateo Kovačić partnered Mišić in midfield.

The defensive line also saw significant reshuffling. Joško Gvardiol dropped to left back, while Ivan Smolčić came in on the right to replace Josip Stanišić. Josip Šutalo and Marin Pongračić formed the central defensive partnership.

Spain’s Luis de la Fuente also made notable changes, leaving captain Rodri, Dani Olmo, and Ferran Torres on the bench from the start. However, Lamine Yamal started and immediately posed a threat to the Vatreni.

Lineups

CROATIA: Livaković – Smolčić, Šutalo, Pongračić, Gvardiol – Mišić, Kovačić – Marco Pašalić, P. Sučić, Perišić – Beljo

SPAIN: Unai Simón – Pubill, Cubarsí, Huijsen, Cucurella – Zubimendi, Ruiz, Lopez – Yamal, Oyarzabal, Baena

Match report

The spectacle in Seville kicked off at 20:45, and Spain wasted no time, scoring with their very first attack as Baena and Cucurella combined to release Lamine Yamal on the edge of the box, who fired into the far corner in the second minute.

Croatia struggled to gain any foothold in the early stages. Cucurella and Baena continued to cause problems down the left, with another chance in the fourth minute falling to Baena from 16 meters, only for Livaković to hold comfortably. Oyarzabal also threatened after a slick Yamal assist, and Cubarsí tested Livaković from range as Spain dominated. Pongračić, who had a nervy opening, picked up a yellow card in the 19th minute.

Croatia’s first meaningful attacking moment came in the 17th minute when Perišić crossed to the far post for Marco Pašalić, but his header was comfortably gathered by Unai Simón. The Vatreni gradually found their footing and managed to settle into the match, though Spain remained firmly in control.

The 28th minute brought a moment of Croatian joy. Perišić delivered a pinpoint cross and Dion Drena Beljo rose to meet it with a header that beat Simón, scoring his first senior international goal and drawing Croatia level. The celebrations were short-lived. Within three minutes, Yamal found space on the left and picked out Pubill in the center, who headed calmly into the net to restore Spain’s lead. Pubill’s first international goal put the hosts back in front at 2-1.

Spain continued to press before the break. Fermín López struck the post with a superb effort from the edge of the box, while Oyarzabal had a goal disallowed for offside. Half time arrived with Spain deserving their advantage, Baena fortunate to still be on the pitch after a series of sharp reactions to refereeing decisions.

Bilić made one change at half-time with Luka Vušković replacing Pongračić. Spain began the second half with more of the same, though Croatia created their first real chance of the half in the 50th minute when Sučić played in Marco Pašalić, whose effort was blocked and won a corner.

De la Fuente made his first substitutions in the 57th minute, bringing on Merino and Pedri for Fermín and Fabián Ruiz. Croatia responded three minutes later with a double change of their own, with Ante Budimir and Mario Pašalić replacing Beljo and Kovačić.

The third goal came in the 63rd minute and it was Yamal again. The teenager burst clear of the Croatian defense, rounded Livaković one-on-one, and slotted the ball into the near post where it bounced into the net. Croatia showed spirit and continued to push, with Ivanović — who had replaced Perišić in the 72nd minute — firing narrowly wide from distance in the 77th minute. Pedri also drew a fine save from Livaković late on.

In the 81st minute, Luka Modrić received a warm reception from the Seville crowd as he was introduced from the bench. The veteran captain tried his luck in the 90th minute, getting into the box and shooting from ten meters, but fired straight at Simón.

By then, the result had long been decided. A minute before the final whistle, Nico Williams wrapped up a convincing Spanish victory. Merino played him in on the left side of the penalty area; Williams held off Šutalo and finished precisely past Livaković to make it 4-1.

This was Croatia’s first defeat in the new edition of the Nations League. After two rounds, they hold third place in Group A3. This was also Slaven Bilić’s first defeat since returning to the Croatia bench.

Croatia plays its next match on Saturday, October 3rd, when they welcome England to Rujevica.

World.title: Croatia and USA to Strengthen Ties Across Multiple Sectors
World.content:
September the 29th, 2026 – Croatia and the USA are set to strengthen ties across multiple sectors, from tourism to investments, energy and tech.

The recent Economic Forum in New York, organised by the Croatian Chamber of Economy (HGK) and the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ), brought together around 70 American and 35 Croatian companies, including 15 from the tourism sector.

Domagoj Puljizovic reports for Poslovni that over 100 business people from both sides of the Atlantic took part, with the goal of strengthening economic cooperation between Croatia and the USA, connecting companies, opening new business partnerships and creating opportunities for investment and business expansion on the American market. Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković also attended the forum together with entrepreneurs from Croatia and the USA, discussing the further development of economic relations between the two countries. B2B meetings were also in focus, enabling direct company connections and the presentation of opportunities for future cooperation.

important croatian companies took part

President of the Croatian Chamber of Economy Luka Burilović emphasised that some of the most important Croatian companies from the energy, food industry and defence sectors participated in the economic delegation. “The strongest Croatian companies from energy, the food industry and defence are taking part in the economic delegation. Some of them are already present in the USA, including Orqa, Končar, Infobip, HS Produkt, Metamorfoza, Podravka and many others. Interest in cooperation is high, and the potential is even greater. This is confirmed by the impressive turnout, both in number and composition, of more than 100 businesspeople from the American side,” said Burilović.

new business bridges

He added that the partnership between Croatia and the USA is strengthening year by year, and that existing cooperation agreements provide an important framework for its further development. As one of the important steps in strengthening economic cooperation, he highlighted the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement, which was signed almost four years ago but has not yet entered into force. Its application is expected to reduce business costs and administrative barriers and further encourage investments, especially in the IT sector.

Prime Minister Plenković emphasised that Croatia wants to further develop its partnership with the USA in areas of strategic importance for future economic development – from energy and technology to industry and innovation. “We see particular potential in energy, digital technologies and artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, the defence industry, research and development, and high-tech investments. The expanded LNG terminal on Krk will reach a capacity of 6.1 billion cubic metres per year, and more than two-thirds of the gas arriving at Krk comes from the USA,” said Plenković.

croatia’s blossoming ict sector

He also highlighted the importance of Croatia’s ICT sector, whose globally successful companies confirm the potential of domestic knowledge, talent and innovation. He stressed that Croatia should be viewed not only as a market of 4 million people, but also as a safe and stable base for access to the European Union market of 450 million consumers.

“We want to connect Croatian and American companies, capital, technology and knowledge even more strongly. We want to further develop tourism sustainably, with investments in higher-quality accommodation, infrastructure, services and stronger air connections with the USA. We are building new transatlantic value chains and opening space for an even stronger economic partnership between Croatia and the USA,” the Prime Minister said.

further tourism opportunities

Tourism was one of the important topics of the forum. Croatian service exports to the USA have amounted to almost one billion euros in recent years, and a significant part of the revenue is generated precisely in this area, along with IT and consulting services. HTZ Director Kristjan Staničić said that the American market shows great interest in Croatia’s tourism offer, especially the premium segment and high value-added products.

“The USA is Croatia’s most important long-haul market, with great potential. American guests are among our tourists with the highest average spending, they increasingly visit Croatia throughout the year, and interest in investing in Croatian tourism is also growing,” said Staničić. He added that discussions were also held on continuing cooperation to improve air connectivity between the USA and Croatia. He also highlighted the promotion of Croatia through a new promotional video featuring John Malkovich, which is being shown on Times Square in New York, one of the world’s most famous tourist locations.

World.title: Largest Thermal Baths in Croatia Open As Of Today
World.content:
September the 29th, 2026 – The largest thermal baths in Croatia have opened their doors today, putting Bjelovar and the massive Wellovar project in the spotlight.

Construction lasted 23 long months, and it is the most complex pool complex in Croatia due to its energy, heating, air-conditioning and cooling systems. Poslovni reports that the geothermal baths called Wellovar in Bjelovar will be officially opened today on the occasion of City Day. The thermal baths themselves will be available to the general public in about ten days, Mayor Dario Hrebak announced on Monday.

Today marks 270 years of the city of Bjelovar and the Wellovar project is the largest project in its history, and all of the necessary occupancy permits for the baths have been obtained. The complex has five indoor and five outdoor pools, including an Olympic-size one, four saunas, a gym, sports and recreational facilities, and a restaurant. The outdoor pools will open only next year in May because it’s currently too cold.

According to Terme Bjelovar director Zvonimir Žarec, there are currently 47 employees at the baths, and lifeguards will also be hired shortly. Žarec said that in the last seven to eight months he has spoken with more than a thousand candidates, and a large part of the employees have returned to Bjelovar from other places.

Three hours of swimming on a weekday will cost seven euros, and a full-day ticket 16 euros on weekdays or 21 euros at weekends and on public holidays. Pensioners, persons with disabilities, war veterans, students and secondary-school pupils will pay five euros for three hours of swimming in the morning hours. A full-day family ticket for two adults and two children will cost 44 euros on weekdays or 56 euros at weekends and on public holidays.

Around 600 guests are expected at the ceremonial opening and session, and the arrival of Prime Minister Andrej Plenković and Speaker of the Croatian Parliament Gordan Jandroković has also been announced.

World.title: First Croatian Green Hydrogen Plant Being Built at Rijeka Refinery
World.content:
September the 29th, 2026 – The very first Croatian green hydrogen plant is being built at the large Rijeka Refinery, and it’s one of INA’s key investments.

Croatia will soon get its first commercial plant for the production of green hydrogen. Morski reports that the INA industrial complex at the Rijeka Refinery is currently a major construction site, and the first molecules of this more environmentally friendly energy source are expected at the beginning of next year, according to HRT. This is otherwise one of INA’s key investments, worth more than 60 million euros, which significantly strengthens Croatia’s energy position on the European map.

1,500 tonnes of hydrogen per year

Designed in accordance with the best global practices and technologies already applied worldwide, the new hydrogen production plant will use electricity from its own power plant. “Similar plants have already been implemented around the world, and ours is being built to the highest standards,” emphasised Una Radulović Zekić, Director of Health, Safety and Environment at INA. The planned annual capacity is 1,500 tonnes of green hydrogen. It will primarily be used for the needs of the refinery itself, but depending on demand, it will also be available for placement on the commercial market.

This project is part of a broader modernisation cycle of the Rijeka plant, within which the construction of a facility for processing heavy residues was recently completed. This enables the processing of a significantly wider range of crude oil and completely eliminates the need to import semi-finished products, while overall diesel production will increase by up to 30 percent. Goran Pleše, Operational Director of Refining and Marketing at INA, emphasises that with the completed modernisation, both Rijeka and Croatia are gaining a much more favourable market position.

kostrena demands higher environmental standards

Despite these large investments, the local community points to long-standing open environmental problems. Residents of Kostrena have been struggling for decades with unpleasant odours and occasional sea pollution. “Kostrena has been burdened by all kinds of industry in the area for decades. We expect INA and others to move in the direction of relief and to respect the highest standards of environmental protection, safety and transparency,” said the mayor of the Municipality of Kostrena, Dražen Vranić.

a new system of protective barriers for a cleaner sea

Responding to environmental challenges, INA points out that the construction of an extensive system of protective barriers is also underway, which should prevent further leakage of hydrocarbons into the marine area. The project envisages the drilling of a total of 75 boreholes, of which 54 are new and 21 existing. The entire system is designed to pump pollutants at the lowest point and thus permanently prevent contact of hydrocarbons with the sea. Completion of the works and the first concrete results are expected in the spring.
