Mother See calls report ‘an act of political retribution’

“The ‘report’, compiled using public funds and based on accusations and defamatory claims circulated on social media and in the media, is an act of political retribution, vindictiveness and unacceptable interference in the internal life of the Church,” the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin said.

The clergy called on the Armenian authorities to build Church-state relations on the basis of mutual respect, a clear separation of powers and the primacy of national interests. They also called for:

“an end to the persecution of clergy and the popularly elected Catholicos of All Armenians through fabricated accusations and defamation;

action strictly within the framework of the Constitution, national legislation and international law, in line with proclaimed democratic principles, guaranteeing freedom of conscience, religion and belief in the country and strengthening social solidarity rather than division;

existing problems and disagreements to be resolved through dialogue, without preconditions and without resorting to futile ultimatum-style rhetoric.”

According to the Mother See’s statement, the authorities are attempting to artificially create a crisis within the Church:

“Any initiatives to reform the Church that are driven by political arbitrariness, manipulation or coercion are unacceptable. Efforts to address the challenges facing the Armenian Church and improve its functioning are carried out exclusively on the basis of decisions by the Church’s highest canonical governing bodies.”

Expert commentary

According to religious freedom expert Izabella Sargsyan, the government has no right to interfere in the Church’s internal affairs or prepare reports of this kind.

She argues that the report is unacceptable from the standpoint of legality, ethics and human dignity:

“This is not simply about freedom of religion or belief, or about an abuse of power by the government. It concerns personal data and the publication of names, including that of a minor who was allegedly subjected to sexual abuse.”

International humanitarian law and human rights expert Anna Melikyan stressed that Armenia’s Constitution clearly defines the relationship between the government and religious organisations, including their freedom of activity, separation from the state and autonomy:

“Freedom and autonomy mean that the government has no right to interfere in the internal affairs of a religious organisation, including its choice of governance system or efforts to bring it into line with canonical and ethical norms.”

She insists that neither the executive nor the legislature can decide who should lead a religious organisation or what internal rules it should adopt unless a criminal or administrative offence has been identified:

“If there are facts that provide reasonable grounds to suspect clear criminal or administrative offences, there are other mechanisms for responding to them – through criminal or administrative proceedings.”

The human rights expert says the confrontation between the government and the Church should be viewed in terms of the legality of the government’s actions in order to prevent possible unlawful interference.

She says an effective system of checks and balances should operate in a democratic state to prevent governments from being tempted to overstep their powers:

“All states and governments face this temptation, and if they encounter no resistance, they will seize as much power as they can.”

World.title: Azerbaijan’s Meydan TV case: ‘Investigator, prosecutor and judge in this case is Ilham Aliyev’
World.content:
Journalist testifies in Meydan TV case

On 28 September, journalist Shamshad Agha, founder and editor-in-chief of the Arqument.az website, testified at Baku Court on Grave Crimes in the Meydan TV case. He rejected the charges against him, said there were inconsistencies in the criminal case materials and linked his arrest to his journalistic work.

In his testimony to the court, the journalist also said he had been subjected to violence during his detention and threatened that members of his family would be brought to a police station unless he disclosed the password to his phone.

“The 30-volume criminal case is based entirely on groundless accusations. This whole collection of papers they call a ‘criminal case’ has been fabricated,” Shamshad Agha said.

On 6 December 2024, Meydan TV journalists Ramin Deko (Jabrayilzade), Aynur Ganbarova (Elgunesh), Aysel Umudova, Aytaj Ahmadova (Tapdig), Khayala Aghayeva and Natig Javadli were detained. They were charged under Article 206.3.2 of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code with smuggling committed by a group of people acting in prior conspiracy. The criminal proceedings against them became known as the “Meydan TV case”. Journalists Shamshad Agha, Nurlan Libre, Fatima Movlamli, Ulviya Ali and Ahmad Mukhtar were later also arrested in connection with the case. In August this year, the charges against the journalists were expanded, with additional charges brought under other articles of the Criminal Code.

Meydan TV says the arrests are linked to its journalists’ critical reporting.

The full version of the article is available in the Azerbaijani-language section.

Who am I?

I am Shamshad Agha – Shamshad Islam oglu Aghayev, a citizen of Azerbaijan, a journalist and poet who has faced repression at the hands of the political and ideological heirs of Stalinism.

I was born on 1 September 1982 in the village of Shivla in Lerik District. My childhood unfolded against the backdrop of the pain the Karabakh conflict brought to those close to me. I grew up during the so-called “transition period”, tending lambs on mountain slopes with a book in my hands.

My father worked as a teacher for 40 years. His library and the books he gave me largely shaped my worldview and my understanding of injustice and the need to resist it.

At school, we studied literature from the period of Stalinist repression. The fate of intellectuals who fell victim to the “Red Terror” instilled in me a deep rejection of Stalinism and shaped my attitude towards its political and ideological heirs.

I particularly remember the words of repressed Azerbaijani writer Yusif Vazir Chamanzaminli: “I learnt to resist oppression and injustice from my mother.” My mother taught me the same. If I lose her while I am in prison and cannot attend her funeral, I am certain she will know that I did not side with injustice and oppression.

Azerbaijan’s state television recently broadcast a film about literary critic Seyid Huseyn, who was repressed under Stalin. Because of his family ties to one of the leaders of Azerbaijan’s independence movement and his closeness to an opposition party, he was executed after a 20-minute trial, while his wife was sentenced to eight years in exile.

And this is being shown by the state television of a country whose authorities today, in my view, persecute women and imprison them for writing and speaking the truth. I am certain that if the Siberian camps still existed today, they would be sent there too.

That is the irony of history and fate.

When did I become involved in public and political life?

I became actively involved in public and political life during my university years. In 2003, I was an activist in the student movement. Following the presidential election, whose results I considered unfair, pressure on politically active students at the university intensified. In solidarity with the opposition Musavat party, which was facing pressure at the time, several other students and I joined the party.

At the same time, I wrote articles, short stories and poetry, which were published in regional and national publications. While still a student, I joined the Union of Writers of Azerbaijan, but later left it and, together with like-minded writers, established an independent literary association.

In 2007, I graduated with honours from Lankaran State University and spent three years teaching Azerbaijani language and literature at the school I had once attended. At the same time, I continued working with media outlets and reporting on problems in the region.

In 2010, I committed myself fully to journalism, and in 2014 I established the independent website Arqument.az, of which I remain founder and editor-in-chief.

In 2016, together with Akif Gurbanov and Alasgar Mammadli, we founded the School of Democracy to train young journalists. Today, many of its founders, teachers and graduates are in prison on charges that I consider politically motivated.

Today, journalists, civil society representatives, activists and politicians facing repression by the Azerbaijani authorities are the voice of the country’s disenfranchised citizens

In my view, Abzas Media, Toplum TV and Meydan TV remain among the last platforms for freedom of expression in Azerbaijan. I am proud of my work with these independent media outlets and of my colleagues who are now on trial or in prison.

Journalism begins with doubt and courage. My colleagues have reported on the consequences of war, spoken out against restrictions on media freedom and continued their work even from prison. Some have received international recognition, while others have trained a new generation of journalists.

It is partly thanks to colleagues like these that I remain who I am. I’m glad you’re here, guys.

Why was I arrested?

In 2022, when Azerbaijan adopted a new law “On Media”, I actively opposed it and described it as a “death sentence for independent media”. I believed the authorities were seeking to push independent journalism out of the public sphere because, despite the considerable resources available to state and pro-government media, the public continued to trust independent sources of information.

While working as a presenter at Toplum TV, I heard even officials and MPs acknowledge that audiences placed greater trust in information from independent media. Meydan TV, which was established outside the country, also continued to overcome restrictions on access to information. In my view, the authorities chose to confront independent media through pressure rather than competition. The new law and the creation of a media register were part of this process. The Venice Commission also criticised the law. Many journalists, experts and civil society representatives who opposed it subsequently ended up in prison.

After the arrests of Abzas Media staff, I was approached, according to my account, by representatives of the security services who offered me co-operation, praising my professionalism and saying they needed my views as an expert. I refused. Further attempts were then made to contact me through intermediaries, and I later received a warning that I could be arrested. Despite this, I continued to refuse to co-operate.

Later, Russian Foreign Intelligence Service chief Sergei Naryshkin said after a visit to Baku that he had discussed joint action with the Azerbaijani side against Western-oriented media outlets and organisations. Soon afterwards, Sputnik Azerbaijan published an article mentioning me and Arqument.az, which I head, including our critical stance towards Russia over its war against Ukraine.

I saw this as a warning that I was about to be arrested. At the time, I continued meeting friends and defending my detained colleagues, and received several verbal warnings telling me to back down. But I could not do so. Otherwise, I would not have been able to look my colleagues – or former participants in our journalism training programmes who were already in detention – in the eye.

I did not back down out of heroism, but out of shame

One police officer told me that many people were afraid to protest because even mentioning certain names could have serious consequences. I replied that it was not about courage. We speak out because we are ashamed to remain silent in the face of injustice. It is this feeling that compels us to overcome our fear.

In my view, an authoritarian system seeks to suppress such civic courage by portraying independent journalists as people who supposedly “work for foreign powers”. But we are here because we spoke about what was happening in our own country.

How was I arrested?

At around 1am on 5 February 2025, I was detained near Neftchilar metro station. I say that I was beaten during my detention as officers demanded the password to my phone, and that I was denied medication for high blood pressure.

I was then taken to my home, where my brother and underage daughter were present. According to my account, one of the officers hit me when I told my family that I had been detained. I was not shown a court order authorising the search. Officers searched the flat and seized computers, phones, press cards and documents.

After finding no money in the flat, they again demanded my password and threatened to take my brother and daughter to the police station. To make them stop, I gave them the password. Despite my requests, my lawyer was not allowed to be present during the search.

At the Baku Main Police Department, I was asked to provide the password to my computer. I say that I was again subjected to violence, but I did not disclose the password. I refused to give evidence without a lawyer present.

After being questioned in the presence of my lawyer, during which I said my prosecution was politically motivated, I was placed in a temporary detention centre. On 6 February, Judge Rafael Sadigov ordered that I be remanded in custody. I consider the decision political and hold President Ilham Aliyev responsible for it.

After the court hearing, I was transferred to the Baku pre-trial detention centre. The stories of prisoners I met there reinforced my belief that the judicial and law-enforcement systems are unjust.

All this is happening in the 21st century in a country that is a member of the Council of Europe.

In my view, the existing system has an interest in the constant production of criminal cases, while investigative bodies seek to preserve their influence and privileges. Yet the state should not only prosecute alleged offenders but also address the causes of crime.

When a country has so many criminal cases and prisoners, society should consider the quality of governance. Where violence becomes an acceptable tool, it is difficult to speak of justice.

Every day in the pre-trial detention centre, I hear people praying and cursing those they believe are responsible for injustice. I wonder whether all this will ever end, and I am certain that it will. The authorities may try to drown out discontent through controlled media and entertainment, but in my view, one day it will turn into open protest.

Azerbaijan’s problems are not limited to media freedom and political rights. The country also faces serious social problems. According to official statistics, around 2.9 million people have registered medical conditions – almost a third of the population. I believe that talk of stability and victories conceals deep problems within society.

In my view, journalists are turned into political hostages precisely because they write about these problems. Meanwhile, those who investigate corruption and the transfer of state funds abroad are accused of receiving money from overseas. It is particularly disheartening that society often tolerates corruption and injustice. But I am certain this will not always be the case.

Alleged irregularities in the criminal case

I believe the 30-volume criminal case is based entirely on groundless accusations and was compiled in violation of the law. The prosecution alleges that I falsified documents but, in my view, has failed to provide convincing evidence.

In court, I pointed out that under Article 52.3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, criminal case materials must be drawn up on specially numbered forms. I asked for these to be presented to the court, but it emerged that no such forms existed. On this basis, I believe the legal requirements governing the preparation of the case were not followed.

In my view, the prosecutor’s office should have discontinued the case, but instead effectively endorsed the alleged violations. I therefore hold both the prosecution representatives and the leadership of the prosecutor’s office responsible for them.

As a result, I believe that neither the 30 volumes of case materials nor the 600-page indictment based on them has proper legal validity. I maintain that numerous provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure were violated during the investigation and preparation of the charges. That is why, in seeking to prove my innocence, I am constantly forced to refer to domestic and international law, while the investigation and the court, in my view, disregard its requirements.

Under rulings by the Plenum of Azerbaijan’s Supreme Court and the case law of the European Court of Human Rights, detaining a person requires evidence linking them to an offence and specific grounds for their detention. I believe the prosecution has provided no such evidence and that my detention is therefore unlawful.

At almost every hearing, I point to alleged violations and file motions, but the court rejects them. In my view, the charges are politically motivated and the case is not being examined objectively.

The investigator, prosecutor and judge in this case is Ilham Aliyev.

If President Ilham Aliyev has evidence that I was involved in smuggling or falsified documents, let him present it to the court. I am confident that an objective examination of the case materials will establish my innocence.

There are numerous contradictions in the case materials. I had never met Ulvi Tahirov and saw him for the first time in court. We had never communicated, and his testimony does not mention my name. Investigators have also presented no evidence linking me to Ramin Jabrayilzade, who, according to the case materials, was found with €38,000 when he was detained.

A record dated 16 January 2025 already identifies me as a defendant, even though I was not detained as a suspect until the night of 5 February. I was also linked to €40,000 from the Abzas Media case, although I am being tried as part of the Meydan TV case.

Investigators also cite my telephone conversations with Aynur Ganbarova, although their content has not been established. Another piece of purported “evidence” was a document stating that I had allegedly received €1,370, but a forensic examination commissioned by investigators found that the signature on it was not mine. An examination of my phones, laptop and storage devices also found no material of significance to the investigation.

I also consider the charge of illegal business activity to be unfounded: Arqument.az was officially registered in 2015, while I registered with the tax authorities as an individual in 2017. Investigators have also failed to specify which documents I allegedly falsified and used.

The claim that I repeatedly travelled abroad in 2024 and engaged in smuggling is also untrue: I did not leave the country at all that year.

I therefore believe that investigators have failed to present convincing evidence to support the charges of smuggling, illegal business activity, money laundering, document forgery and tax evasion.

As you can see, the prosecution has presented no evidence that I received grants from any organisations, engaged in money laundering or was involved in smuggling. Nevertheless, I remain in custody on the grounds that I might abscond from the investigation.

I consider this argument unfounded. In July 2024, as part of the Toplum TV case, an investigator conveyed through another witness that he wanted to question me. I called him myself and voluntarily went to the Baku Main Police Department the following day, where I gave evidence as a witness. If I had intended to abscond, why would I have contacted the investigator myself and gone in for questioning?

I was subsequently banned from leaving the country. The investigator justified the restriction by saying that I would allegedly be arrested in the near future. However, eight months passed, and I was eventually detained not in connection with the Toplum TV case but the Meydan TV case. According to my account, the investigator later said that if I had not been arrested in this case, another reason would have been found because the decision to arrest me had already been made.

I therefore consider the entire process unlawful and an act of politically motivated repression. In a country where political will takes precedence over the law, it is difficult to speak of a fair trial.

As Tolstoy wrote, when those who are supposed to uphold justice themselves commit injustices and show no respect for the law, human life or universal values, sooner or later this leads to grave consequences.

World.title: Local man in Abkhazia confesses to killing Russian tourist
World.content:
Killing of Russian tourist in Abkhazia

A local man in Abkhazia who allegedly killed a Russian tourist has confessed to the crime following his arrest. Edgar Abukhba had previously served a prison sentence for a serious offence – rape involving extreme violence.

Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry said it had detained a suspect in the killing of Russian national Amina Bikbova.

Amina Bikbova

A 26-year-old woman from Orenburg, Russia, was on holiday in the Abkhaz city of Gagra, where she met 25-year-old local fruit seller Edgar Abukhba.

The two exchanged messages for a couple of days. Then, on 24 September, Abukhba invited her for coffee, according to Amina’s friend. She has not been seen since and did not contact her family.

Concerned about their daughter’s disappearance, her parents contacted Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry.

A day later, the ministry announced that it had detained a suspect in the killing of the Russian tourist. He was identified as Edgar Abukhba.

Edgar Abukhba

Abukhba initially denied any involvement in Amina Bikbova’s disappearance. He said they “had coffee, and later a guy came to pick her up and drove her away”.

He later confessed to the killing and told investigators where he had hidden the body.

According to Abukhba’s account, after coffee he took the woman to the rented apartment where he was staying. They had sex, after which he strangled her.

He then planned to dump her body in the Bzyb River. But he was unable to carry the body all the way to the river, so he left it, wrapped in a blanket, on the riverbank.

Edgar Abukhba had previously committed a similar crime.

In July 2019, he lured a Russian tourist into the former Abkhaz Council of Ministers building in Sukhum and raped her with extreme violence. He then tried to kill her, striking her repeatedly on the head with a brick. The woman survived, but was left permanently disabled.

A lower court sentenced him to 19 years in prison. However, Abkhazia’s Supreme Court, hearing his appeal, took into account that Abukhba was 17 at the time of the crime and was therefore considered a minor.

His sentence was reduced from 19 to nine years in prison.

Abukhba was released on 2 February 2024.

If Abukhba is found guilty of killing Russian tourist Amina Bikbova, he could now face a life sentence.

Commentary

Sukhumi blogger Ruslan Shakov published a commentary asking whether the killing could have been prevented and whether anything could have been done to stop Abukhba from committing another serious sexual offence.

“The more I look into Amina’s story, the fewer questions I have about ‘who specifically released Edgar Abukhba’ and the more I have about what happened after his release.

“It is important to understand that there was no single judge who simply decided to cut his sentence.

“Abukhba was sentenced to nine years for raping a Russian tourist, robbery and causing grievous bodily harm. The case then went through several levels of court. Because of the way sentences are enforced in Abkhazia, he was actually released on 2 February 2024, after serving about 4½ years.

The nine-year sentence itself was not formally reduced. But that is not really the main question.

What happened to him after he was released?

Abkhazia has a law providing for administrative supervision of people released from prison. And this is where I have questions.

Were any monitoring or preventive measures put in place after Abukhba’s release? Who is responsible for assessing the risk that someone who has committed such a violent crime could do it again, and how is that risk assessed?

I am not saying that administrative supervision would necessarily have saved Amina. No one can know that. But when someone who has committed such a crime returns to society, the work should not end on the day of his release.

A systemic reform of the security system is needed: reviewing certain provisions of criminal law, tighter controls on firearms, and strengthening the Interior Ministry in terms of personnel and technical capacity. […]

And then there are the comments directed at Amina.

Yes, it can be said that you should not go to the home of someone you barely know. But a risky decision does not make someone responsible for their own murder.

Amina may not have known who she was dealing with or what was in his past. The authorities did.

At the same time, I disagree with attempts to attribute the crime of one individual to all of Abkhazia. After the family reported her disappearance, law enforcement identified and detained a suspect and found the woman’s body. The investigation is continuing.

But good police work after a killing does not remove the main question: could something have been done before it happened?

And here I would like to see not a search for one guilty agency or one particular person, but an honest examination of what needs to change in the law and across the security system to prevent similar cases from happening again.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: ‘Which neighbouring country would you visit?’ Tbilisi street poll – VIDEO
World.content:
Travel poll in Georgia

We asked people on the streets of Tbilisi which of Georgia’s neighbouring countries they would like to visit and why.

We also asked whether they had previously travelled to any countries in the region, why they chose those destinations and what impressions they came away with.

The answers vary widely. Turkey is mentioned most often, with respondents drawn by its picturesque coastline and the Bosphorus. Many also say they would be happy to visit Armenia or Azerbaijan, while some look further afield and name more distant countries in the region.

Russia is rarely mentioned in a positive context. Instead, it is named by almost every respondent when asked which neighbouring country they would not like to visit.

Through this survey, we sought to find out how well people in Georgia know the countries of the South Caucasus and their other neighbours, what interests them about these countries and what stereotypes they hold about them.

World.title: SOCAR, ExxonMobil sign deal to explore for oil and gas in Azerbaijan’s Middle Kura Basin
World.content:
Oil and gas investment in Azerbaijan

At the second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in Baku, SOCAR and ExxonMobil signed a production-sharing agreement for the exploration and development of unconventional hydrocarbon resources in the Middle Kura Basin. A final investment decision was also made on the full-field development of the Absheron gas field.

Speaking on 26 September about investment priorities for the coming decade, Ilham Aliyev said the oil and gas sector would retain a leading role.

What will ExxonMobil look for in the Middle Kura Basin?

The agreement provides for the exploration, development and production of unconventional hydrocarbon resources in the Middle Kura Basin. According to SOCAR, the companies will each hold a 50% stake in the project through their subsidiaries, with ExxonMobil acting as operator.

The project does not involve the development of an existing offshore field in the Caspian Sea, but rather the exploration of the oil and gas potential of an onshore basin. Bloomberg has linked the project to shale oil and gas production. It has also been reported that the project is awaiting parliamentary approval.

Aliyev said successful exploration “could lead to another oil and gas boom in Azerbaijan”.

Published information does not specify when commercial production could begin, targeted annual production levels, confirmed recoverable reserves or the project’s overall budget. The precise size and boundaries of the contract area have also not been disclosed.

For Azerbaijan, the significance of the agreement lies in bringing ExxonMobil’s technology and expertise in developing unconventional hydrocarbon resources into the search for new reserves. However, the basin’s resource potential and the commercial viability of development will have to be established before its possible economic impact can be assessed.

Absheron: annual gas production set to quadruple

SOCAR, TotalEnergies and XRG have taken a final investment decision on the full-field development of the Absheron gas and condensate field. According to TotalEnergies, which operates the project, the company holds a 35% stake. SOCAR also owns 35%, while XRG holds 30%.

Under the company’s plan, annual gas production will increase from 1.5bn to 6bn cubic metres, while daily condensate production will rise from 12,000 to 47,000 barrels. The new phase of development is expected to begin in 2029.

In his speech, Aliyev spoke of an additional 5bn cubic metres of gas within three to four years. However, the figures presented by the company imply an increase in annual production of 4.5bn cubic metres.

TotalEnergies says the gas produced will be supplied to the domestic market and Turkey.

GDP diversifying, but energy still dominates exports

Discussing the country’s future economic model, Aliyev said “oil and gas will retain a leading role in our economy”, adding that the revenues generated would be reinvested in the economy.

The president said the non-oil sector accounted for more than 70% of GDP, while, according to him, oil and gas still made up more than 90% of exports.

According to calculations by Marja based on State Customs Committee statistics, oil and gas products accounted for 71.22% of goods exports in January-August 2026.

Electricity, data centres and logistics

Aliyev linked the development of renewable energy to efforts to reduce domestic gas consumption and free up additional volumes for export. He also referred to the expansion of power transmission lines for electricity exports and projects to lay submarine cables across the Caspian and Black seas.

The president identified supplying electricity to data centres and artificial intelligence systems as a priority and said an Azerbaijan-Kazakhstan fibre-optic cable would become operational by the end of the year. Documents relating to the Oracle Alloy project were also exchanged at the forum. According to SOCAR, Caspian Mind AI will serve as the local operator.

In transport, the government aims to increase transit freight volumes from an expected 16m tonnes in 2026 to at least 25m tonnes by 2030. Discussing food and water security, Aliyev highlighted water shortages and the need to reduce dependence on food imports, while also calling for investment in agriculture.

What does the $10.8bn package actually represent?

According to the Economy Ministry, 23 documents covering projects worth a combined $10.8bn were signed at the forum. The ministry says these projects are planned for implementation.

However, the documents represent projects at different stages of development. A final investment decision has been taken on Absheron. The ExxonMobil agreement establishes the contractual framework for exploration and subsequent development. A framework agreement with Comstock provides for studying opportunities to liquefy US gas and sell it on international markets. A memorandum with Apollo concerns assessing potential investments, conducting due diligence and preparing final agreements.

Published information does not provide a full breakdown of the $10.8bn figure among individual projects, a financing timetable or details of how much has already been formalised as binding financial commitments. There is therefore no basis for treating the entire amount as a guaranteed inflow of foreign investment.

Aliyev described the government’s approach to investment policy as follows:

“All we have to do is create favourable conditions.”

The economic results of the forum will ultimately depend on the actual investment made in the announced projects, as well as growth in production and non-oil exports.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s president sees no serious effects of climate change, but UN report says otherwise
World.content:
Climate change in Azerbaijan

President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev says the country has yet to feel the serious effects of climate change. He bases this assessment on the snow cover he observes in the mountains during winter. However, the latest climate documents that Azerbaijan itself has submitted to the UN show that the country is already facing serious consequences of the climate crisis.

According to official data, the average temperature has risen by 1.1°C over the past 23 years, water resources have declined by around 15%, droughts have become longer, the Caspian Sea has fallen by more than two metres, and the number of frost days and the area covered by glaciers in the mountains have decreased.

On 26 September, President Ilham Aliyev addressed climate change while discussing food security at the second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in Baku. He commented on the issue:

“We have not yet felt the effects of climate change. I go skiing every winter and see that the snow levels in our mountains remain the same. Perhaps the snow is melting somewhere, but not in Azerbaijan.”

Aliyev then reiterated that Azerbaijan “has not yet been affected by climate change”. Yet in the very next sentence of the same speech, the president noted that water shortages required greater attention to food security.

However, the president’s broad assessment contradicts official climate documents prepared by Azerbaijan itself.

What does the government document in force in 2026 say?

One of the most recent sources is NDC 3.0, a document Azerbaijan submitted under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Azerbaijan submitted it in November 2025, and an updated version appeared in August 2026.

The document paints a very different picture from the one Aliyev presented on 26 September:

“Azerbaijan is seriously affected by the climate crisis.”

The document lists rising temperatures, changing weather patterns, land degradation, shrinking water resources and the falling level of the Caspian Sea among the effects of the climate crisis. It notes that these processes threaten biodiversity, water resources, agriculture, economic development and people’s well-being.

This is therefore not merely a matter of future projections. Azerbaijan’s official climate document describes changes that are already taking place.

Azerbaijan has already warmed by 1.1°C

According to NDC 3.0, the average temperature in Azerbaijan has risen by 1.1°C over the past 23 years.

In 2023, the country’s average temperature reached 14.6°C, 1.9°C above the climatic norm. The Baku region has also recorded a significant increase in indicators measuring heatwaves with temperatures above 35°C.

These figures are consistent with data previously published by the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources. The ministry reported that temperatures across the country during the first 20 days of June 2024 were 4.8°C above the climatic norm.

These figures do not simply reflect weather conditions in a particular month or year. They show changes against a backdrop of long-term warming.

What about Aliyev’s example of snowfall?

It is unclear which mountain and elevation the president was referring to, or which years he was comparing. It is therefore impossible to independently verify whether the snow levels he observes while skiing have actually changed.

However, heavy snowfall over several winter seasons does not, in itself, reflect a long-term climate trend.

More importantly, data from Azerbaijan’s own government point to changes already taking place in the country’s mountainous regions.

The 2024 National Adaptation Plan states that temperatures have risen across the country in recent decades, while the number of frost days in winter has declined. This trend is particularly pronounced in mountainous areas. The plan also includes a separate section titled “Glacier melting”, which states that observations by the National Hydrometeorological Service indicate that glaciers are melting at an accelerating rate.

The same issue came up in 2020 at a meeting on water management chaired by Aliyev. At the time, Ecology Minister Mukhtar Babayev told the president that rising temperatures in Azerbaijan’s mountainous regions had led to “a decline in the number of frost and snowy days”.

An earlier report that Azerbaijan submitted to the UN states that the total area of glaciers in the Gusarçay river basin shrank from 4.9 sq km to 2.4 sq km over approximately 110 years.

Therefore, the amount of snow at a particular ski resort in a single season cannot serve as an indicator of long-term changes in the country’s mountain ecosystems.

Water resources have already declined

Another detail in Aliyev’s speech effectively points to an existing problem: the president identifies “water shortages” as a risk to food security.

According to Azerbaijan’s NDC 3.0 document, the country’s water resources have declined by approximately 15% over recent decades. Total precipitation over the past decade has fallen by around 3.4% compared with the 1971–2000 climatic norm.

In December 2025, Deputy Ecology Minister Umayra Taghiyeva cited another figure at a UN event: the volume of water flowing into the country had fallen by 30%. This figure reflects a decline in the amount of water entering Azerbaijan, rather than a reduction in the country’s total water resources.

Furthermore, around 67–70% of Azerbaijan’s river flow originates outside the country, making it vulnerable both to climate change and to changes in the use of transboundary water resources.

Droughts are becoming longer

NDC 3.0 states that over the past 30 years, the number of occurrences of hot, dry winds has increased 14-fold, while the duration of droughts has increased by more than 20%. The document also notes that the number of hailstorms has more than tripled over the past decade.

Azerbaijan’s 2024 National Adaptation Plan, which uses calculations covering a slightly different period, states that droughts have become 19% longer.

World Bank modelling suggests that even under a relatively optimistic climate scenario, a significant share of agricultural land in central Azerbaijan will face the risk of water shortages by 2050.

According to the projections, unless adaptation measures are introduced, yields of some rain-fed crops — those grown primarily using rainfall rather than irrigation — could fall by 30% in 2051–2060 compared with

The Caspian Sea has fallen by more than two metres

According to the Azerbaijani government’s NDC 3.0 document, the level of the Caspian Sea has fallen by more than two metres over the past 30 years.

The document attributes this to several factors: reduced river inflows, increased evaporation caused by rising temperatures, and other geological factors. It notes that these processes are already posing risks to coastal infrastructure and ecosystems.

It would therefore be inaccurate to attribute the Caspian Sea’s falling level solely to climate change. However, Azerbaijan’s official document identifies rising temperatures and increased evaporation as factors contributing to the process.

What conclusions can we draw from the official data?

Aliyev’s personal observation about snowfall in the mountains cannot be disproved using the available public data. He did not specify a particular location, measurements or a period for comparison.

However, the broader conclusion he draws from this observation — namely, his claim that “Azerbaijan has not yet been affected by climate change” — contradicts the data in documents that the Azerbaijani government itself has submitted to the UN.

These documents record changes that have already occurred: a 1.1°C rise in temperature, declining water resources, longer droughts, fewer frost days in the mountains, melting glaciers and a falling Caspian Sea level.

Moreover, Azerbaijan’s NDC 3.0 document, which remains in force in 2026, describes a situation very different from the one the president presented in his speech: Azerbaijan “is seriously affected by the climate crisis”.

Climate change in Azerbaijan

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: September 30, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 30. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called 'Iron Fist' in response to Armenian armed forces on September 27, 2020, Trend reports.

The 44-day second Karabakh war brought an end to 30-year occupation of Azerbaijani lands and the restoration of country's territorial integrity.

Trend presents chronicle of Azerbaijan's second Karabakh war for September 30, 2020:

- President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva met with wounded soldiers.

- President of the European Council Charles Michel made a phone call to President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev.

- The Armenian armed forces used the Tochka-U high-precision tactical ballistic missile system. However, due to the unsuitability and poor quality of the Armenian troops' military equipment, three of the fired missiles didn't explode.

- The Azerbaijani Army disabled one S-300 anti-aircraft missile system of the Armenian armed forces during the fighting in the Shushakand village of the Khojaly district.

- The Armenian armed positions of the 1st Battalion of the 5th Motorized Rifle Regiment Tartar district's Hasangaya settlement and the 1st Battalion of the 6th Motorized Rifle Regiment stationed in the Talish direction were destroyed. The enemy's military equipment in the Jabrayil direction of the front was destroyed. The Azerbaijani Army units subjected the 4th battalion of the Armenian armed forces in the Fuzuli direction, to heavy artillery fire. The command post of the 41st separate regiment of the 18th motorized rifle division was also fired upon. The troop control was completely broken.

- The personnel of the 2nd Battalion of the seventh Mountain Rifle Regiment of the 10th Mountain Rifle Division of the 1st Combined Arms Army of Armenia in Tonashen, suffered big losses and left their defensive positions without permission. A blow was struck at the headquarters of the 5th Mountain Rifle Regiment in the Aghdere settlement of the division.

- The Azerbaijani Army conducted operations to destroy Armenian manpower and military equipment, surrounded in the Aghdere and Tartar directions, as well as continued the cleansing of the territory. Suffering significant losses in manpower and military equipment, the enemy couldn't cope with the evacuation of the dead and wounded.

- Some 46 civilians have been injured, and 14 have been killed as a consequence of heavy artillery shelling of Azerbaijani densely populated areas.

World.title: King of Bahrain receives credentials of Azerbaijani ambassador
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 29. King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa of Bahrain has received the credentials of Azerbaijan's newly appointed Ambassador Javidan Huseynov,during an official ceremony in Bahrain on September 29, Trend reports.

King Hamad welcomed Huseynov along with newly appointed ambassadors from South Korea, Algeria, Kuwait and Türkiye.

The King highlighted the strong bilateral relations between Bahrain and Azerbaijan and wished the Azerbaijani ambassador success in further strengthening cooperation and friendship between the two countries.

On October 17, 2025 President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, has signed a law approving the establishment of the embassy in Bahrain.

Under the decree, the Cabinet of Ministers of the Republic of Azerbaijan was instructed to address logistical and financial matters related to the operation of the Azerbaijani Embassy in the Kingdom of Bahrain (Manama) and to take necessary measures arising from the order.

By another decree signed by President Ilham Aliyev on February 27, 2026 Javidan Huseynov has been appointed Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Azerbaijan to Bahrain.

World.title: Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva meet with Prefect of Dicastery for Interreligious Dialogue of Holy See (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 29. On September 29, Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, and Alena Aliyeva met with Cardinal George Jacob Koovakad, Prefect of the Dicastery for Interreligious Dialogue of the Holy See.

Cardinal George Jacob Koovakad fondly recalled his visit to Azerbaijan and the hospitality he received during his stay. He noted that he had been received by President Ilham Aliyev and highlighted the special importance of the meetings he held during the visit.

The Cardinal emphasized that, at a time when the world is witnessing war, violence, and messages of hatred, Azerbaijan’s model of interfaith solidarity and peace sends a powerful message to the international community.

Leyla Aliyeva stressed the importance of mutual support, joint efforts, and broader dialogue on culture, religion, and human values amid challenging global developments.

The meeting also included discussions on the Heydar Aliyev Foundation’s projects in the Vatican and future joint programs under the Memorandum of Understanding signed with the State Committee for Work with Religious Organizations.

World.title: Finance presenter Alan Kohler retiring after three decades at ABC
World.content:
After a brilliant 31-year career as the ABC's finance guru, Alan Kohler has decided to hang up his boots at the end of the year.

With a successful career in print before moving to television, Kohler has been one of the most influential journalists Australia has ever produced, as a former editor of The Australian Financial Review (AFR) and The Age and as an incisive columnist on all affairs financial.

"I love the ABC, always have, even more so after I joined it," he told ABC staff in a statement.

" I find it very hard to imagine this wonderful place not being part of my life, but I'm 74 and it's time to spend more time with my family, including the six grandchildren. "

Alan Kohler (left) speaks with then-treasurer Paul Keating in 1984, during Kohler's time as editor of The Australian Financial Review. (Supplied)

Kohler joined the public broadcaster in 1995 as business and economics correspondent for the 7.30 Report and went on to host Inside Business.

For the past 24 years, he has been the lead 7pm News finance presenter, unravelling the mysteries of financial markets for the audience with a format all his own that has often begun with: "Now, here's an interesting graph."

ABC managing director Hugh Marks said Kohler had made an extraordinary contribution to the organisation and the nation.

Alan Kohler swapped the studio for the home office during COVID-19 pandemic. (Supplied)

"For decades, he has helped Australians make sense of complex issues with insight, clarity and a uniquely engaging style, always delivered with warmth, humour and that trademark cheeky grin.

"I can't thank Alan enough for everything he has given to the ABC and our audiences. While this marks the end of an incredible chapter, it is certainly not the end of Alan's contribution, just the beginning of a new one."

Kohler hosted Inside Business for many years. He currently writes a weekly column and hosts a podcast, That's Business, every Friday.

While he is a distinguished editor, Kohler's biggest impact on the nation has been as a communicator.

After several stints as the chanticleer columnist for the AFR, he joined The Sydney Morning Herald (SMH) and The Age as senior business columnist, working with your correspondent during my time as SMH business editor.

Alan Kohler worked as a journalist in Darwin during Cyclone Tracey. (Supplied)

A canny entrepreneur, he had by that stage already launched The Eureka Report and later left Fairfax Media when he added online news service Business Spectator to the mix.

Throughout his various incarnations, he has remained steadfastly loyal to the ABC and to his audience and is expected to continue his association with one-off specials.

World.title: Why Daniel Tupou is a Sydney Roosters grand final specialist
World.content:
The Roosters boast a galaxy of stars for Sunday's NRL decider against Newcastle, but veteran winger Daniel Tupou might be the only one who could call himself a grand final specialist.

Not that he ever would — at 35, Tupou has been a firm believer that actions speak louder than words for many years now, and those actions demand his automatic inclusion in any discussion about an all-time Roosters XVII.

A win over the Knights will make Tupou, already the club's highest-ever tryscorer and only a few games shy of being their most capped player, the first Rooster to win four premierships with the club since the 1940s.

He's the only player to have appeared in all three grand final wins under coach Trent Robinson, although calling what Tupou has done merely "appearing" sells him short.

Back in 2013, in just his second year of first grade, Tupou went skywalking to score a spectacular try in the Tricolours' win over a Manly side containing future teammate Daly Cherry-Evans.

Tupou has been making his mark in grand finals for more than a decade. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Back then, Tupou was like so many of his teammates are now — young and hungry in his first grand final, with everything to prove.

"I can't remember much, to be honest it's a bit of a blur, it was such a long time ago. Most of these boys are where I was in 2013 — I was the same age then as Rob Toia is now," said Tupou.

"He's (Cherry-Evans) has never brought it up. I might not bring it up this week, not until after the game on Sunday at least."

That try was just the 17th of Tupou's career, and his 199th in the preliminary final win over the Dolphins is proof he can still fly.

But that and his calm demeanour are about the only things that are still the same after all this time, with Tupou himself having become one of the best wingers of the modern era in the years since.

His performances in the club's back-to-back premiership wins in 2018-19 are living proof of that transformation from skinny aerial specialist to a truly complete flanker.

In the first victory, a comprehensive win over Melbourne, he scored the opening try and worked like a dog from the backfield, running for the second-most metres of any Roosters player.

In the second, a 14-8 war with Canberra, he was unlucky not to become the first winger to win the Clive Churchill Medal as man of the match.

Tupou ran for a team-high 185 metres from 17 carries and saved several tries with perfect defensive decision-making before making the break and throwing the final pass for James Tedesco's premiership-winning score.

It's as good a game as a winger has ever played in a grand final, but when Tupou explains how he finds his best form on the season's biggest day, he makes it sound maddeningly simple.

"You have to stay calm and collected. Enjoy the week and the hype around it, enjoy the atmosphere once we hit the field but embrace the vibe, embrace the energy," said Tupou.

"There's a lot of stuff to tick off, but you have to enjoy every bit of it.

"Just stay present. Don't overthink, be where your feet are."

It's the advice he'll give the grand final rookies on Sunday, even though the Roosters have plenty of premiership experience on hand.

Victor Radley and James Tedesco both played in 2018-19, Nat Butcher and Angus Crichton were both there for the latter and Spencer Leniu won three titles with Penrith.

This Rooster has been the NRL's best forward in 2026 Fresh off another act of blunt-force artistry, there can be no doubt that Roosters prop Naufahu Whyte has been the best forward in the NRL in 2026.

But given 15 of the 22 players named on Tuesday have yet to play in a grand final, they have a fair share of first-timers.

None could ask for a better example of how to make the most of it than Tupou, whose deeds under the brightest of lights have made him a stone-cold living legend of the club he'll once again try to bring to glory on Sunday.

"It's in the preparation. We've worked so hard during the year to earn this moment," said Tupou.

"It's nothing less than what we've already done, we just have to stay consistent."

World.title: Aussie skipper Molineux a chance to play home series despite injury
World.content:
Australia will give captain Sophie Molineux every chance to play in white-ball matches against Bangladesh and New Zealand, as she battles a hip injury.

Molineux was named to captain Australia's side for ODIs against Bangladesh and T20s against New Zealand next month, despite the injury.

Fast bowler Darcie Brown has been sidelined with a back injury that also has her in doubt for the WBBL, while fellow quick Lucy Hamilton will miss the ODIs with a quad strain.

Molineux proves inspired choice Sophie Molineux is praised for her leadership ability after guiding Australia to its Women's T20 World Cup victory.

But it is Molineux's fitness that is of most interest ahead of the opening ODI in Brisbane on October 9.

The Victorian put aside a history of frustrating blows to have a stellar first six months as captain, culminating in Australia's T20 World Cup win in England.

"Sophie has been named in the squad but has been managing a hip injury," chief national selector Shawn Flegler said.

"Her involvement in the series will continue to be assessed over the coming days.

"Lucy suffered a mild quad strain at training, but we're hopeful she'll recover in time to be fit and firing for the T20 series."

If Molineux is ruled out, selectors will have to make a call between vice-captains Tahlia McGrath and Ashleigh Gardner to lead the side.

Australian squad:

Sophie Molineux (c), Ashleigh Gardner (vc), Tahlia McGrath (vc), Nicola Carey, Kim Garth, Lucy Hamilton, Alana King, Phoebe Litchfield, Beth Mooney, Ellyse Perry, Megan Schutt, Annabel Sutherland, Georgia Voll, Georgia Wareham

World.title: Union, community say $500k 'woefully inadequate' for Alice Springs College
World.content:
The Australian Education Union (AEU) says half a million dollars will not be enough to cover all necessary infrastructure upgrades at the new Alice Springs high school merger.

From the start of 2027, Centralian Middle School (CMS) and Centralian Senior College (CSC) will merge to become the Alice Springs College on the current CMS site in Gillen.

The school community has raised concerns that many classrooms, the hall and the library will be too small to fit extra students, while science and computer labs and the home economics kitchen need upgrading.

Brian Gray says $500,000 "does not buy a lot of school". (Supplied: Australian Education Union)

AEU NT branch president Brian Gray said the school needed repainting, had an ineffective air-conditioning system, broken or repeatedly breaking lifts meaning the school was inaccessible and more than the allocated $500,000 was needed for renovations.

"In a climate in which millions have been spent on truancy officers and hundreds of millions to upgrade prisons and build work camps, why has the same financial commitment not been given to invest in the young people of Alice Springs and build them the school they can be proud of and deserve?" Mr Gray said, quoting union members.

"We've had this fantastic announcement of $14 million to build these new sports facilities right next door to the CMS site.

" $14 million buys you a heck of a lot of oval, $500,000 doesn't buy you a lot of school. "

$14.5m NT sports complex The Gillen Oval Multi-Sport Precinct has been green-lit and could become a shop window for Indigenous soccer players, former Manchester United star and Danish international Jesper Olsen says.

He said the school community also wanted certainty around how exactly the $500,000 would be spent and when upgrades would be complete, information which had so far been unclear to staff and families.

'Significant need' for funding

CSC school council chair and a parent of children at both CMS and CSC Rachel Neary said $500,000 was "woefully inadequate", but schools in Palmerston had been provided more than $100 million to update science labs, tech areas and home economic rooms.

"We're not advocating for taking money off schools in Darwin, but actually what we're asking for … is needs-based funding and what we have at the new emerging Alice Springs College is significant need," she said.

"We sit in the lowest 3 per cent nationally in terms of our student outcomes and grades. So it's a school where there's a significant amount of need."

Rachel Neary says this is an opportunity to expand the school to support central Australian students. (ABC Alice Springs: Samantha Jonscher)

Mr Gray said there were 1,700 children in public primary schools in Alice Springs and only about 700 in public high schools, so the merger was an opportunity for the NT government to create a school that would keep children in public education.

"Alice Springs College needs to be a school that supports [students] to reach their fullest potential as the future leaders of this town," he said.

Ms Neary said the merger was a once-in-a lifetime opportunity.

"We could really create something significant for young people in Central Australian region," she said.

Money amount uncertain

Department of Education acting deputy chief executive Miranda Watt said more funding would be provided to the Alice Springs College, which would likely be used for updating areas such as science labs and disability access, similar to what was delivered to Driver Secondary School and Rosebury Secondary School in Palmerston.

"[The amount of funding] is yet to be decided, but there's certainly a commitment that that will happen," she said.

Centralian Middle School in Alice Springs will become the new Alice Springs College. (ABC Alice Springs: Xavier Martin)

Ms Watt defended the school's current infrastructure, saying CMS had in previous years had more than 1,000 students, with the only infrastructure changes since then being that some walls had been removed to open up spaces.

"So by putting those additional walls in and updating the spaces to be a little bit more contemporary, it means that many students could attend," she said.

She said while the school's hall may be inadequate for the influx of extra students, there were plenty of other large areas that could be used for assemblies.

World.title: Breaking: Man taken to Geraldton hospital as WA police respond to 'serious incident'
World.content:
A man in his 30s has been taken to Geraldton Regional Hospital with serious injuries following what police say is a "serious incident" just east of the town in Western Australia's Midwest.

Police said they were responding to an incident early this morning involving people known to each other in Moonyoonooka on the outskirts of Geraldton, more than 400 kilometres north of Perth.

Significant police resources had been deployed to the areas of Moonyoonooka and Utakarra, they said.

Police have told people to stay clear of the area. (ABC News: Chloe Henville)

St John WA said they were called to the area around 1am.

"St John WA has taken a man in his 30s to Geraldton Hospital from an incident in this location," a spokesperson said.

Police said the man's injuries were "non-life-threatening".

Forensic officers on scene

Two police forensic officers could be seen working at Giles Park, just off Moonynooka Yuna Road.

Police forensic officers are at the scene gathering evidence. (ABC News: Chloe Henville)

The road remains open.

About 100 metres to the north, a police vehicle has blocked off Allen Road.

Witnesses have reported seeing police tactical response vehicles heading north towards the area, which includes the local airport and speedway.

102.5 ABC Perth caller Penny said she was driving south from Gingin, 77 kilometres north of Perth, around 5:30am when she saw a convoy of police vehicles heading towards the town.

"It was an [armoured police vehicle] and about six undercover LandCruisers with lights flashing," she said.

Police have advised people to stay clear of the area and wait for further advice.

World.title: $15b data centre next to tip could be among Australia's largest
World.content:
A $15 billion data centre is being proposed for a site near Wagga Wagga in south-western New South Wales.

Canberra-based CDC Data Centres intends to build the 1.4-gigawatt development on council-owned land next to a landfill facility on Ashfords Road at Gregadoo, 15 kilometres from the regional centre.

If approved, it would be one of the biggest planned data centres in Australia, behind Anthropic's $32 billion proposal at Dalby in Queensland, Syncline Energy's 2.4 gigawatt hub in north-west Melbourne and a 185-hectare site slated for a data centre near Darwin.

CDC chief executive Greg Boorer said Wagga Wagga was a perfect regional location.

"It's sandwiched between renewable energy zones, it's got significant spare capacity in the grid, there's a university, a skilled workforce and it's proximate to Canberra where we're headquartered," he said.

Mr Boorer said CDC has been in discussions with Wagga Wagga City Council for about nine months, with the proposed purchase of the site progressing.

In a statement the council said the proposal represents a potentially generational economic, investment and workforce opportunity for Wagga Wagga and the wider region.

"Council recognises that the Wagga Wagga community will have questions and concerns about data centres generally, as well as the location of the proposal and its potential impacts," the statement said.

Greg Boorer is confident sourcing finance for the data centre will not be an issue. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

A scoping report lodged with the NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure shows the company plans to build four single-storey buildings on the site, each about the size of a supermarket distribution centre.

The site is about a kilometre from Transgrid's Wagga Wagga substation, which is critical given the amount of electricity required to power the site.

CDC proposes to fund its own connection and network augmentation to the grid.

According to its scoping report, cooling of the data centres would use mechanical infrastructure such as chiller decks and pump rooms designed to minimise water consumption.

Nine rural dwellings are near the proposed data centre, three within a 500-metre radius.

"The location is excellent because you're a long way from homes and people. It's next to a rubbish tip where people don't want to necessarily live anyway," Mr Boorer said.

The report also cites plans for a closed-loop radiator system to minimise water use, 384 back-up diesel generators, on-site diesel storage amounting to 6,400 tonnes, and two large-scale batteries.

In January a fire at the landfill facility escaped, burning through 55ha of surrounding land.

Mr Boorer said the fuel would not be stored in one location.

"Diesel is really difficult to burn, and that's why it's a good and safe way of powering the generators," he said.

"We've looked at other alternative fuels, but there's just not a supply available."

Community engagement

The proposed development has been deemed state significant by the NSW government, and CDC said it was working its way through planning requirements, with community engagement expected to begin soon.

The scoping report identifies the visual impact of the data centres on the rural landscape, noise impacts, water demand and security issues and the loss of agricultural land as matters of interest to the community.

Plans for a data centre on Sydney's North Shore were withdrawn on Monday amid community anger about the project, while consultation processes at another proposed data centre at Moss Vale in the Southern Highlands have come under scrutiny due to a threat of legal action from its developer.

"I completely understand this is change. It's different, and people have lots and lots of questions," Mr Boorer said.

"We'll be doing lots of community engagement and education sessions, so people realise there are lots of forms and operators of data centres.

"We need to make sure they're in the right locations, so we're not competing for different resources with communities."

The layout of CDC Data Centres' proposed Gregadoo facility. (Supplied: NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure)

Homegrown data centres 'imperative'

Mr Boorer said, if approved, the Gregadoo data centre would be CDC's first regionally based venture, with its other data centres in Auckland, Canberra, Melbourne, Sydney and Perth.

Wagga Wagga already hosts a smaller-scale 300-kilowatt data centre owned by Leading Edge, which also has sites in Newcastle, Albury, Tamworth, Dubbo and Coffs Harbour.

Mr Boorer said the company would need to source finance for the project, but was confident it would not be an issue.

"For economic prosperity and cyber-resilience, it's imperative we actually have these capabilities in Australia, to leverage for our own benefit, but also to protect our systems," he said.

"It really is one of the new industries of this century."

World.title: Saved by the Bell actor Dennis Haskins dies at 75
World.content:
Dennis Haskins, the actor best known for playing the affable principal Richard Belding on the hit NBC sitcom Saved by the Bell, has died aged 75.

"It's a tragic loss," his agent, Jay Schachter, said in a statement.

"Everyone loved Mr Belding and those of us who got to know Dennis, loved him even more. He was a great person, and he loved, I mean absolutely LOVED his fans.

"He always had time for them, no matter what. He was my client and dear friend for over 20 years, and I will miss him terribly. I'm heartbroken."

Saved by the Bell, which ran from 1989 to 1993, centred on the antics of a group of students at the fictitious Bayside High in Southern California.

Taking a page from the comedy movie Ferris Bueller's Day Off, the school often appeared to be run more by the teens than their hapless principal. The show was both ridiculed and embraced for its zany plots.

Lark Voorhies, who played Lisa Turtle on the show, paid tribute to Haskins in an Instagram post, saying she was heartbroken.

"Knowing Dennis Haskins for almost 40 years has been one of the truest blessings of my life, which makes losing him hurt so deeply," she wrote.

"We shared so much history together from our earliest days, and through it all, he remained a fabulous person, a loyal friend, and someone with such a kind, gentle heart."

Haskins was born and raised in Chattanooga, Tennessee.

According to a biography posted by the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, he was active in the school's drama club and helped found a community theatre group.

Before his television career, he was a music manager, agent and concert promoter, and his clients included Tom Jones and Gregg Allman, according to his biography on IMDb.

Haskins later went on to have guest roles in The Twilight Zone and Magnum, PI in the 1980s.

World.title: Queensland government department loses $800k in cyber attack
World.content:
The Queensland government department delivering the state's first cyber security strategy lost more than $800,000 in a cyber attack, a new report has revealed.

The Customer Services, Open Data and Small and Family Business department plays a lead role in strengthening the state government's cyber security capabilities.

In the department's latest annual report, the entity noted it lost $809,000 in public money as a result of an external cyber attack in July 2025.

A department spokesperson said no payment was made "to those responsible".

"The systems of a third-party telecommunication provider were accessed illegally for financial gain," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"Immediate steps were taken to contain and investigate the incident, and security controls have been further strengthened."

The review, released on Friday, said no government data or sensitive information was compromised during the incident.

"The department blocked the attack and engaged a third party to mitigate any further exposure," the report said.

The entity is responsible for setting the cyber security policy and guidance for the state's public sector and for managing whole-of-government cyber security services.

"The Queensland government is committed to protecting the security and resilience of its systems and services," the spokesperson said.

Thousands of cyber security events

In the Transport and Main Roads Department's annual report, the entity said it reviewed more than 9,000 suspicious activities in the last financial year.

The department also investigated more than 3,000 cyber security events.

The Department of Transport and Main Roads investigated more than 3,000 cyber security events in the last financial year. (Supplied: Transport and Main Roads Queensland)

"These efforts supported early threat detection, reduced operational impacts and informed ongoing improvements to security controls," the report said.

A transport department spokesperson said the entity continues to enhance its cyber security capability through continuous monitoring, staff awareness programs, security assurance activities, and targeted initiatives aligned with the state's cyber security strategy.

It said the department actively monitors and investigates suspicious activities to protect the state's transport services, information systems, and customer data.

Under legislative requirements, the department notifies individuals when an incident results in an eligible privacy breach.

In March, the Queensland Audit Office published a report that examined and tested the effectiveness of a state government, local government, and statutory body's IT security controls.

Cybersecurity audit exposes gaps in government systems in Qld The report found increasing frequency and sophistication of cyber attacks could expose government entities that had weak cybersecurity.

The audit gained the "highest level of access" to two government entities in the state.

It did not name the entities "to avoid publicly identifying any security vulnerabilities".

The report found that the increasing frequency and sophistication of cyber attacks could expose entities that had weak cybersecurity.

It recommended all public sector entities and local governments review and, where needed, update their policies to ensure there is appropriate guidance about identifying, assessing, and monitoring third-party cyber security risks and developing mitigation controls.

In the Customer Services department's "cyber security leadership role", it agreed to all relevant recommendations and progressed actions, including initiatives to strengthen whole‑of‑government cyber security capability.

World.title: Consortium named frontrunner to build Brisbane’s 2032 Olympic stadium
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics Consortium named frontrunner to build Brisbane’s 2032 Olympic stadium Cameron Atfield September 30, 2026 — 10:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The consortium behind some of Australia’s best-known sporting venues has emerged as the frontrunner to build Brisbane’s proposed Olympic stadium, with the state authority overseeing the project selecting the BESIX Watpac and John Holland joint venture for the final stage of contractor negotiations. The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority announced on Wednesday morning the consortium had won out over a Built-Sacyr partnership to move to the next stage of the early contractor involvement (ECI) process, which began almost a year ago on October 31, 2025. GIICA chief executive Simon Crooks said the first phase of the ECI had been a thorough process. A large section of Victoria Park has been excavated for the Olympic stadium build. BMD “We are satisfied that the process has delivered the best-possible contractor for this second and final phase,” he said.



“Engaging two highly experienced construction teams in the design phase has meant we were able to rigorously test buildability, sequencing, risk and opportunity early. “This collaborative process supports our commitment to delivering an outstanding Brisbane Stadium, while ensuring value for money and confidence in an on-time, responsible and appropriate build for Queenslanders.” The stadium will be the new home of three-peat AFL premiers Brisbane Lions. Cox Architecture Together, BESIX Watpac and John Holland have delivered a host of landmark stadium projects across Australia. BESIX Watpac built Suncorp Stadium, barely two kilometres from the Victoria Park site, as well as the doomed Gabba and Queensland Country Bank Stadium in Townsville. John Holland, meanwhile, built the Melbourne Cricket Ground’s Shane Warne Stand, Marvel Stadium in the same city, the Sydney Football Stadium and the under-construction Penrith Stadium.



BESIX Watpac chief executive Mark Baker said the company had “never been more ready” to help shape Queensland’s Olympic legacy. “With a track record of delivering every major stadium in Queensland without missing an opening, a century of local heritage and our Brisbane-based headquarters, we are proud to progress the next stage of development for Brisbane Stadium,” he said. Stadium work at Victoria Park. BMD Consortium partner Nick Miller, the chief executive of John Holland, said they were “ready to hit the ground running” to deliver Brisbane a home of AFL, cricket and the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. GIICA chairman Stephen Conry said the authority was pleased with the stadium’s progress.



“It will enable Brisbane to be a serious player in a nationally and globally competitive market for major events,” he said. “Comprehensive design, procurement and early works are continuing at pace to deliver the new stadium precinct that will enhance Victoria Park, connecting it to the rest of the city and allowing far more people to enjoy it, rather than just a few.” GIICA’s annual report, tabled last Friday, reveals the agency expanded rapidly during 2025-26 as responsibility for the venue program intensified. The authority reported 81 staff, up from a full-time equivalent workforce of 52 a year earlier, and said it had adopted an integrated delivery model with delivery partner Unite32 – a consortium led by Laing O’Rourke and AECOM.



Related Article Exclusive

Infrastructure How Brisbane 2032 is driving Australia’s next infrastructure boom The report also showed the authority recorded a $493.6 million operating surplus largely driven by the transfer of Victoria Park land and assets into its control, with total assets reaching $550.5 million by June 30. GIICA said all venue milestones during 2025-26 were delivered within approved timeframes and scope, with procurement and planning activities progressing across Brisbane and regional Queensland venues. But it warned there were risks to keeping to its $7.1 billion budget, jointly funded by the state government and the Commonwealth. Risks cited in the report included escalating construction costs, market capacity constraints, inflationary pressures and supply chain disruptions.
