World.title: One day after public flag celebrations Neale tells Lions: ‘Make me a Magpie’
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 One day after public flag celebrations Neale tells Lions: ‘Make me a Magpie’ Michael Gleeson September 30, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Days after celebrating his third successive premiership, dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale has officially told Brisbane he will move to Collingwood as a free agent. In case you thought you already knew this, let’s be clear. Neale on Wednesday morning made official the previous reports anticipating his move to Collingwood by formally telling his club he wanted to go to the Magpies. Neale leaves Brisbane with two Brownlow medals and three premierships. Getty Images He told the Lions of his intentions the day after he and his premiership teammates were feted at a public fan event in Brisbane. That he had not been offered a new contract at Brisbane in his free agency year suggests the only question was which club the free agent would choose, not whether he would leave.



After a very public and acrimonious marriage break up Neale has endured a tumultuous year. Despite his wife and children moving back to Perth, Neale has opted not to ask for a move to Western Australia, fearing he would feed the circus circling his personal life. He has instead taken a three-year deal at Collingwood at slightly less than $1 million a season. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘We have nothing but gratitude:’ Lions give Collingwood-bound Neale their blessing In August Neale was revealed to have toured Collingwood’s facilities ahead of playing against Carlton the next day. Reports also suggested there had been discussion of what number he would wear and so which locker he would have. Essendon, West Coast and Collingwood all approached Neale once it became clear he felt he needed to leave Brisbane. Fremantle, the club he began his career at, said if he wanted to return they would make it happen, but that would be a tight squeeze financially for the grand finalists. He also met with St Kilda coach Ross Lyon – his former coach at Fremantle with whom he maintains a good relationship – but they agreed a move there was not the right fit for Neale or the club.



Lions president Andrew Wellington told this masthead after Saturday’s win that, regardless of him leaving, the Lions would always value Neale not only for his three flags and two Brownlow medals but the impact of his arrival when the Lions were battling to win matches. Related Article Exclusive

AFL 2026 AFL considering changes to free agency system “It was a really important platform for turning the club around, and if you look at his performances in grand finals and big games, he has been incredible, so we have got nothing but gratitude for what he has done for our club,” Wellington said. Neale was fortunate to play in Saturday’s grand final having initially been banned by the AFL tribunal for an intentional strike to the stomach of Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan in the preliminary final, only for that decision to be watered down to a fine by the AFL appeals board. “Lachie has been a great player for the Brisbane Lions, and we thank him for his incredible contribution over his eight seasons,” Lions list manager Dom Ambrogio said.



“We understand Lachie’s reasons for wishing to explore free agency and we wish him all the best for the next chapter of his career.” The club said it will further celebrate and recognise Neale’s contribution to the club in the coming days. The free agency period opens on Friday and the AFL will confirm what compensation the Lions will receive for Neale. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Boy, 16, among trio charged with Sydney student’s mistaken identity murder
World.content:
Two men and a 16-year-old boy extradited from Victoria have been charged with the mistaken identity murder of a university student shot dead in his bed in Sydney’s south-west. Marco Tapia, 23, was killed when a group of assailants stormed his family’s Glen Alpine home in the early hours of September 1. Police have since confirmed the wrong address was targeted in the allegedly botched organised crime killing. Marco Tapia was shot dead while in bed at his family’s Sydney home. Detectives are yet to identify the intended target of the botched attack, but are investigating if the trio was contracted to target a Coconut Cartel member. Tapia had no links to organised crime. Vaifaalie Tuafuti, 23, Omar Mohamed, 22, and a 16-year-old boy who cannot be identified for legal reasons have been charged with murder, two counts of special aggravated break and enter and committing a serious indictable offence, and possessing an unauthorised prohibited firearm.



All three are due to face court on Wednesday. Detectives will allege in court that the trio broke into the Glen Alpine home before shooting Tapia in his bed. One of the trio is alleged to have been armed with a pistol. The trio was extradited from Victoria on September 18, along with a 26-year-old woman, Amenah Abusud. The trio charged with murder were earlier extradited from Victoria. NSW Police Abusud has not been charged with Tapia’s murder, but she has been charged with criminal group and accessory offences.



Police alleged during an extradition hearing in Melbourne Magistrates Court this month that the group worked for the notorious Alameddine crime family in a recent spate of violence against rival group the Coconut Cartel. The trio has also been charged over a home invasion in Hurstville, in Sydney’s south, and the shooting several cars in nearby Turrella the night before Tapia was killed. Loading Ballistic analysis found discharged cartridge cases at the two scenes were “positively matched” to the Glen Alpine crime scene where a firearm was found, a NSW Police officer testified in court. The court was told the Victorians left their Airbnb at Campbelltown, in Sydney’s south-west about 1.50am on September 1 and returned about 4am, “where they appear to be in a rush to collect their belongings before all leaving”.



Two boys, aged 14 and 16, were earlier charged with allegedly staging vehicles and providing the weapon. They remain in custody and are due to face court again on November 13. With Lachlan Abbott Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Almost half the Greens partyroom is contesting in leadership showdown
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Almost half the Greens partyroom is contesting in leadership showdown Nick Newling September 30, 2026 — 8:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Greens senator David Shoebridge will challenge for the party leadership on a joint ticket with Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May as his deputy, setting up a rare three-way contest for the future of the party ahead of a vote this week. Shoebridge and Hodgins-May will face off against another joint ticket led by NSW senator Mehreen Faruqi and deputy candidate Nick McKim, from Tasmania, as well as veteran South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Young who is currently expected to run on a leader-only ticket. Greens leadership contenders David Shoebridge and Mehreen Faruqi, both senators for NSW. Alex Ellinghausen In a statement, Shoebridge and Hodgins-May said they “do not seek to reform Labor, but replace them” as they shared their intention to grow the party, push for climate action and create distance from the United States and “the 1 per cent”. Greens MPs will meet in Sydney over the next two days for a pre-planned “retreat” in which they will vote for a leader after the unexpected resignation of current leader Larissa Waters. Waters cited worsening chronic kidney disease for her shock retirement.



The Greens have typically sought a consensus candidate before leadership votes, with Waters promoted following last May’s election in an unopposed ballot. However, the pool of candidates for this week’s vote represents almost half of the 11-person party room, giving six parliamentarians who are not running the power to decide. Both Shoebridge and Faruqi are staunch critics of Australia’s relationship with the United States and will prosecute hard-left positions on economics and foreign policy. Shoebridge served as a NSW state MP for the Greens from 2010 to 2022, before moving to federal parliament at the 2022 election. He is the parliament’s primary opposer of the AUKUS treaty, arguing that proximity to the United States and President Trump represents a sovereign risk to Australia. Hodgins-May is one of the Green’s two millennial senators and a relative newcomer to parliament, joining in 2024 to fill a casual vacancy left by retiring Victorian senator Janet Rice. She has taken a position of more prominence recently, making repeated media appearances on behalf of the party.



In her pitch for the leadership, Faruqi said the Greens needed to grow, highlighting a “broken” economic model that was hurting voters. The senator has ventilated her frustration that the Greens have not seen a boost in the polls since the election, amid the ascendancy of One Nation, compared to the rise of populist left-wing leaders in the UK such as Greens leader Zack Polanski and the New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Hanson-Young, the first Green to put their hand up for leadership candidacy, raised the threat of a “hate peddling” One Nation, and highlighted protection of the environment in her pitch to party members. Hanson-Young said on Tuesday she was contacting her colleagues to seek their support. Loading Former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather wrote to Greens colleagues on Tuesday calling for party members to have a say in the vote for the new leader: “The selection of a new leader comes at a time of genuine debate and disagreement about the future strategic and political direction of the party. That debate couldn’t have higher stakes”. He said the Greens received almost 2 million votes last election, yet the direction of the party’s leadership would be determined by just 11 elected representatives. World.title: ‘You’re thinking kangaroos, aren’t you?’ Thurston, Thaiday try to solve Brisbane Olympics puzzle
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics ‘You’re thinking kangaroos, aren’t you?’ Thurston, Thaiday try to solve Brisbane Olympics puzzle Dominique Tassell September 30, 2026 — 8:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s day two of the staggered unveiling of the Brisbane 2032 Games emblems, and the state is one piece closer to seeing the final design – though two of six pieces is proving largely a guessing game. NRL legends Johnathan Thurston and Sam Thaiday revealed another piece of the emblem at Castle Hill Lookout in Townsville on Wednesday morning. Johnathan Thurston holds the second piece of the mystery Brisbane 2032 emblems. Dominique Tassell Thurston admitted he had “no idea” what the emblems – one for the Olympics and one for the Paralympics – could be. “I was thinking maybe they could have been two ears of a kangaroo as the emblem,” he said. “You know, you think of Australia, you’re thinking kangaroos, aren’t you?



“But I also like the Sunshine State idea.” The former North Queensland Cowboys hero said the impact on Townsville from co-hosting events in 2032 would be huge. Sam Thaiday and Thurston examine the piece. Dominique Tassell The city hoped to host soccer preliminaries at North Queensland Stadium, with sailing in the Whitsundays using a mix of existing facilities and temporary stands. “This is what Townsville was built for – with the stadium that we’ve got now, it’s attracting world-class events,” Thurston said.



“We had Pink here last year or the year before. We’ve got the Foo Fighters, we’ve got Guns N’ Roses coming, so we’re starting to attract world-class artists, and now we’ve got events such as the Olympics. Thaiday: I’m looking forward to seeing Rockhampton next, so we can start to put some of these puzzle pieces together.” Dominique Tassell “It’s one of the biggest events in the world. To have those events here right in our backyard, I know that everyone will show up for it.” Thaiday theorised the second piece of the Games emblems could be a flame or a leaf. “I’m looking forward to seeing [what’s unveiled in] Rockhampton next, so we can start to put some of these puzzle pieces together,” he said.



Thaiday said he was incredibly excited to see events run in his home town. “As a young kid, my actual dream was to go to the Olympics. “Now I can help out and be involved, and go and be a spectator and be a fan. I think that’s the beautiful thing about where my life is at the moment. I’m a fan. “This is a great opportunity to inspire the next generation, put the iPad down, go outside, find something that you love and enjoy. “Who knows, JT and I might even ... if there’s lawn bowls at the Olympics we could make a team.



Related Article Road to Brisbane 2032 One piece of Brisbane 2032 Games emblems revealed in world-first “Thurston and TNT, we’re dynamite. We’ve got theme songs and everything ready to go.” Retired swimmer Ian Thorpe and Paralympic swimmer Grant “Scooter” Patterson unveiled the first piece of the emblems for both the Olympic and Paralympic Games on Tuesday at Cairns Esplanade Lagoon, kicking off a multi-day rollout stretching across the state. It was a long ray-like golden design, prompting speculation it could be part of a Sunshine State-inspired design, or part of a crocodile, turtle or even Queensland’s official flower, the Cooktown orchid. It is the first time the emblems have been revealed in pieces.



Four more pieces of the emblem are left to be unveiled, followed by a final reveal of how they come together on Monday morning in Brisbane. Two emblems will be revealed, one for the Olympic Games and one for the Paralympic Games, though they will likely be very similar. They are traditionally separate, though Paris 2024 had a joint emblem. Each of the Games has featured its own emblem since Paris 1924, though Athens 1896 had its own coat of arms. The emblems signify the ethos of each Games. Brisbane 2032’s theme, unveiled late last year, is: Believe. Become. Belong.



The Games’ organising committee said it signified a series of commitments. Believe: “We believe in the power of sport and our Australian spirit. Together, they unlock our limitless potential, grit and heart to go further than we ever imagined.” Belong: “Everyone is welcome at our Games. Every person is celebrated, creating a playing field that’s fair and fun.” Become: “This is our moment and our move. Together, we’ll harness the magic of the Games to become stronger, taking us into an exciting new era.” Cairns will also likely host soccer preliminaries for Brisbane 2032 at Barlow Park. The Cairns Convention Centre has also been earmarked as a possible venue for indoor sport events.



The next stop on the tour, Rockhampton, is slated to host rowing, canoe sprints, paracanoe and paralympic rowing events on the Fitzroy River. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

The consortium behind some of Australia’s best-known sporting venues has emerged as the frontrunner to build Brisbane’s proposed Olympic stadium, with the state authority overseeing the project selecting the BESIX Watpac and John Holland joint venture for the final stage of contractor negotiations. The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority announced on Wednesday morning the consortium had won out over a Built-Sacyr partnership to move to the next stage of the early contractor involvement (ECI) process, which began almost a year ago on October 31, 2025. GIICA chief executive Simon Crooks said the first phase of the ECI had been a thorough process. A large section of Victoria Park has been excavated for the Olympic stadium build. BMD “We are satisfied that the process has delivered the best-possible contractor for this second and final phase,” he said.



“Engaging two highly experienced construction teams in the design phase has meant we were able to rigorously test buildability, sequencing, risk and opportunity early. “This collaborative process supports our commitment to delivering an outstanding Brisbane Stadium, while ensuring value for money and confidence in an on-time, responsible and appropriate build for Queenslanders.” The stadium will be the new home of three-peat AFL premiers Brisbane Lions. Cox Architecture Together, BESIX Watpac and John Holland have delivered a host of landmark stadium projects across Australia. BESIX Watpac built Suncorp Stadium, barely two kilometres from the Victoria Park site, as well as the doomed Gabba and Queensland Country Bank Stadium in Townsville. John Holland, meanwhile, built the Melbourne Cricket Ground’s Shane Warne Stand, Marvel Stadium in the same city, the Sydney Football Stadium and the under-construction Penrith Stadium.



BESIX Watpac chief executive Mark Baker said the company had “never been more ready” to help shape Queensland’s Olympic legacy. “With a track record of delivering every major stadium in Queensland without missing an opening, a century of local heritage and our Brisbane-based headquarters, we are proud to progress the next stage of development for Brisbane Stadium,” he said. Stadium work at Victoria Park. BMD Consortium partner Nick Miller, the chief executive of John Holland, said they were “ready to hit the ground running” to deliver Brisbane a home of AFL, cricket and the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. GIICA chairman Stephen Conry said the authority was pleased with the stadium’s progress.



“It will enable Brisbane to be a serious player in a nationally and globally competitive market for major events,” he said. “Comprehensive design, procurement and early works are continuing at pace to deliver the new stadium precinct that will enhance Victoria Park, connecting it to the rest of the city and allowing far more people to enjoy it, rather than just a few.” GIICA’s annual report, tabled last Friday, reveals the agency expanded rapidly during 2025-26 as responsibility for the venue program intensified. The authority reported 81 staff, up from a full-time equivalent workforce of 52 a year earlier, and said it had adopted an integrated delivery model with delivery partner Unite32 – a consortium led by Laing O’Rourke and AECOM.



Related Article Exclusive

Infrastructure How Brisbane 2032 is driving Australia’s next infrastructure boom The report also showed the authority recorded a $493.6 million operating surplus largely driven by the transfer of Victoria Park land and assets into its control, with total assets reaching $550.5 million by June 30. GIICA said all venue milestones during 2025-26 were delivered within approved timeframes and scope, with procurement and planning activities progressing across Brisbane and regional Queensland venues. But it warned there were risks to keeping to its $7.1 billion budget, jointly funded by the state government and the Commonwealth. Risks cited in the report included escalating construction costs, market capacity constraints, inflationary pressures and supply chain disruptions. World.title: Simple ways to help improve your home Wi-Fi
World.content:
Sponsored Technologynbn Simple ways to help improve your home Wi-Fi Advertorial for nbn September 30, 2026 — 9:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It wasn’t that long ago that the family computer was the only device in the house using the internet. Today, the average broadband household has 25 connected devices: smart TVs, gaming consoles, phones, security cameras, electric vehicles and laptops. This reflects how many Australian households now stream, game, study and work online – often at the same time. Is your home-internet keeping up? iStock So, what do you do when your home internet isn’t keeping up? It rarely points to a fault in the underlying network. As households connect more devices and spend more time online, the setup inside the home can play a bigger role than most people realise. In fact, nbn research shows 51 per cent of nbn users have not made a change to their in-home internet equipment or setup in the past two years. Here are a few simple places to start. Wi-Fi router placement



Your Wi-Fi router is one of the hardest-working devices in the house, but it’s often one of the most overlooked. Where it sits may have a surprising impact on your internet experience. It works best with a clear line of sight to the devices using it. nbn’s advice is to put it somewhere central, open and raised at waist height if you can, rather than in a cupboard, behind the television or on the floor. Then look at what surrounds it. Walls and large objects between your router and devices can weaken the signal, which is why a central, open location often works best. Large appliances, metal objects and mirrors may also affect how the signal travels. Water can absorb the signal too, so avoid placing the router near a fish tank where you can. Some household devices, including microwaves and baby monitors, may cause interference. Try moving the router a couple of metres. A small shift may be enough to notice a difference. Run multi-room speed tests This is the step many people miss. Testing in one spot tells you very little. Testing in several rooms can help show where the problem might be. Start beside your Wi-Fi router, using a speed test app or browser-based speed test. Then repeat the test in the rooms where the internet feels slowest.



If speeds are slower than expected everywhere, connect a laptop to the router with an Ethernet cable and test again. This takes Wi-Fi out of the picture and can help show whether the issue is with your internet connection or your home setup. If the wired test is closer to the speeds you expect for your plan, the issue may be linked to something inside the home, such as Wi-Fi coverage, interference or older equipment. If the wired test is also slower than expected, discuss it with your internet provider. Check the equipment age Like smartphones, Wi-Fi routers can start to feel their age. They may still work, but newer models are usually built to handle more, including faster internet plans over the nbn® network, more connected devices and more people online at the same time. If you’ve recently changed to a faster plan through your internet provider, consider checking whether your router is still the right fit. The model number is usually on a sticker underneath; a quick online search can tell you when it was released, which Wi-Fi generation it uses, and whether the manufacturer is still providing important firmware and security updates. If your router is over five years old, it may be time to ask your internet provider whether it is still right for your plan.



Consider mesh Wi-Fi signal can weaken the further it travels, especially through thick walls, brick, concrete or other dense materials in your home. If your speed tests dropped off sharply in particular rooms, a mesh network may help spread coverage more evenly through the house. Mesh systems use extra units, called nodes, to carry the signal into harder-to-reach areas in your home. It’s worth considering in homes with three or more bedrooms, or across multiple storeys. Plug in when it counts Wi-Fi gives you flexibility, but for devices that stay in one place, a cable can sometimes work better. For online gaming, high-definition streaming or moving large files, an Ethernet cable connected directly from your device to the Wi-Fi router may help provide a more stable connection and less lag*.



It suits anything that stays put, such as a desktop computer, a games console or a smart television. Check the cable, too: older or lower-grade cabling can lead to slower speeds, and nbn recommends at least CAT 6 for anything new. If you want extra Ethernet points installed, discuss the right option for your setup with a registered cabler. None of the above recommendations require a new plan. A few practical adjustments to what is already in the house may improve speed, coverage and reliability, and the speed test will tell you whether they worked. Discover nbn’s practical tips for improving your home internet setup at nbn.com.au/optimise *Your home network setup is one part of your overall internet connection. Your experience also depends on your nbn® technology, and factors outside nbn’s control (like your internet provider and plan, usage during busy periods and the number of concurrent online devices at your premises). If you’re still concerned by the performance of your service, we recommend speaking to your service provider.

World.title: One day after public flag celebrations Neale tells Lions: ‘Make me a Magpie’
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 One day after public flag celebrations Neale tells Lions: ‘Make me a Magpie’ Michael Gleeson September 30, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Days after celebrating his third successive premiership, dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale has officially told Brisbane he will move to Collingwood as a free agent. In case you thought you already knew this, let’s be clear. Neale on Wednesday morning made official the previous reports anticipating his move to Collingwood by formally telling his club he wanted to go to the Magpies. Neale leaves Brisbane with two Brownlow medals and three premierships. Getty Images He told the Lions of his intentions the day after he and his premiership teammates were feted at a public fan event in Brisbane. That he had not been offered a new contract at Brisbane in his free agency year suggests the only question was which club the free agent would choose, not whether he would leave.



After a very public and acrimonious marriage break up Neale has endured a tumultuous year. Despite his wife and children moving back to Perth, Neale has opted not to ask for a move to Western Australia, fearing he would feed the circus circling his personal life. He has instead taken a three-year deal at Collingwood at slightly less than $1 million a season. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘We have nothing but gratitude:’ Lions give Collingwood-bound Neale their blessing In August Neale was revealed to have toured Collingwood’s facilities ahead of playing against Carlton the next day. Reports also suggested there had been discussion of what number he would wear and so which locker he would have. Essendon, West Coast and Collingwood all approached Neale once it became clear he felt he needed to leave Brisbane. Fremantle, the club he began his career at, said if he wanted to return they would make it happen, but that would be a tight squeeze financially for the grand finalists. He also met with St Kilda coach Ross Lyon – his former coach at Fremantle with whom he maintains a good relationship – but they agreed a move there was not the right fit for Neale or the club.



Lions president Andrew Wellington told this masthead after Saturday’s win that, regardless of him leaving, the Lions would always value Neale not only for his three flags and two Brownlow medals but the impact of his arrival when the Lions were battling to win matches. Related Article Exclusive

AFL 2026 AFL considering changes to free agency system “It was a really important platform for turning the club around, and if you look at his performances in grand finals and big games, he has been incredible, so we have got nothing but gratitude for what he has done for our club,” Wellington said. Neale was fortunate to play in Saturday’s grand final having initially been banned by the AFL tribunal for an intentional strike to the stomach of Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan in the preliminary final, only for that decision to be watered down to a fine by the AFL appeals board. “Lachie has been a great player for the Brisbane Lions, and we thank him for his incredible contribution over his eight seasons,” Lions list manager Dom Ambrogio said.



“We understand Lachie’s reasons for wishing to explore free agency and we wish him all the best for the next chapter of his career.” The club said it will further celebrate and recognise Neale’s contribution to the club in the coming days. The free agency period opens on Friday and the AFL will confirm what compensation the Lions will receive for Neale. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Boy, 16, among trio charged with Sydney student’s mistaken identity murder
World.content:
Two men and a 16-year-old boy extradited from Victoria have been charged with the mistaken identity murder of a university student shot dead in his bed in Sydney’s south-west. Marco Tapia, 23, was killed when a group of assailants stormed his family’s Glen Alpine home in the early hours of September 1. Police have since confirmed the wrong address was targeted in the allegedly botched organised crime killing. Marco Tapia was shot dead while in bed at his family’s Sydney home. Detectives are yet to identify the intended target of the botched attack, but are investigating if the trio was contracted to target a Coconut Cartel member. Tapia had no links to organised crime. Vaifaalie Tuafuti, 23, Omar Mohamed, 22, and a 16-year-old boy who cannot be identified for legal reasons have been charged with murder, two counts of special aggravated break and enter and committing a serious indictable offence, and possessing an unauthorised prohibited firearm.



All three are due to face court on Wednesday. Detectives will allege in court that the trio broke into the Glen Alpine home before shooting Tapia in his bed. One of the trio is alleged to have been armed with a pistol. The trio was extradited from Victoria on September 18, along with a 26-year-old woman, Amenah Abusud. The trio charged with murder were earlier extradited from Victoria. NSW Police Abusud has not been charged with Tapia’s murder, but she has been charged with criminal group and accessory offences.



Police alleged during an extradition hearing in Melbourne Magistrates Court this month that the group worked for the notorious Alameddine crime family in a recent spate of violence against rival group the Coconut Cartel. The trio has also been charged over a home invasion in Hurstville, in Sydney’s south, and the shooting several cars in nearby Turrella the night before Tapia was killed. Loading Ballistic analysis found discharged cartridge cases at the two scenes were “positively matched” to the Glen Alpine crime scene where a firearm was found, a NSW Police officer testified in court. The court was told the Victorians left their Airbnb at Campbelltown, in Sydney’s south-west about 1.50am on September 1 and returned about 4am, “where they appear to be in a rush to collect their belongings before all leaving”.



Two boys, aged 14 and 16, were earlier charged with allegedly staging vehicles and providing the weapon. They remain in custody and are due to face court again on November 13. With Lachlan Abbott Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Almost half the Greens partyroom is contesting in leadership showdown
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Almost half the Greens partyroom is contesting in leadership showdown Nick Newling September 30, 2026 — 8:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Greens senator David Shoebridge will challenge for the party leadership on a joint ticket with Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May as his deputy, setting up a rare three-way contest for the future of the party ahead of a vote this week. Shoebridge and Hodgins-May will face off against another joint ticket led by NSW senator Mehreen Faruqi and deputy candidate Nick McKim, from Tasmania, as well as veteran South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Young who is currently expected to run on a leader-only ticket. Greens leadership contenders David Shoebridge and Mehreen Faruqi, both senators for NSW. Alex Ellinghausen In a statement, Shoebridge and Hodgins-May said they “do not seek to reform Labor, but replace them” as they shared their intention to grow the party, push for climate action and create distance from the United States and “the 1 per cent”. Greens MPs will meet in Sydney over the next two days for a pre-planned “retreat” in which they will vote for a leader after the unexpected resignation of current leader Larissa Waters. Waters cited worsening chronic kidney disease for her shock retirement.



The Greens have typically sought a consensus candidate before leadership votes, with Waters promoted following last May’s election in an unopposed ballot. However, the pool of candidates for this week’s vote represents almost half of the 11-person party room, giving six parliamentarians who are not running the power to decide. Both Shoebridge and Faruqi are staunch critics of Australia’s relationship with the United States and will prosecute hard-left positions on economics and foreign policy. Shoebridge served as a NSW state MP for the Greens from 2010 to 2022, before moving to federal parliament at the 2022 election. He is the parliament’s primary opposer of the AUKUS treaty, arguing that proximity to the United States and President Trump represents a sovereign risk to Australia. Hodgins-May is one of the Green’s two millennial senators and a relative newcomer to parliament, joining in 2024 to fill a casual vacancy left by retiring Victorian senator Janet Rice. She has taken a position of more prominence recently, making repeated media appearances on behalf of the party.



In her pitch for the leadership, Faruqi said the Greens needed to grow, highlighting a “broken” economic model that was hurting voters. The senator has ventilated her frustration that the Greens have not seen a boost in the polls since the election, amid the ascendancy of One Nation, compared to the rise of populist left-wing leaders in the UK such as Greens leader Zack Polanski and the New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Hanson-Young, the first Green to put their hand up for leadership candidacy, raised the threat of a “hate peddling” One Nation, and highlighted protection of the environment in her pitch to party members. Hanson-Young said on Tuesday she was contacting her colleagues to seek their support. Loading Former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather wrote to Greens colleagues on Tuesday calling for party members to have a say in the vote for the new leader: “The selection of a new leader comes at a time of genuine debate and disagreement about the future strategic and political direction of the party. That debate couldn’t have higher stakes”. He said the Greens received almost 2 million votes last election, yet the direction of the party’s leadership would be determined by just 11 elected representatives. Staying with the assistant treasurer’s appearance on ABC TV this morning, Mulino said balancing the cyber threats posed by AI while at the same time considering how best to deploy AI to bolster Australia’s cybersecurity was “a constant work in progress”.

“It’s almost a battle on both sides. There’s AI being used in terms of creating cyber threats, and there’s AI on the defence side. So it’s a constant process that we need to undertake,” he said.

“I think that what was highlighted with the Medicare breach is that we do need to lean in more in this area. Fortunately, no sensitive data was stolen, but I think the fact that AI, so OpenAI, has apologised is a very good sign.”

Mulino said the government’s parliamentary inquiry on artificial intelligence was an important step in the process of ensuring Australia’s preparedness to tackle AI threats.

“It shows the government is bringing AI right to the centre of decision making and the coordination of policy.”

World.title: Psychologist who worked with OT, Youth Court charged with sexual offences against young men
World.content:
A man at the centre of a police investigation into alleged historical sexual offending is a psychologist who has had "significant involvement" with young men referred by various agencies including Oranga Tamariki and the Youth Court, RNZ can reveal.

It can now be reported that Ban Teik Tan, who is known as Ricki Tan, is before the courts facing 17 charges. The charges include unlawful sexual connection with a boy aged 12-16 and indecent assault on a boy aged between 12-16.

The charges relate to five complainants and date between 1996 to 2005. Tan has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Tan, who has been a registered psychologist in New Zealand since 1995, has had his practising certificate suspended.

In a statement to RNZ, Tan confirmed police had laid charges of historic sexual offending against him.

"I absolutely deny those allegations. I am innocent.

"Because the matter is before the court, I will not comment further. I respect the role of the court and will defend myself following the advice of my lawyer Ethan Huda, barrister of Christchurch. I request everyone to respect the court process and to avoid any speculation or pre-judgement."

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

The 63-year-old's case was called in the Christchurch District Court before Judge Michael Crosbie last month in relation to Tan's application for continued name suppression. Crosbie declined his application, however Tan was given 20 working days to file an appeal in the High Court.

Tan filed an appeal on Friday last week, but then on Wednesday he abandoned it.

Crosbie's judgment, released to RNZ, said Tan had "significant involvement" with young men who were referred to him by various organisations, including Oranga Tamariki (OT) and through the Youth Court.

Crosbie said the allegations against Tan were "very much at an early stage".

"Police enquiries have identified links between Mr Tan and multiple agencies and programmes through which he had access to children and young people. Oranga Tamariki has advised that records identify Mr Tan as having had professional involvement with more than approximately 100 young persons.

"While there is no suggestion that Mr Tan offended against those young persons, having identified the breadth of Mr Tan's involvement with such persons in his professional role, Police are concerned that there may be further potential complainants and are embarking on a thorough investigation."

Crosbie said he understood Police would be attempting to contact those identified by OT as having had contact with Tan.

At the suppression hearing, Tan's lawyer Ethan Huda said Tan was seeking name suppression on the ground that publication of his name would give risk to a fair trial.

Huda said there were two unique features of the case. This included that police would be approaching some people with what he referred to as a "scripted questionnaire" to "elicit" information from them.

He said police would identify Tan to the people spoken to as part of their approach.

"Police believe without identifying [the man] they cannot carry out the questionnaire in the way they would like to."

Huda submitted Tan's name should not be published until police had finished administering the questionnaire.

He also wanted to know what the questionnaire would say.

In response, Crown prosecutor Courtney Martyn spoke of the approach that police were using as part of their investigation and what groups of people police would approach.

Martyn said the defendant had "considerable involvement with a great deal of young people…"

"The police aren't going around recruiting complainants or recruiting potential complaints," Martyn said.

She said at no stage would the police be trying to elicit complaints.

"What they're going to be saying is police are conducting an investigation into [the defendant] and as part of that investigation we are speaking to people who may have had contact with him and we understand you're one of those people."

Police would not be discussing any further details or specific allegations.

Crosbie said he did not accept that Police were "eliciting" complainants in the course of the investigation.

"It is not uncommon for Police to contact individuals who may hold relevant information concerning a person under investigation, particularly in the early information-gathering stages of an investigation.

"In attempting to contact individuals identified as potentially having relevant information, Police are carrying out ordinary investigative functions. Accordingly, I do not accept that this is a "unique" feature of this case."

He said that even if an individual came forward with allegations involving Tan, police were still required to investigate the complete, properly review the allegations and then ensure there was sufficient evidence to charge Tan.

"It is not as simple as 'eliciting a complainant' and them then giving false evidence against Mr Tan."

Crosbie declined Tan's application.

Tan was featured in an article on the New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) website in 2023 in relation to his role with NZDF's Youth Development Unit (YDU).

"Originally from Malaysia, Mr Tan is a registered psychologist who has lived in New Zealand for over 40 years. He's worked in Child Protection, Youth Justice, Youth Forensic Mental Health and Corrections before coming to the Youth Development Unit, based at Whenuapai Air Force Base, in 2014."

Oranga Tamariki deputy chief executive Thomas Ronan earlier told RNZ the agency had been made aware by police that they were investigating allegations of historical offending by a 63-year-old man.

World.title: KiwiRail boosts underlying surplus in face of large impairment charge from City Rail link
World.content:
State owned rail company KiwiRail has posted a full-year deficit after tax of just over $1.4 billion.

However a large part of that is due to an impairment charge related to the Auckland City Rail Link.

The company's underlying result for the year saw it post a surplus of $162 million, slightly ahead of its forecast.

Operating revenues came in at just over $1.1b, up 5 percent on the previous year.

Freight revenue increased by 11 percent to $504.4m, with 3 percent growth in freight volumes.

The company said its statutory result was significantly impacted by non-cash impairment charges required under accounting standards, with the primary driver of this charge being a $1.19b impairment of City Rail Link assets.

Chair Suzanne Tindal said the results for FY26 were encouraging.

"They reflect daily decisions being made by many people across the organisation and in the field to do things better than they did last year."

Tindal said KiwiRail contributes an estimated $3.3b of value to New Zealand annually.

"We move around a quarter of the country's export freight, connect the North and South Islands through Interislander, support more than 24 million metro passenger journeys each year".

Rail Minister Winston Peters has also welcomed the result and issued congratulations to every rail worker, including Board Chair Suzanne Tindal, the newest apprentices, and everyone in between.
